### Additional Info

## Measurements

**CPU** (5 s samples, mean of 10):

```
containerd   ~96 % of one core
dockerd      ~94 % of one core
split        ~80 % user time, ~20 % system time
```

**Context switches:** dockerd 16,185/s, containerd 16,021/s — together 32,206 of
the system's 46,901/s (**69 %**), almost entirely voluntary.

**Syscalls per process:** ~48,000/s.

```
epoll_pwait  ~13,400/s
futex         ~8,600/s
nanosleep     ~5,800/s
read          ~5,700/s
write         ~5,100/s
```

**A single fd pair carries essentially all of it.** Per-fd breakdown over 5 s:

```
dockerd fd 9   27,105 reads + 24,369 writes    <- everything else < 100
dockerd fd 7    1,803 +  1,798                 (Go runtime eventfd)
```

`ss -xp` confirms the peer:

```
/run/containerd/containerd.sock
  dockerd fd 9  <-->  containerd fd 13
```

**Throughput:** 33,824,204 bytes in 5 s over 22,470 writes = **6.8 MB/s**.

**It is continuous, not periodic.** Bytes/second over 15 s:

```
7.69  7.31  5.90  8.41  5.92  8.20  5.93  8.20  6.33
7.42  7.84  7.09  6.31  7.78  6.63   (MB)
```

**The payload is image metadata.** Readable fragments captured from the write
buffers include `mediaType`, `//github.com/cirruslabs/docker-images-flutter` (the
`org.opencontainers.image.source` label of an image present on the host), package
names such as `imagemagick` and `docker-cli-compose`, and content digests.

**perf profile of dockerd** is dominated by Go GC — and is unchanged whether the
heap is 696 MB or 121 MB:

```
7.56 %  runtime.tryDeferToSpanScan
3.52 %  runtime.mallocgcSmallScanNoHeader
3.15 %  runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers
3.03 %  runtime.scanObjectsSmall
```

**Goroutine dumps** (SIGUSR1) show nothing spinning: dockerd has 279 goroutines,
almost all waiting (148 IO wait, 72 sync.Cond.Wait — 70 of those are the
per-container fifo/bytespipe log pipeline). containerd has 165, with **two**
`streamNamespaceInterceptor` goroutines, i.e. two open streams.

## The load scales with the number of images

This is the strongest hint at the cause.

| action | total CPU |
|---|---|
| baseline (98 images, 450 build cache entries) | 223 % |
| after `docker image prune` + `builder prune` (→ 29 images) | 182 % |
| after full `systemctl restart docker` | 199 % |
| after containerd.io 2.2.6 → 2.3.4 | 187 % |
| after docker-ce 29.6.2 → 29.7.2 | 191 % |
| after removing 10 more unused images (→ 27) | **164 %** |

Only image removal ever helped, and it helped twice, in proportion.

## Ruled out

| hypothesis | ruled out by |
|---|---|
| container churn | 0 container events in 180 s |
| external API clients | only 2 connections to docker.sock: dockerd itself and systemd socket activation |
| health checks | 16 exec cycles/minute — three orders of magnitude too few |
| log processing | container logs grow ~1 KB per 5 s; journald 140 lines/min |
| cgroup stat collection | would be system time; 80 % is user time |
| memory leak | RSS stable (+4 KB in 60 s) |
| accumulated daemon state | full restart dropped RSS 696 → 121 MB, CPU unchanged |
| containerd version | 2.2.6 → 2.3.4, no change |
| engine version | 29.6.2 → 29.7.2, no change |

## Commands used

```sh
# per-fd read/write breakdown
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write /comm=="dockerd"/ { @w[args->fd] = count(); }
             tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read  /comm=="dockerd"/ { @r[args->fd] = count(); }
             interval:s:5 { exit(); }'

# identify the peer
readlink /proc/$(pidof dockerd)/fd/9      # -> socket:[INODE]
ss -xp | grep INODE

# throughput
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write /pid==CONTAINERD_PID && args->fd==13/
             { @bytes = sum(args->count); @n = count(); } interval:s:5 { exit(); }'

# per-second profile (shows it is continuous, not periodic)
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write /pid==CONTAINERD_PID && args->fd==13/
             { @b = sum(args->count); } interval:s:1 { print(@b); clear(@b); }'

# payload sampling
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write /pid==CONTAINERD_PID && args->fd==13 && args->count>200/
             { printf("%s~", str(args->buf, 180)); }'
```

## Notes

- Not reproduced deliberately on a second host; observed continuously on this one
  for 26 days across two version upgrades.
- Not tested with the classic (graph driver) image store — the host has not been
  switched back.
- Hostname and Docker ID removed from the `docker info` output above.

body_text:
The daemon-wide `--experimental` flag and `experimental` key in `daemon.json` gate unrelated
features under one global switch. This makes it difficult to graduate, deprecate, or remove
features independently.

New experimental features should use granular `--feature NAME[=true|false]` flags or entries
in the `features` map in `daemon.json`, as introduced in #48167.

Remove daemon-wide experimental mode in Docker Engine v30 after resolving its remaining
consumers.

Related history: 
- #26713

## Required work

### Resolve remaining experimental features

- [ ] Resolve checkpoint/restore lifecycle under #36433.
  - [ ] Deprecate the checkpoint restore parameters accepted by `POST /containers/{id}/start`.
  - [ ] Remove checkpoint restore in v30.
  - [ ] Decide whether checkpoint create/list/delete should also be removed.
  - [ ] If checkpoint creation remains, move it behind a granular feature flag instead of
daemon-wide experimental mode.
- [ ] Resolve legacy builder squash under #34565 and #38657.
  - [ ] Prefer removing legacy builder `--squash`, or explicitly decide to retain it.
  - [ ] If retained, move it behind a granular feature flag.
- [ ] Resolve the Swarm plugin task runtime introduced behind experimental mode in #34455.
  - [ ] Decide whether to remove or stabilize `TaskTemplate.Runtime = "plugin"`.
  - [ ] If retained as experimental, give it a granular feature flag.

### Deprecate daemon-wide mode

- [ ] Deprecate the `--experimental` daemon flag with a v30 removal warning.
- [ ] Deprecate the `experimental` key in `daemon.json`.
- [ ] Direct users and developers to `--feature` and the `features` configuration map.
- [ ] Deprecate the associated API indicators:
  - [ ] `Experimental` in `GET /version`.
  - [ ] `ExperimentalBuild` in `GET /info`.
  - [ ] `Docker-Experimental` response headers.
- [ ] Deprecate corresponding Go API and client fields.
- [ ] Update the API changelog, daemon documentation, and release notes.

### Remove in v30

- [ ] Remove `--experimental` and the `experimental` configuration key.
- [ ] Remove `Config.Experimental` and `Daemon.HasExperimental`.
- [ ] Remove global experimental route handling.
- [ ] Remove the experimental response middleware and `Docker-Experimental` header.
- [ ] Remove the deprecated `/version` and `/info` fields, with appropriate API-version
compatibility handling.
- [ ] Remove corresponding client fields and detection logic.
- [ ] Remove or replace `WithExperimental` test helpers and experimental test-environment
propagation.
- [ ] Remove obsolete documentation and tests.
- [ ] Coordinate corresponding output and detection changes with `docker/cli`.

### Description

`TestContainerRestartPolicyUserDefinedNetwork` (in `integration/container/restart_test.go`) failed intermittently in CI during the 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-12 scan window.

**Failure evidence:**

| Run | Branch | Job | Result |
|-----|--------|-----|--------|
| [34475195808](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34475195808/job/102864240772) | `trixie_me_trixie_you` | `vm (template:oraclelinux-8, ...) / integration` | ❌ FAIL (12.20s) |
| [34475195808](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34475195808/job/102864240856) | `trixie_me_trixie_you` | `vm (template:oraclelinux-8, ...) / integration (rootless)` | ❌ FAIL (12.27s) |

**Passing evidence (same 72h window, independent master runs):**

| Run | Branch | Job | Result |
|-----|--------|-----|--------|
| [34598138516](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34598138516/job/103258676163) | `master` | `vm / integration` | ✅ PASS (3.44s) |
| [34598138516](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34598138516/job/103258676213) | `master` | `vm / integration (rootless)` | ✅ PASS (3.22s) |
| [34508344173](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34508344173/job/102975994463) | `master` | `vm / integration` | ✅ PASS (3.48s) |
| [34508344173](https://github.com/moby/moby/actions/runs/34508344173/job/102975994477) | `master` | `vm / integration (rootless)` | ✅ PASS (3.17s) |

**Classification:** Flaky — the test consistently passes (~3s) on master across multiple independent runs in the same window, but failed (~12s, ~4x the normal duration) on the `trixie_me_trixie_you` experimental/WIP branch, both in the rootless and non-rootless job variants of the same run. The longer duration before failure suggests a timing/readiness race (e.g. waiting for the user-defined network or container restart to settle) rather than a deterministic logic bug, consistent with typical restart-policy test flakiness in this package (see also #52551).

No existing tracking issue was found for this specific test via search of `moby/moby` issues (open or closed) or the flaky-tests epic (#37306, closed).

The current DIND-based CI practically limits the host distribution to Debian userspace + irregular system configuration (systemd, udevd, resolved, etc.) + irregular kernel (Ubuntu, or Oracle on Lima workflows).
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/8210b0babaed17fbe706a4c5e8c7d0b9c6aba2a1/Dockerfile#L4
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/8210b0babaed17fbe706a4c5e8c7d0b9c6aba2a1/.github/workflows/test.yml#L35
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/8210b0babaed17fbe706a4c5e8c7d0b9c6aba2a1/.github/workflows/vm.yml#L46-L47

To cover "real" host OSes with their standard configuration, we have to consider de-DINDifying the CI.
I suggest beginning with de-DINDIfying `./integration/container ./integration/build ./integration/system` executed in `vm.yml`.

- - -

openSUSE's test script might be useful for reference https://github.com/os-autoinst/os-autoinst-distri-opensuse/blob/master/tests/containers/docker_engine.pm

- - -

### Description

Running the Docker daemon on a system where there's also a networkmanager wifi hotspot running, seems to destroy the hotspot routing such that connecte hotspot clients can no longer reach the internet.

### Reproduce

1. Activate NetworkManager hotspot
2. Have clients connect
3. Before starting the docker service, do a test to try to reach something from a connected hotspot client, e.g. `ping example.com`. At this point, it should work fine. If it doesn't, fix your setup first.
4. On the hotspot host, use `service docker start`
5. Now try to do something like `ping example.com` on the client. You should get host resolution or package loss errors.
### Expected behavior

Docker shouldn't cause any trouble for the hotspot.

body_text:
### Description

On Docker Engine 29.x with the **containerd image store** (the default for fresh installations), `docker push` aborts a multi-gigabyte layer with:

```text
failed commit on ref "layer-sha256:<digest>": failed to do request:
Put "https://<registry>/v2/<repo>/blobs/uploads/<uuid>.patch?digest=sha256%3A<digest>":
net/http: timeout awaiting response headers
```

The same image, pushed to the same registry from the same network, **succeeds** when the daemon is configured with `"features": { "containerd-snapshotter": false }` (classic `overlay2` graph driver). In that configuration the client waits for the registry and the push completes.

The trigger is a registry that takes longer than 30 seconds to **return response headers** for the final blob commit request. The byte upload itself completes quickly; the registry then spends minutes checksumming and finalizing the blob server-side before responding. We observed several minutes for a single multi-GB layer against a commercial artifact-repository product. The classic path tolerates this; the containerd path does not.

### Expected behaviour

Pushing an image through the containerd image store should be at least as tolerant of a slow registry as the classic graph-driver path — either by not imposing a response-header timeout on the blob-commit request, by retrying on that timeout, or by exposing the timeout as a daemon configuration option.

### Actual behaviour

The push aborts on the first occurrence, with no retry and no backoff.

The cause appears to be a **hardcoded 30-second `ResponseHeaderTimeout`** on the HTTP transport used by the containerd image store's registry client:

- `containerd/containerd`, `core/remotes/docker/registry.go`, `DefaultHTTPTransport()`:

  ```go
  func DefaultHTTPTransport(defaultTLSConfig *tls.Config) *http.Transport {
      return &http.Transport{
          // ...
          TLSHandshakeTimeout:   10 * time.Second,
          ExpectContinueTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
          ResponseHeaderTimeout: 30 * time.Second,   // <-- applies to the blob commit PUT
      }
  }
  ```

- `moby/moby`, `daemon/hosts.go`, `(*Daemon).RegistryHosts()` reaches that transport via `hostconfig.ConfigureHosts(...)`, and `daemon/containerd/resolver.go` (`newResolverFromAuthConfig`) passes the resulting `RegistryHosts` straight into `docker.NewResolver`.

Thirty seconds is the entire budget the registry is given to checksum and finalize a blob that may be several gigabytes. We are not aware of any `daemon.json` key that exposes this value.

The classic path has no equivalent limit. `moby/moby`, `daemon/pkg/registry/registry.go`, `newTransport()` sets `TLSHandshakeTimeout` and `IdleConnTimeout` but deliberately sets **no** `ResponseHeaderTimeout`, so it waits for the registry for as long as the connection stays alive. That single difference accounts for the whole behavioural gap between the two image stores.

Two further details confirm which code path is in play:

1. The error string `failed commit on ref "layer-sha256:..."` originates from containerd's pusher (`core/remotes/docker`), not from the classic `docker/distribution` client.
2. The classic path emits `Retrying in N seconds` lines before failing. Those lines are absent here — the containerd path gives up immediately.

One caveat on our own measurements, in case it helps anyone triaging a similar report: in our production failure the abort was logged about five minutes after the previous `Pushed` line, which initially led us to suspect a five-minute timeout. With five concurrent uploads in flight, that interval is simply when the large blob's data transfer finished and its commit `PUT` was issued; the abort follows 30 seconds later. The 30-second constant is consistent with everything we observed.

### Impact

This is not an exotic configuration. Because the containerd image store is enabled **by default on fresh installations of Docker Engine 29.0 and later**, while hosts upgraded in place keep `overlay2`, a fleet of build agents silently diverges: newly provisioned agents fail a push that older agents complete successfully, with an identical Dockerfile, identical engine version, and an identical `--no-cache --pull` build. In our case two agents differed in no other relevant respect (same engine 29.7.2, same containerd, same runc, same DNS, same route, comparable TLS/connect timings to the registry), and the storage backend was the only variable.

The only workaround we found is to disable the containerd image store — that is, to opt **out** of the new default. That is the outcome we would like to avoid; see the questions at the end.

---

### Steps to reproduce

This reproduction is fully self-contained. It needs only a throwaway VM, Docker Engine 29.x, the public `registry:2` image, and `mitmproxy`. No commercial registry is required — the slow blob commit is simulated deterministically.

#### 1. Build a large, incompressible single-layer image

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.bigblob
FROM ubuntu:24.04
RUN dd if=/dev/urandom of=/big.bin bs=1M count=6000
```

`/dev/urandom` is required: a file of zeros compresses to almost nothing and the resulting blob would never be large enough to matter.

#### 2. Start a local registry

```bash
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry --restart=always registry:2
```

#### 3. Put a proxy in front of it that delays only the blob-commit request

```python
# slow_commit.py
# Run with:
#   mitmdump -s slow_commit.py --mode reverse:http://127.0.0.1:5000 -p 5001
import time
from mitmproxy import http

def request(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None:
    # Delay only the final blob commit: PUT .../blobs/uploads/<uuid>?digest=sha256:...
    if flow.request.method == "PUT" and "digest" in flow.request.query:
        time.sleep(60)   # anything above the hardcoded 30s ResponseHeaderTimeout
```

Delaying only the commit is deliberate. It leaves the byte upload running at full speed and isolates exactly the behaviour a slow registry exhibits: fast transfer, slow finalization.

#### 4. Run A — containerd image store (fails)

```bash
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json >/dev/null <<'EOF'
{
  "features": { "containerd-snapshotter": true },
  "insecure-registries": ["127.0.0.1:5001"]
}
EOF
sudo systemctl restart docker

docker info -f 'driver={{.Driver}} status={{.DriverStatus}}'
# expected: driver=overlayfs status=[[driver-type io.containerd.snapshotter.v1]]

docker build -f Dockerfile.bigblob -t 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1 .
time docker push 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1
```

**Result:** aborts 30 seconds after the commit `PUT` is issued, with `failed commit on ref "layer-sha256:..." : ... net/http: timeout awaiting response headers`. No retry lines are emitted.

#### 5. Run B — classic overlay2 (succeeds)

Only the feature flag changes. Same image, same registry, same delay.

```bash
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json >/dev/null <<'EOF'
{
  "features": { "containerd-snapshotter": false },
  "insecure-registries": ["127.0.0.1:5001"]
}
EOF
sudo systemctl restart docker

docker info -f 'driver={{.Driver}}'
# expected: driver=overlay2

docker build -f Dockerfile.bigblob -t 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1 .
time docker push 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1
```

**Result:** the push waits out the full 60-second delay and completes successfully.

`sudo journalctl -u docker -f` during both runs shows the underlying HTTP exchange and the presence or absence of retries.

#### Notes on the reproduction

The layer size is **not** the trigger and can be reduced substantially — a large layer is only what makes a real registry slow enough to cross the threshold in practice. The trigger is purely `time.sleep(n)` with `n > 30`. Conversely, setting `n < 30` makes both runs pass, which is a useful negative control.

---

### Related upstream work

containerd's resolver has since gained `doWithTransportRetries` in `core/remotes/docker/resolver.go`, which retries transient transport errors — explicitly including response-header timeouts — up to `maxAttempts = 5`. If we are reading this correctly, an engine built against a containerd containing that change should no longer exhibit the failure. Confirmation of that, and of which engine release will carry it, would be very helpful.

---

### Questions

The reason for opening this issue is less about the workaround (which we have) and more about how to stay on the new default:

1. **Is the 30-second `ResponseHeaderTimeout` intentional for the blob-commit request, and can it be made configurable?** Thirty seconds is a reasonable default for a manifest `HEAD` or a token request, but the commit `PUT` is a request whose entire purpose is to wait for server-side finalization of a potentially multi-gigabyte blob. Either exempting that request from the timeout, or exposing the value through `daemon.json`, would resolve this class of failure. Today there appears to be no supported way to adjust it without recompiling.

2. **Can the containerd push path adopt the same retry/backoff semantics as the classic path?** The asymmetry between the two backends is the surprising part: identical engine, identical registry, different resilience, with nothing in `docker info` suggesting that pushing behaviour would differ.

3. **What is the recommended configuration for a fresh Docker Engine 29.x installation that must push very large layers to a slow-finalizing registry, while keeping the containerd image store?** We would prefer not to set `"features": { "containerd-snapshotter": false }` on every newly provisioned host, because that means permanently opting out of the default and out of the direction the project is moving in. Is there a supported way to influence the registry client used by the containerd image store from `dockerd` — for example per-registry host configuration, `hosts.toml`-style settings, or any timeout tuning — that we have missed?

4. **Is any of this documented?** The behavioural difference between the two image stores on push is not mentioned on the containerd image store page, which currently describes the switch as transparent for most users. A note about large-blob push semantics would have saved us a considerable amount of diagnosis.

---

### Output of `docker version`

```text
Client:
 Version:     29.7.2
 API version: 1.55

Server:
 Engine:
  Version:     29.7.2
  API version: 1.55
 containerd:
  Version:     v2.3.4
 runc:
  Version:     v1.4.3
```

### Output of `docker info` (relevant excerpt, failing configuration)

```text
Server Version: 29.7.2
Storage Driver: overlayfs
 driver-type: io.containerd.snapshotter.v1
Cgroup Driver: systemd
Cgroup Version: 2
containerd version: v2.3.4
runc version: v1.4.3
Kernel Version: 6.17.0-35-generic
Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
OSType: linux
Architecture: x86_64
CPUs: 8
Total Memory: 31.3GiB
Live Restore Enabled: false
Firewall Backend: iptables
```

### Additional environment details

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS virtual machines, on-premises, no HTTP proxy configured for the daemon, no `userns-remap`. Before the change, `/etc/docker/daemon.json` did not exist on either host. The reference host that succeeds is the same engine version, upgraded in place from an earlier release, and therefore still on `overlay2`.

Thirty seconds is the entire budget the registry is given to checksum and finalize a blob that may be several gigabytes. We are not aware of any `daemon.json` key that exposes this value.

The classic path has no equivalent limit. `moby/moby`, `daemon/pkg/registry/registry.go`, `newTransport()` sets `TLSHandshakeTimeout` and `IdleConnTimeout` but deliberately sets **no** `ResponseHeaderTimeout`, so it waits for the registry for as long as the connection stays alive. That single difference accounts for the whole behavioural gap between the two image stores.

Two further details confirm which code path is in play:

1. The error string `failed commit on ref "layer-sha256:..."` originates from containerd's pusher (`core/remotes/docker`), not from the classic `docker/distribution` client.
2. The classic path emits `Retrying in N seconds` lines before failing. Those lines are absent here — the containerd path gives up immediately.

One caveat on our own measurements, in case it helps anyone triaging a similar report: in our production failure the abort was logged about five minutes after the previous `Pushed` line, which initially led us to suspect a five-minute timeout. With five concurrent uploads in flight, that interval is simply when the large blob's data transfer finished and its commit `PUT` was issued; the abort follows 30 seconds later. The 30-second constant is consistent with everything we observed.

### Impact

This is not an exotic configuration. Because the containerd image store is enabled **by default on fresh installations of Docker Engine 29.0 and later**, while hosts upgraded in place keep `overlay2`, a fleet of build agents silently diverges: newly provisioned agents fail a push that older agents complete successfully, with an identical Dockerfile, identical engine version, and an identical `--no-cache --pull` build. In our case two agents differed in no other relevant respect (same engine 29.7.2, same containerd, same runc, same DNS, same route, comparable TLS/connect timings to the registry), and the storage backend was the only variable.

The only workaround we found is to disable the containerd image store — that is, to opt **out** of the new default. That is the outcome we would like to avoid; see the questions at the end.

---

### Steps to reproduce

This reproduction is fully self-contained. It needs only a throwaway VM, Docker Engine 29.x, the public `registry:2` image, and `mitmproxy`. No commercial registry is required — the slow blob commit is simulated deterministically.

#### 1. Build a large, incompressible single-layer image

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.bigblob
FROM ubuntu:24.04
RUN dd if=/dev/urandom of=/big.bin bs=1M count=6000
```

`/dev/urandom` is required: a file of zeros compresses to almost nothing and the resulting blob would never be large enough to matter.

#### 2. Start a local registry

```bash
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry --restart=always registry:2
```

#### 3. Put a proxy in front of it that delays only the blob-commit request

```python
# slow_commit.py
# Run with:
#   mitmdump -s slow_commit.py --mode reverse:http://127.0.0.1:5000 -p 5001
import time
from mitmproxy import http

def request(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None:
    # Delay only the final blob commit: PUT .../blobs/uploads/<uuid>?digest=sha256:...
    if flow.request.method == "PUT" and "digest" in flow.request.query:
        time.sleep(60)   # anything above the hardcoded 30s ResponseHeaderTimeout
```

Delaying only the commit is deliberate. It leaves the byte upload running at full speed and isolates exactly the behaviour a slow registry exhibits: fast transfer, slow finalization.

#### 4. Run A — containerd image store (fails)

```bash
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json >/dev/null <<'EOF'
{
  "features": { "containerd-snapshotter": true },
  "insecure-registries": ["127.0.0.1:5001"]
}
EOF
sudo systemctl restart docker

docker info -f 'driver={{.Driver}} status={{.DriverStatus}}'
# expected: driver=overlayfs status=[[driver-type io.containerd.snapshotter.v1]]

docker build -f Dockerfile.bigblob -t 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1 .
time docker push 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1
```

**Result:** aborts 30 seconds after the commit `PUT` is issued, with `failed commit on ref "layer-sha256:..." : ... net/http: timeout awaiting response headers`. No retry lines are emitted.

#### 5. Run B — classic overlay2 (succeeds)

Only the feature flag changes. Same image, same registry, same delay.

```bash
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json >/dev/null <<'EOF'
{
  "features": { "containerd-snapshotter": false },
  "insecure-registries": ["127.0.0.1:5001"]
}
EOF
sudo systemctl restart docker

docker info -f 'driver={{.Driver}}'
# expected: driver=overlay2

docker build -f Dockerfile.bigblob -t 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1 .
time docker push 127.0.0.1:5001/test/bigblob:1
```

**Result:** the push waits out the full 60-second delay and completes successfully.

`sudo journalctl -u docker -f` during both runs shows the underlying HTTP exchange and the presence or absence of retries.

#### Notes on the reproduction

The layer size is **not** the trigger and can be reduced substantially — a large layer is only what makes a real registry slow enough to cross the threshold in practice. The trigger is purely `time.sleep(n)` with `n > 30`. Conversely, setting `n < 30` makes both runs pass, which is a useful negative control.

---

### Related upstream work

containerd's resolver has since gained `doWithTransportRetries` in `core/remotes/docker/resolver.go`, which retries transient transport errors — explicitly including response-header timeouts — up to `maxAttempts = 5`. If we are reading this correctly, an engine built against a containerd containing that change should no longer exhibit the failure. Confirmation of that, and of which engine release will carry it, would be very helpful.

---

### Questions

The reason for opening this issue is less about the workaround (which we have) and more about how to stay on the new default:

1. **Is the 30-second `ResponseHeaderTimeout` intentional for the blob-commit request, and can it be made configurable?** Thirty seconds is a reasonable default for a manifest `HEAD` or a token request, but the commit `PUT` is a request whose entire purpose is to wait for server-side finalization of a potentially multi-gigabyte blob. Either exempting that request from the timeout, or exposing the value through `daemon.json`, would resolve this class of failure. Today there appears to be no supported way to adjust it without recompiling.

2. **Can the containerd push path adopt the same retry/backoff semantics as the classic path?** The asymmetry between the two backends is the surprising part: identical engine, identical registry, different resilience, with nothing in `docker info` suggesting that pushing behaviour would differ.

3. **What is the recommended configuration for a fresh Docker Engine 29.x installation that must push very large layers to a slow-finalizing registry, while keeping the containerd image store?** We would prefer not to set `"features": { "containerd-snapshotter": false }` on every newly provisioned host, because that means permanently opting out of the default and out of the direction the project is moving in. Is there a supported way to influence the registry client used by the containerd image store from `dockerd` — for example per-registry host configuration, `hosts.toml`-style settings, or any timeout tuning — that we have missed?

4. **Is any of this documented?** The behavioural difference between the two image stores on push is not mentioned on the containerd image store page, which currently describes the switch as transparent for most users. A note about large-blob push semantics would have saved us a considerable amount of diagnosis.

---

The reference host that succeeds is the same engine version, upgraded in place from an earlier release, and therefore still on `overlay2`.

### Description

`docker exec -it` injects a single stray NUL byte (`0x00`) into the attached output stream on essentially every invocation. The byte lands at a variable position — sometimes before any command output, sometimes after it (at session teardown) — which suggests it's tied to the exec session's connection open/close handling rather than to the command or its output itself.

This is reproducible with the most minimal possible command (`echo`), with a fully cleared environment (`env -i`), with both `bash` and `sh`, across multiple hosts, and container base images — so it does not appear to depend on the container's OS, shell, or any user configuration.

In interactive use, this stray byte is normally invisible (terminals silently discard NUL). But when the attached process is producing live, cursor-addressed terminal output (e.g. a test runner redrawing progress in place with ANSI cursor-positioning escape sequences, or printing multi-byte UTF-8 characters), the stray byte can land mid-escape-sequence or mid-character, corrupting the terminal's rendering for the remainder of the session (extra/incorrect line wrapping, misplaced cursor, garbled output) until the user runs `reset`.

### Reproduce

```bash
script -qec "docker exec -it <container> env -i sh -c 'echo minimal_env_test'" /tmp/nul_test.typescript < /dev/null
cat -A /tmp/nul_test.typescript

Replace <container> with the name/ID of any running container.

Expected output (cat -A, so $ marks end-of-line and ^M is a literal CR):
minimal_env_test^M$

Actual output — a stray NUL (rendered by cat -A as ^@) appears, either before or after the real output:
^@minimal_env_test^M$
or
minimal_env_test^M$
^@$



### Expected behavior

No NUL bytes

### docker version

```bash
Environment matrix

All reproduced with the exact command above (only the shell/image varied):

│           Host            │         Container image         │ Shell │            docker version            │

│ WSL2 (Ubuntu)             │ custom Ubuntu 22.04-based image │ bash  │ Docker version 29.4.0, build 9d7ad9f │
├───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Linux VM (CI build agent) │ same Ubuntu 22.04-based image   │ bash  │ Docker version 29.4.0, build 9d7ad9f │
├───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ WSL2 (Ubuntu)             │ alpine                          │ bash  │ Docker version 29.4.0, build 9d7ad9f │
├───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Linux                     │ alpine                          │ sh    │ Docker version 29.7.2, build a7dcaa6 │
└───────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┴───────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Additional Info


- Using env -i rules out any shell startup file (.bashrc, /etc/profile, BASH_ENV, etc.) as the source.

### Description

When I tag an image and start a container using that tag, executing the prune command removes the tag, resulting in a discrepancy between the information displayed by the `ps` command before and after the operation.

### Reproduce

1.docker tag fd2d3e51789e test2
2.docker run -itd test2:latest bash
3.docker ps
4.docker image prune -a
5.docker ps

### Expected behavior

prune cmd should retaining the tagged image currently in use

Created with: Astra (AI), under my supervision and review.

Candidate fix: https://github.com/moby/swarmkit/pull/3297

## Description

A valid unassigned task can remain Pending and desired Running after its eligible node returns. A service-level label update advances the service revision without replacing the task. If another scheduling pass occurs while the node is unavailable, the task is dropped from the scheduler's retry queue. An untouched control service recovers; force-updating the affected service creates a replacement that runs.

Related to [moby/moby#36699](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/36699), especially the [2023 node-restart report](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/36699#issuecomment-1784992254) and [2024 follow-up](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/36699#issuecomment-1977596175). Those later reports have similar symptoms but do not establish the metadata-update/revision trigger. The original 2018 issue concerns tasks desired Shutdown; this report concerns tasks still desired Running. This is not a claim to resolve all of #36699.

## Reproduce

The [disposable lab harness](https://github.com/Mazyod/swarm-pending-task-repro) creates labelled DinD daemons and cleans up only its own resources. It requires a local Linux-container Docker engine supporting privileged DinD. The original stock reproducer is pinned at `be601541949e509f65b1096e4ca0c760202364b9`:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Mazyod/swarm-pending-task-repro.git
cd swarm-pending-task-repro
git checkout be601541949e509f65b1096e4ca0c760202364b9
./scripts/run.sh pause 29.8.1
./scripts/run.sh restart 29.1.5
```

The smaller scenario performs these steps inside a disposable single-node Swarm:

1. Cache `busybox:1.37` and set the node's scheduling availability to Pause.
2. Create services `control` and `updated`, each running `busybox:1.37 sleep 600`; wait for both tasks to become Pending and record their IDs.
3. Run `docker service update --detach --label-add repro.revision=1 updated`. Its task ID remains unchanged.
4. Run `docker node update --label-add repro.tick=1 <node>` to trigger another scheduler pass while scheduling is still paused.
5. Set node availability back to Active. The original control task runs; the updated service's original task stays Pending.
6. Run `docker service update --detach --force updated`. A new task ID reaches Running.

The worker-restart scenario first runs both services on a separate worker using a hostname constraint. It stops that worker's DinD container, waits for Down and replacement Pending tasks, updates only one service's label, triggers a scheduler pass by creating an unrelated service, and starts the same worker. Only the untouched control recovers on stock Engine.

## Expected behavior

Both still-valid Pending tasks remain eligible for scheduling and run after node recovery.

Actual: the updated service's original Pending task remains unassigned and desired Running while the control runs. The lab observes five seconds after control recovery, and the source regression directly verifies loss of the retry queue entry.

- `docker:29.8.1-dind`: `docker@sha256:3f3c01aaaebf7cce837356b688b7c059a4749f10bd7660dec7c58fc454a283f0`
- `busybox:1.37`: `busybox@sha256:9db7b59979c38555a39def84a31fb98b5296952f9e3afd4f6f11f05b07adfab0`

One matching scheduler message from the 29.8.1 pause run:

```text
time="2026-09-18T11:15:04.855048722Z" level=debug msg="task belongs to old revision of service" module=scheduler node.id=5zow56i4ep3rwzvrlg9x9dk4d task.id=sw8i16alhabowfjz5pc4tu0uf
```

In [SwarmKit's scheduler](https://github.com/moby/swarmkit/blob/1fd637ba5cc32ff30d1dd2bdb14997bd4f424b46/manager/scheduler/scheduler.go#L926-L977), `noSuitableNode` takes the older-revision branch whenever `service.SpecVersion.Index > task.SpecVersion.Index`. For a task still desired Running, it neither transitions to Shutdown nor reaches `enqueue` in the other branch. The task remains in the store but disappears from later retries. The branch was introduced in [SwarmKit #2998](https://github.com/moby/swarmkit/pull/2998) to retire obsolete tasks desired Shutdown.

A candidate SwarmKit fix adds the desired-Shutdown condition to the older-revision branch. Its regression fails on stock because the task is missing from `unassignedTasks`, then passes with the fix and verifies assignment of the same task ID after node recovery. The full scheduler package, full scheduler race check, and full SwarmKit root-module suite pass on Go 1.27.1 linux/amd64, including the existing obsolete-task shutdown regression.

For runtime validation, built stock and patched managers from Moby `464cd50c3d9e92877d56940ea160de6fca7bea23` (29.8.1), vendoring SwarmKit `ad0357aedfca72c288abb8395ec5603e1136a9e5`. The scheduler file matches the tested SwarmKit HEAD byte-for-byte. The stock build reproduces both scenarios; the patched build recovers the same Pending task IDs in both, including with a stock worker. These are laboratory builds, not a released fix. A SwarmKit PR and a later Moby dependency update/backport are separate steps.

### Description

The Docker daemon crashed with a nil-pointer fault inside the container health-check monitor. The crash killed the daemon process; systemd restarted it within seconds, but containers with `restart: unless-stopped` did **not** resume — leaving a compose stack silently `Exited (0)` with no crash-loop in container logs.

This is a background daemon task (periodic health probe). There was no CLI/API activity, OOM, kernel OOM, or host restart at the time.

### Reproduce

No deterministic repro — the panic fired from the periodic health probe in steady state (~6 days healthy, 11 compose containers, mix of `CMD` / `CMD-SHELL` healthchecks, intervals 5s/10s).

1. Run a compose project with several healthchecked containers and `restart: unless-stopped`.
2. Leave it in steady state (hours to days).
3. Observe dockerd SIGSEGV in `handleProbeResult` → `Container.CommitInMemory` with no client trigger.
4. After systemd restarts dockerd, previously-running `unless-stopped` containers remain `Exited (0)`.

Likely requires the health-probe commit path plus something that leaves a map field's `reflect.Type` invalid (see analysis). Suggested tests: concurrent stop/remove during `handleProbeResult`/`CommitInMemory`, and fuzzing the JSON round-trip deepcopy.

### Expected behavior

- A fault while committing one container's health state should not take down the entire daemon.
- After an ungraceful daemon death, containers that were running with `unless-stopped` should come back (or the daemon should log clearly that they were left exited because they looked "intentionally stopped").
- A nil/invalid `reflect.Type` during JSON deepcopy of a freshly allocated `Container` should be treated as a recoverable error, not `throw("fault")`.

### docker version

```
Docker Engine: 29.7.2 (API 1.55)
Package: .deb from download.docker.com
Go version (engine module): go 1.26.3 (moby/moby@docker-v29.7.2 go.mod)
Built with containerd snapshotter enabled
OS/Arch: linux/amd64
```

Full `docker version` dump available on request.

### docker info

```
Storage driver: overlayfs (containerd snapshotter)
Swarm: inactive
1 daemon, no cluster
Host uptime at crash: 11 days
No memory pressure / OOM events, CPU load ~0
OS: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS (noble-class)
Kernel: 7.0.0-30-generic x86_64
```

Full `docker info` dump available on request.

### Additional Info

#### Crash log (`journalctl -u docker.service`)

```
Sep 19 10:05:37 node-4-dell-optiplex-3050 dockerd[1271]: unexpected fault address 0x0
Sep 19 10:05:37 node-4-dell-optiplex-3050 dockerd[1271]: fatal error: fault
Sep 19 10:05:37 node-4-dell-optiplex-3050 dockerd[1271]: [signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x80 addr=0x0 pc=0x5881fa00d52e]
Sep 19 10:05:37 node-4-dell-optiplex-3050 dockerd[1271]: goroutine 6642075 gp=0x30c3ade18960 m=220 mp=0x30c3ad323808 [running]:
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... runtime.throw({0x5881fc612c1c?, 0x18?})
     /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:1229
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... runtime.sigpanic()
     /usr/local/go/src/runtime/signal_unix.go:945
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... reflect.(*rtype).common(...)
     /usr/local/go/src/reflect/type.go:356
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... reflect.(*rtype).Elem(0x30c3ad830979?)
     /usr/local/go/src/reflect/type.go:769
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... encoding/json.(*decodeState).object(...)
     /usr/local/go/src/encoding/json/decode.go:691
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... encoding/json.(*decodeState).value / .object / .unmarshal
     (decode.go 380/767/777/183)
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... encoding/json.(*Decoder).Decode
     /usr/local/go/src/encoding/json/stream.go:75
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon/container.(*Container).CommitInMemory(0x30c3af07f088, 0x30c3ac606808)
     /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/container/container.go:311
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.handleProbeResult(...)
     /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:242
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.monitor(...)
     /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:320
Sep 19 10:05:37 ... github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.(*Daemon).updateHealthMonitor.gowrap1()
     /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:361
```

Line numbers match **docker-v29.7.2** / **Go 1.26.5**:

- `CommitInMemory` container.go:311 is `json.NewDecoder(&buf).Decode(&deepCopy)` after encoding the live container:
  https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.7.2/daemon/container/container.go#L300-L324
- `encoding/json` decode.go:691 is `elemType := t.Elem()` in the **map** branch of `object()`:
  https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.5/src/encoding/json/decode.go#L690-L693
- `runtime.sigpanic` signal_unix.go:945 is the `throw("fault")` path, not `panicmem()`:
  https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.5/src/runtime/signal_unix.go#L929-L945

#### What this is (and is not)

`CommitInMemory` does **not** unmarshal health-probe command output. It JSON-encodes the whole `Container`, then JSON-decodes into a fresh `var deepCopy Container` so the in-memory replica can be updated without a disk checkpoint. `handleProbeResult` already holds `c.Lock()` and already drops the result if the monitor `done` channel is closed.

So this is a deepcopy of container metadata on every successful/failed probe (every 5s/10s per healthchecked container), and the crash is while decoding a JSON **object into a map field** of that fresh copy (`t.Elem()` on the map's `reflect.Type`).

A concurrent stop/remove of the *live* container is a weak explanation for a nil `*rtype` here: the decode target is a zero `Container` on the stack, and map element types come from compile-time field descriptors (`MountPoints map[string]*MountPoint`, plus nested maps on `Config` / `NetworkSettings` / `State`). A nil `*rtype` at `t.Elem()` is closer to **corrupt or typed-nil `reflect.Type` metadata** than to a missing probe JSON blob.

#### Why `recover()` in `monitor` would not have saved this process

The log is `fatal error: fault` / `runtime.throw`, not a recoverable `panic("invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference")`.

Go 1.26.5 only converts a SIGSEGV at addr `< 0x1000` into `panicmem()` when `si_code` is `0`, `SEGV_MAPERR`, or `SEGV_ACCERR`. This crash has **`code=0x80` (`SI_KERNEL`) and `addr=0x0`**, so the runtime prints `unexpected fault address 0x0` and `throw("fault")`. That cannot be recovered in `monitor`.

Same `SI_KERNEL` + addr `0x0` + `throw("fault")` signature as golang/go#80933 (nil type pointer in runtime type-assert cache; discussion there also leans toward memory corruption).

#### Consequence amplification (`unless-stopped`)

`unless-stopped` is implemented as "restart unless `HasBeenManuallyStopped`" (`daemon/container/container.go` `ShouldRestart`, `restartmanager.ShouldRestart`). `handleContainerExit` also treats `daemon.IsShuttingDown()` as "manually stopped" for that check.

After this crash, containers were `Exited (0)`. Exit 0 + `unless-stopped` looks like an intentional stop, so the restarted daemon left the stack down until a manual `docker compose up -d`. In this incident that was a ~6h user-facing outage (reverse proxies 502) with a healthy-looking host.

Related but different stack: #50234 (`cmdProbe.run` / Docker 24, EOL). Related restart-policy footgun: #41302 / moby/moby#53415 (`HasBeenManuallyStopped` set too broadly).

#### Suggested directions

1. Stop using `encoding/json` round-trip as a hot-path deepcopy in `CommitInMemory` (or isolate map decode so a bad `reflect.Type` becomes an error, not a process-killing fault).
2. Do not let a health-monitor fault take down dockerd: even if `recover()` cannot catch `throw("fault")`, reducing unsafe reflect/json on this path still shrinks blast radius. `debug.SetPanicOnFault` is not a real fix.
3. On daemon restore after an ungraceful exit, do not treat `unless-stopped` + exit 0 as "user stopped this". Distinguish "stopped by user/compose" from "daemon was killed while it ran", and log a clear warning when containers are left exited for that reason.
4. Operator workaround today: `"live-restore": true` so containers keep running across dockerd death; `restart: always` is a poorer substitute because it also undoes an intentional `compose stop` after a later daemon restart.

Happy to attach the full journald excerpt, `docker version`, and `docker info` if useful.

body_text: ### Description - As is evident, the location mentioned at https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/binaries/#install-server-and-client-binaries-on-windows ( https://download.docker.com/win/static/stable/ ) contains only pre-built binaries for Windows x64. - - Specifically, to enable the use of Moby on the Windows ARM64 GitHub Actions runner (as seen in https://github.com/version-fox/vfox-flutter/pull/24 ), I had to manually write a PowerShell 7 script to install Git and Go, and then manually compile the Moby source code. Logic is like, ```powershell $git = "$env:TEMP\git-installer.exe" & curl.exe -fsSL -o $git "https://github.com/git-for-windows/git/releases/download/v2.55.0.windows.5/Git-2.55.0.5-arm64.exe" Start-Process $git -Wait -ArgumentList '/VERYSILENT', '/NORESTART', '/SP-', '/SUPPRESSMSGBOXES' $mobyVersion = '29.8.1' $root = 'C:\vfox-docker' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $root | Out-Null $goMsi = "$env:TEMP\go.msi" & curl.exe -fsSL -o $goMsi 'https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.1.windows-arm64.msi' & msiexec.exe /i $goMsi /quiet /norestart Remove-Item $goMsi $env:GOPATH = Join-Path $root 'gopath' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $env:GOPATH | Out-Null $env:PATH = "C:\Program Files\Go\bin;$env:GOPATH\bin;$env:PATH" $moby = Join-Path $root 'moby' git clone --depth 1 --branch "docker-v$mobyVersion" https://github.com/moby/moby.git $moby go install github.com/tc-hib/go-winres@v0.3.1 $env:DOCKERCLI_VERSION = $mobyVersion $env:VERSION = $mobyVersion Push-Location $moby & .\hack\make.ps1 -Client -Daemon Pop-Location $bin = Join-Path $moby 'bundles' $env:PATH = "$bin;$env:PATH" $dataRoot = Join-Path $root 'data' $log = Join-Path $root 'dockerd.log' $dockerdArgs = "--data-root `"$dataRoot`" --debug --exec-opt isolation=process" Start-Process -FilePath (Join-Path $bin 'dockerd.exe') -ArgumentList $dockerdArgs -RedirectStandardOutput $log -RedirectStandardError (Join-Path $root 'dockerd.err.log') docker info ``` - Providing PowerShell 7 scripts for compiling and installing Moby on Windows ARM64 clearly helps developers streamline this process.

body_text:
### Description

On Docker Engine 29.8.0 (`3ce5872`), an ordinary Swarm service backend addition sets the **host network namespace** `net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode` to `0` even though Docker's load-balancer IPVS service is in its separate LB sandbox namespace. Repeated writes during service rollouts override a host LVS-DR director's intentional `conn_reuse_mode=2`. In our three-node cluster a Keepalived IPVS health gate observed 0 on all nodes during an unstable service deploy and the active public VIP entered FAULT. One earlier VIP flap indirectly restarted the host DNS resolver and broke an offsite PostgreSQL backup. We saw 28 VI_1 FAULTs across the nodes since September 21; we do not assert that each historical fault has this same cause because the old gate lacked invariant logging.

### Reproduce

1. On a Swarm node running a host IPVS director, establish `sysctl -w net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode=2` and record `readlink /proc/1/ns/net`, `readlink /proc/$(pidof dockerd)/ns/net`, and host sysctl. The dockerd namespace must equal the host's.
2. Roll a service with default VIP endpoint mode and an overlay backend, while polling the **host** sysctl and journaling the host IPVS gate. Our bapi unstable deploy #219 at 2026-09-24 11:58Z yielded `UNHEALTHY: net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode is 0, expected 2` on all three nodes. On brovs1 `VI_1` and `VI_DEVOPS` entered FAULT at 11:58:03Z and regained MASTER at :11. The original 02:05 incident predates invariant logging, so its precise invariant is unknown.
3. The host timer repairs this to 2 once per second but repeated resets can be sampled by a two-second Keepalived health check. The competing writes are visible even without any Docker daemon restart.

Source: [service_linux.go:94-100,158-170](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/service_linux.go#L158-L170) uses `ipvs.New(sb.Key())` for the LB sandbox, then calls `sb.osSbox.ApplyOSTweaks(sb.oslTypes)` on every backend addition **outside** `Namespace.InvokeFunc`. [namespace_linux.go:568-584](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L568-L584) hardcodes mode 0, while [knobs_linux.go:19-47](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/kernel/knobs_linux.go#L19-L47) writes through the calling thread's `/proc/sys`. [`Namespace.InvokeFunc`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L317-L367) has the correct `LockOSThread`/`netns.Set` mechanism, but this call does not use it. No specific syscall trace was captured. Both [29.8.1](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.1/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L569-L584) and [master](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/libnetwork/service_linux.go#L168-L170) retain this behavior.

### Expected behavior

Adding a backend to Docker's LB sandbox must not repeatedly overwrite the host namespace's unrelated IPVS policy. Apply sandbox-local tweaks inside the sandbox netns, and document or offer an opt-out for any genuinely required host-global tuning. This should protect hosts running their own IPVS director without changing Docker's sandbox behavior.

{"repository": "moby/moby", "task_candidate_id": 17040, "repository_id": 173, "issue_number": 53766, "github_issue_id": 5574934724, "html_url": "https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/53766", "created_at": "2026-09-24T21:43:34+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "Swarm LB backend updates reset host IPVS conn_reuse_mode, disrupting independent host IPVS director", "body_text": "### Description

On Docker Engine 29.8.0 (`3ce5872`), an ordinary Swarm service backend addition sets the **host network namespace** `net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode` to `0` even though Docker's load-balancer IPVS service is in its separate LB sandbox namespace. Repeated writes during service rollouts override a host LVS-DR director's intentional `conn_reuse_mode=2`. In our three-node cluster a Keepalived IPVS health gate observed 0 on all nodes during an unstable service deploy and the active public VIP entered FAULT. One earlier VIP flap indirectly restarted the host DNS resolver and broke an offsite PostgreSQL backup. We saw 28 VI_1 FAULTs across the nodes since September 21; we do not assert that each historical fault has this same cause because the old gate lacked invariant logging.

### Reproduce

1. On a Swarm node running a host IPVS director, establish `sysctl -w net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode=2` and record `readlink /proc/1/ns/net`, `readlink /proc/$(pidof dockerd)/ns/net`, and host sysctl. The dockerd namespace must equal the host's.
2. Roll a service with default VIP endpoint mode and an overlay backend, while polling the **host** sysctl and journaling the host IPVS gate. Our bapi unstable deploy #219 at 2026-09-24 11:58Z yielded `UNHEALTHY: net.ipv4.vs.conn_reuse_mode is 0, expected 2` on all three nodes. On brovs1 `VI_1` and `VI_DEVOPS` entered FAULT at 11:58:03Z and regained MASTER at :11. The original 02:05 incident predates invariant logging, so its precise invariant is unknown.
3. The host timer repairs this to 2 once per second but repeated resets can be sampled by a two-second Keepalived health check. The competing writes are visible even without any Docker daemon restart.

Source: [service_linux.go:94-100,158-170](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/service_linux.go#L158-L170) uses `ipvs.New(sb.Key())` for the LB sandbox, then calls `sb.osSbox.ApplyOSTweaks(sb.oslTypes)` on every backend addition **outside** `Namespace.InvokeFunc`. [namespace_linux.go:568-584](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L568-L584) hardcodes mode 0, while [knobs_linux.go:19-47](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/kernel/knobs_linux.go#L19-L47) writes through the calling thread's `/proc/sys`. [`Namespace.InvokeFunc`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.0/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L317-L367) has the correct `LockOSThread`/`netns.Set` mechanism, but this call does not use it. No specific syscall trace was captured. Both [29.8.1](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.8.1/daemon/libnetwork/osl/namespace_linux.go#L569-L584) and [master](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/libnetwork/service_linux.go#L168-L170) retain this behavior.

### Expected behavior

Adding a backend to Docker's LB sandbox must not repeatedly overwrite the host namespace's unrelated IPVS policy. Apply sandbox-local tweaks inside the sandbox netns, and document or offer an opt-out for any genuinely required host-global tuning. This should protect hosts running their own IPVS director without changing Docker's sandbox behavior.

body_text: ### Description IPv6 address literals in image references are accepted since the fix from distribution/distribution#3489 (see #39033), e.g. [::1]:5000/image. However, a link-local IPv6 address with a zone ID is still rejected by the reference parser, so it is impossible to push/pull to a registry reachable only via IPv6 link-local. Use case: several devices on a network with only static link-local IPv6. One device runs an OCI registry (registry:3, host networking, listening on *:5000), the others need to pull/push. Global/ULA addresses are not available. The error comes from the reference parser, before any network connection is attempted. The registry itself is reachable over link-local (curl works, see below). ### Reproduce 1. Run a registry on the host: docker run -d --network host registry:3 2. Run: $ docker pull '[fe80::215:5dff:fea0:7253%eth0]:5000/test:latest' invalid reference format ### Expected behavior The reference is accepted and the client connects to https://[fe80::...%25eth0]:5000/v2/ (zone ID percent-encoded per RFC 6874), or a documented alternative syntax exists for link-local registries. ### docker version ```bash 29.8.1 / 29.8.1 ``` ### docker info ```bash docker info Client: Docker Engine - Community Version: 29.8.1 Context: default Debug Mode: false Plugins: buildx: Docker Buildx (Docker Inc.) Version: v0.37.1 Path: /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-buildx compose: Docker Compose (Docker Inc.) Version: v5.5.1 Path: /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose Server: Containers: 4 Running: 2 Paused: 0 Stopped: 2 Images: 8 Server Version: 29.8.1 Storage Driver: overlay2 Backing Filesystem: extfs Supports d_type: true Using metacopy: false Native Overlay Diff: true userxattr: false Logging Driver: json-file Cgroup Driver: systemd Cgroup Version: 2 Plugins: Volume: local ``` ### Additional Info Suggested direction: allow an optional zone ID in the IPv6 literal of the reference domain regexp (e.g. [fe80::1%25eth0]) and make sure the registry client percent-encodes it when building the URL (Go's net/url and net.Dialer handle zone IDs). If out of scope, a docs note that link-local zone IDs are unsupported would help.

- related: #49784 
- related: #53615
- related: #53864 

With a remote snapshotter (stargz, soci, nydus, overlaybd), `docker pull` doesn't download layer content that the snapshotter fetches lazily from the registry.

The images run, but `docker save` fails, and `docker push` fails unless the missing layers can be cross-repo mounted on the target registry.

This is basically #49784 was fixed by fetching all layer content on pull (#53615), and is intentionally reintroduced for remote snapshotters to keep the benefits of lazy pulling (https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/53877, #53864).


### Workaround

Set `"features": {"lazy-pull": false}` in `daemon.json`, reload the daemon configuration, and pull the image again.

### Description

When `dockerd` starts its own ("managed"/"embedded") containerd, there is no supported way to
customize that containerd's configuration. Everything is hardcoded in Go, and the generated config
file is overwritten on every daemon start.

**Current behavior**

`dockerd` builds the containerd config from a struct and serializes it to
`<exec-root>/containerd/containerd.toml` (i.e. `/var/run/docker/containerd/containerd.toml`),
truncating any existing file:

- `daemon/internal/libcontainerd/supervisor/remote_daemon.go`
  - `Start()` constructs `config.Config` with only `Version`, `Root`, `State`, `GRPC`, `Debug`.
  - `getContainerdConfig()` opens the file with `os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC|os.O_WRONLY` and encodes the
    struct, so hand-edits are lost on the next `dockerd` restart (and on containerd restarts
    performed by the supervisor).
- `daemon/internal/libcontainerd/supervisor/remote_daemon_options.go`: the only knobs are
  `WithLogLevel`, `WithLogFormat`, `WithCRIDisabled`, `WithDetectLocalBinary`.
- `daemon/command/daemon.go` (`getContainerdDaemonOpts`): the only daemon.json field that influences
  this is `cri-containerd`.

Consequences:

1. **No drop-in support.** containerd's own default config sets
   `imports = [defaults.DefaultConfigIncludePattern]` (typically `/etc/containerd/conf.d/*.toml`),
   but the config generated by dockerd is built from an empty `Imports` field, so the drop-in
   directory is silently ignored for the managed instance.
2. **No per-plugin configuration.** There is no way to set anything under `[plugins.*]`, e.g.:
   - CRI runtime options such as `privileged_without_host_devices` /
     `privileged_without_host_devices_all_devices_allowed`
     (needed for VM/sandbox runtimes like Kata/gVisor, where bind-mounting all host devices into a
     "privileged" container is meaningless or unsafe; see also #39697 and
     `containerd/internal/cri/server/container_create.go`),
   - `proxy_plugins` (external snapshotters, see #47444),
   - registry/`config_path`, runtime `options`, `base_runtime_spec` (cf. #45819).
3. **Hardcoded values drift.** dockerd still disables CRI by the containerd v1 plugin URI
   (`io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri`), which no longer matches anything in containerd v2
   (`io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime` / `io.containerd.cri.v1.images`); this had to be patched
   separately in #53564 / #53585 — a symptom of the config being generated from hardcoded strings.

**Workarounds today (and why they are not enough)**

- Run a system containerd on `/run/containerd/containerd.sock`; dockerd detects it
  (`systemContainerdRunning`) and skips starting a managed one, so `/etc/containerd/config.toml`
  and `conf.d/*.toml` apply. This works, but it forces users to install and manage a second daemon
  (systemd unit, upgrades, rootless setups), and it is not viable for the static-binary/container
  images (e.g. `dind`) where the whole point of the managed instance is "just run dockerd".
- Hand-edit `/var/run/docker/containerd/containerd.toml`: lost on the next daemon start.

**Proposal (open to alternatives)**

Give users a supported way to inject configuration into the managed containerd, e.g. one of:

1. Write containerd's default `imports` (or a Docker-specific drop-in dir such as
   `/etc/docker/containerd.d/*.toml`) into the generated config, so users can ship drop-in files.
   Requires a documented precedence rule for fields dockerd must own (`root`, `state`, `grpc.address`).
2. Add an explicit daemon.json field, e.g. `"containerd-config": { ... }` (raw `plugins` map merged
   over the generated config), and/or `"containerd-config-file": "/etc/docker/containerd.toml"`
   used as a base config that dockerd merges its required values over.
3. At minimum, a `--containerd-config-path` flag so the generated file location (and thus a
   pre-seeded config) can be controlled.

Related: #43950 (use containerd's defaults), #45819 (base OCI spec override), #39697
(`privileged-without-host-devices`), #47444 (nix-snapshotter needs `proxy_plugins`),
#53564 / #53585 (CRI plugin URIs).

# Upstream report: Docker containerd filesystem changes resource use

## Observed incident and source evidence

The reporter of [disk-space-saviour issue 22](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/22)
observed 22 concurrent changes requests against one Docker 29.6.1 container
using the containerd image store on an 11.7 GB Ubuntu 24.04 host. The kernel
reported dockerd anonymous RSS of 7,302,520 kB before killing it. Restarting
dockerd then terminated all task containers. The related
[profile](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/21)
records 2,022 seconds in 24 diffs of large image/build trees.

These are the original reporter's observations, not an OOM reproduced in this
checkout. This checkout's Docker daemon uses fuse-overlayfs, so it does not
reproduce the reported containerd backend. We intentionally did not run the
unbounded original reproduction on the shared host.

[ImageService.Changes](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/containerd/image_changes.go)
mounts both the parent image and the container root and calls
`archive.ChangesDirs(containerRoot, imageRoot)`. The call does not pass the
request context to the tree comparison. The endpoint returns the complete
change list; limiting the client's output therefore cannot bound the daemon's
tree-comparison allocation.

## Bounded diagnostic reproduction

Run on a disposable Linux VM with cgroup memory enforcement. Use a new DinD
daemon, without exposing the host Docker socket. Verify that `docker info`
inside it reports the containerd snapshotter. Cap the outer DinD container
at 1 GiB RAM, 1 GiB total memory/swap and 256 PIDs:

```sh
probe="dss-changes-probe-$$"
docker run -d --privileged --name "$probe" \
  --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g --pids-limit=256 \
  -e DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR= docker:29-dind
trap 'docker rm -f "$probe" >/dev/null' EXIT
ready=false
for attempt in $(seq 1 90); do
  if docker exec "$probe" docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    ready=true
    break
  fi
  sleep 1
done
"$ready" || exit 1
docker exec "$probe" docker info
docker exec "$probe" sh -c '
  set -eu
  mkdir -p /tmp/context
  cat > /tmp/context/Dockerfile <<\EOF
FROM busybox:1.37
RUN mkdir /lower && i=0 && while [ "$i" -lt 10000 ]; do \
    echo lower > /lower/f"$i"; i=$((i+1)); done
EOF
  docker build -t changes-probe /tmp/context
  docker run -d --name target changes-probe sleep 600
  docker exec target sh -c "echo upper > /lower/one-new-file"
  time docker diff target > /tmp/diff-single.txt
  wc -l /tmp/diff-single.txt
'
```

The escaped heredoc delimiter preserves the Dockerfile variables literally.
This proposed diagnostic has not run here: our host rejects memory-capped DinD
containers with `cannot enter cgroupv2 ... invalid state` before startup.
Repeat with finite 1,000 and 10,000
lower files, and at most two concurrent requests. Record elapsed time and
the daemon's `/proc/<pid>/status` before/after; the diagnostic does not promise
to reproduce OOM. The memory cap contains any failure to this test daemon.
Wait for readiness before building; remove its container in `finally`/the trap.

## Workarounds and suggested code changes

Clients should serialize requests, cache one snapshot per measurement run,
skip large candidates or low-memory hosts, and prefer direct upperdir usage.
Removing image-layer files creates whiteouts and does not recover image bytes;
remove unused containers/images after work finishes instead.

For the overlay snapshotter, derive changes from upperdir metadata and whiteouts
without walking unchanged lower contents. For other snapshotters, add request
cancellation to tree comparison, bound concurrent expensive comparisons per
daemon, and expose a bounded/streaming changes API or snapshot usage suitable
for individual paths. Document that the current changes endpoint can consume
memory proportional to the compared trees.

## Observed incident and source evidence

The reporter of [disk-space-saviour issue 22](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/22)
observed 22 concurrent changes requests against one Docker 29.6.1 container
using the containerd image store on an 11.7 GB Ubuntu 24.04 host. The kernel
reported dockerd anonymous RSS of 7,302,520 kB before killing it. Restarting
dockerd then terminated all task containers. The related
[profile](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/21)
records 2,022 seconds in 24 diffs of large image/build trees.

These are the original reporter's observations, not an OOM reproduced in this
checkout. This checkout's Docker daemon uses fuse-overlayfs, so it does not
reproduce the reported containerd backend. We intentionally did not run the
unbounded original reproduction on the shared host.

[ImageService.Changes](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/containerd/image_changes.go)
mounts both the parent image and the container root and calls
`archive.ChangesDirs(containerRoot, imageRoot)`. The call does not pass the
request context to the tree comparison. The endpoint returns the complete
change list; limiting the client's output therefore cannot bound the daemon's
tree-comparison allocation.

## Bounded diagnostic reproduction

Run on a disposable Linux VM with cgroup memory enforcement. Use a new DinD
daemon, without exposing the host Docker socket. Verify that `docker info`
inside it reports the containerd snapshotter. Cap the outer DinD container
at 1 GiB RAM, 1 GiB total memory/swap and 256 PIDs:

```sh
probe="dss-changes-probe-$$"
docker run -d --privileged --name "$probe" \
  --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g --pids-limit=256 \
  -e DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR= docker:29-dind
trap 'docker rm -f "$probe" >/dev/null' EXIT
ready=false
for attempt in $(seq 1 90); do
  if docker exec "$probe" docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    ready=true
    break
  fi
  sleep 1
done
"$ready" || exit 1
docker exec "$probe" docker info
docker exec "$probe" sh -c '
  set -eu
  mkdir -p /tmp/context
  cat > /tmp/context/Dockerfile <<\EOF
FROM busybox:1.37
RUN mkdir /lower && i=0 && while [ "$i" -lt 10000 ]; do \
    echo lower > /lower/f"$i"; i=$((i+1)); done
EOF
  docker build -t changes-probe /tmp/context
  docker run -d --name target changes-probe sleep 600
  docker exec target sh -c "echo upper > /lower/one-new-file"
  time docker diff target > /tmp/diff-single.txt
  wc -l /tmp/diff-single.txt
'
```

The escaped heredoc delimiter preserves the Dockerfile variables literally.
This proposed diagnostic has not run here: our host rejects memory-capped DinD
containers with `cannot enter cgroupv2 ... invalid state` before startup.
Repeat with finite 1,000 and 10,000
lower files, and at most two concurrent requests. Record elapsed time and
the daemon's `/proc/<pid>/status` before/after; the diagnostic does not promise
to reproduce OOM. The memory cap contains any failure to this test daemon.
Wait for readiness before building; remove its container in `finally`/the trap.

## Workarounds and suggested code changes

Clients should serialize requests, cache one snapshot per measurement run,
skip large candidates or low-memory hosts, and prefer direct upperdir usage.
Removing image-layer files creates whiteouts and does not recover image bytes;
remove unused containers/images after work finishes instead.

For the overlay snapshotter, derive changes from upperdir metadata and whiteouts
without walking unchanged lower contents. For other snapshotters, add request
cancellation to tree comparison, bound concurrent expensive comparisons per
daemon, and expose a bounded/streaming changes API or snapshot usage suitable
for individual paths. Document that the current changes endpoint can consume
memory proportional to the compared trees.

one can build images using the platform parameter.
ex.: `build --platform=linux/amd64`  

these images can be bundled using manifests.
ex.: `manifest create [name, list, ...]`

at runtime the selector `platform` is read and according to the client machine the right image used to do action.
is there a possibility for a custom selector that can be supplied on the cli.

personally id prefer to use subject from the referral api. add a relationhship that can be addressed directly.
there is also the possibility to add annotations, which currently arent addressable but could be regarded as an alternative.

an exemplatory command would look like:
`run --platform=linux/amd64 --subject=test`

 if there is a feature like this. please let me know.

body_text:
### Description

Since Docker 29.0, when starting a container fails while setting up its network (e.g. a published port can't be bound), the network is removed from the container's saved config: `NetworkSettings.Networks` becomes `{}`, while `HostConfig.NetworkMode` is unchanged. From then on, every start of the container **succeeds with only `lo`**: no `eth0`, no published ports, no error. Only recreating the container recovers it.

A common real-world trigger is the boot race from #39559: a port is published on a specific host IP (here a DNS server on `192.168.1.66:53`), dockerd starts before that IP is configured, and the bind fails with `cannot assign requested address`. Before v29 a later `docker start` brought the container back with its network. Since v29 the container comes back silently without network.

**Cause (from reading the source):** #50945 ("Tidy up when endpoint join fails", first released in v29.0.0) added this to `connectToNetwork` in `daemon/container_operations.go`:

```go
ctr.NetworkSettings.Networks[nwName] = endpointConfig
defer func() {
    if retErr != nil {
        delete(ctr.NetworkSettings.Networks, nwName)
    }
}()
```

That is the right cleanup for `docker network connect`, but the same path runs when a container starts. After a failed start the empty map is checkpointed. On the next start, `updateContainerNetworkSettings` only falls back to `HostConfig.NetworkMode` when `Networks == nil`, not when it is empty. `allocateNetwork` then loops over the empty map and connects nothing, without an error.

That `delete(...Networks, nwName)` is not present in `daemon/container_operations.go` for v20.10.27 through v28.5.2, and is present in docker-v29.0.0 and docker-v29.9.0.

### Reproduce

Runs in a few seconds and uses a documentation IP (`192.0.2.10`) that is not on the host:

```bash
docker network create repro-net
docker create --name repro --network repro-net -p 192.0.2.10:6399:6379 valkey/valkey:9
docker start repro                    # fails: cannot assign requested address (expected)
docker inspect repro --format 'networks={{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
sudo ip addr add 192.0.2.10/32 dev lo
docker start repro                    # succeeds...
docker inspect repro --format 'status={{.State.Status}} networks={{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
docker port repro
# cleanup
sudo ip addr del 192.0.2.10/32 dev lo; docker rm -f repro; docker network rm repro-net
```

Output on 29.9.0:

```
== 1. after create

body_text:
### Description

`docker cp` is performed entirely on the host. It works by mounting the
container rootfs **on the host** and pivoting into that mount. That is sound for
runc and for directory-based snapshotters, but it breaks when a VM-based runtime
(Kata) uses block-device passthrough — which a block-device-backed snapshotter
triggers *unless passthrough is explicitly disabled*: the authoritative mount is
then inside the guest, so the host mount that `docker cp` creates is a second,
independent instance of the same filesystem.

Tested with the `blockfile` snapshotter. `devmapper` reaches passthrough by a
shorter path (its mount source is already a `/dev/mapper/...` block device) and
is expected to behave the same way, but was not tested here.

Both directions then misbehave **silently — exit status 0**. What comes back
depends on timing; observed outcomes for copy-out include:

- **empty contents**, with correct size, mode and timestamps;
- **contents of a different file** — a copy-out returned the data of an
  unrelated file (the mechanism behind this particular case is not established);
- **`No such file or directory`** for a file that exists in the container;
- occasionally the correct contents.

Copy-in writes into the host instance: the container never sees the file, and
the write can **persistently corrupt** the guest's filesystem (demonstrated
below).

This is data loss and data corruption, not an error: `docker cp` reports success
on the command line in every case above. (Whether anything is written to the
daemon log was not checked.)

### Reproduce

```bash
# Requires Docker with containerd-snapshotter + blockfile, and a Kata runtime.
docker run -d --runtime kata --name ktest alpine sleep 3600
docker exec ktest sh -c 'echo PROBE_FROM_GUEST > /probe_guest && sync'

# copy-out: exits 0, but the payload is wrong — empty, stale, or another file's
# contents depending on timing; or the file may not be found at all
docker cp ktest:/probe_guest /tmp/probe_guest && echo "exit=$?"
ls -l /tmp/probe_guest          # size 17 — looks fine
cat /tmp/probe_guest            # may be empty or wrong

# copy-in: exits 0, but the container never sees it
echo CP_FROM_HOST > /tmp/cp_in.txt
docker cp /tmp/cp_in.txt ktest:/cp_in.txt && echo "exit=$?"
docker exec ktest cat /cp_in.txt
# cat: can't open '/cp_in.txt': No such file or directory
```

### Expected behavior

`docker cp` should not silently operate on a non-authoritative view of the
container filesystem. Either:

1. it fails with a clear error when the rootfs is not safely accessible from the
   host, or
2. it transfers through the guest (e.g. `exec` + `tar`, the way `kubectl cp`
   does), which is correct for any runtime and needs no host mount.

Today it does neither: it exits 0 with wrong data, in both directions.

### docker version

{"repository": "moby/moby", "task_candidate_id": 17052, "repository_id": 173, "issue_number": 53930, "github_issue_id": 5825279514, "html_url": "https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/53930", "created_at": "2026-10-13T05:52:05+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "`docker cp` silently returns wrong data and corrupts the container filesystem when it mounts a rootfs the VM guest already has mounted (Kata + block-device passthrough)", "body_text": "### Description

`docker cp` is performed entirely on the host. It works by mounting the
container rootfs **on the host** and pivoting into that mount. That is sound for
runc and for directory-based snapshotters, but it breaks when a VM-based runtime
(Kata) uses block-device passthrough — which a block-device-backed snapshotter
triggers *unless passthrough is explicitly disabled*: the authoritative mount is
then inside the guest, so the host mount that `docker cp` creates is a second,
independent instance of the same filesystem.

Tested with the `blockfile` snapshotter. `devmapper` reaches passthrough by a
shorter path (its mount source is already a `/dev/mapper/...` block device) and
is expected to behave the same way, but was not tested here.

Both directions then misbehave **silently — exit status 0**. What comes back
depends on timing; observed outcomes for copy-out include:

- **empty contents**, with correct size, mode and timestamps;
- **contents of a different file** — a copy-out returned the data of an
  unrelated file (the mechanism behind this particular case is not established);
- **`No such file or directory`** for a file that exists in the container;
- occasionally the correct contents.

Copy-in writes into the host instance: the container never sees the file, and
the write can **persistently corrupt** the guest's filesystem (demonstrated
below).

This is data loss and data corruption, not an error: `docker cp` reports success
on the command line in every case above. (Whether anything is written to the
daemon log was not checked.)

### Reproduce

```bash
# Requires Docker with containerd-snapshotter + blockfile, and a Kata runtime.
docker run -d --runtime kata --name ktest alpine sleep 3600
docker exec ktest sh -c 'echo PROBE_FROM_GUEST > /probe_guest && sync'

# copy-out: exits 0, but the payload is wrong — empty, stale, or another file's
# contents depending on timing; or the file may not be found at all
docker cp ktest:/probe_guest /tmp/probe_guest && echo "exit=$?"
ls -l /tmp/probe_guest          # size 17 — looks fine
cat /tmp/probe_guest            # may be empty or wrong

# copy-in: exits 0, but the container never sees it
echo CP_FROM_HOST > /tmp/cp_in.txt
docker cp /tmp/cp_in.txt ktest:/cp_in.txt && echo "exit=$?"
docker exec ktest cat /cp_in.txt
# cat: can't open '/cp_in.txt': No such file or directory
```

### Expected behavior

`docker cp` should not silently operate on a non-authoritative view of the
container filesystem. Either:

1. it fails with a clear error when the rootfs is not safely accessible from the
   host, or
2. it transfers through the guest (e.g. `exec` + `tar`, the way `kubectl cp`
   does), which is correct for any runtime and needs no host mount.

Today it does neither: it exits 0 with wrong data, in both directions.
