body_text:
I'd like to revisit a long-standing `net.Socket` behavior, following an investigation and proof of concept in libuv: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/5308

This is closely related to [nodejs/node#23858](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/23858), opened in 2018,  where `socket.remoteAddress`, `remotePort`, and `remoteFamily` could already be `undefined` inside the server's connection handler.

That discussion ended without a fix, but a maintainer comment also left room for reconsideration if a stronger technical case could be made.

I've tried to approach this follow-up in that spirit: I traced the behavior through the Node.js and libuv history, examined the relevant Linux kernel semantics, built a libuv proof of concept that preserves the accept-time peer address, and benchmarked its connection-throughput cost.

The findings point to an information-lifetime issue at the libuv layer. Preserving the accept-time address also has a different performance profile from restoring the old unconditional `getpeername()` call.

## What happens

On Unix, libuv accepts incoming TCP connections without requesting the peer sockaddr from `accept()` / `accept4()`. When Node.js later needs the remote address, libuv calls `getpeername()` on the accepted socket.

Normally that works. However, a connection can complete successfully and then be reset before the application processes it. The distinction between obtaining the peer address as part of `accept()` and querying it later with `getpeername()` is part of the original BSD sockets API design, introduced with 4.2BSD in 1983; it is not specific to Linux. The Linux reproducer demonstrates why this distinction matters: `accept()` can still return the peer address even when a subsequent `getpeername()` fails with `ENOTCONN`.

Once the accept-time sockaddr has been discarded, the later query cannot recover it.

A reproducer in the libuv issue demonstrates this using a normal TCP `connect()` followed by an abortive close with `SO_LINGER`.

In one 100,000-connection run using Node.js v26.10.0 / libuv v1.52.1:

```text
upstream:
  Address:    3,268
  Undefined: 96,732

patched:
  Address:   100,000
  Undefined:      0
```

The exact percentage is timing-dependent. The relevant observation is that the connections completed and were accepted, but their peer addresses could become unavailable before the later query. Preserving the sockaddr returned at accept time eliminated that failure mode in this test.

## Historical context

I documented the relevant Node.js and libuv history here: https://github.com/bobnil/libuv-accept-peer-address-poc/blob/main/HISTORICAL_CONTEXT.md

Before the libuv backend, Node's networking code retained the peer address returned by the accept operation.

The first public Node.js/libuv backend retained the accepted fd but did not propagate the accept-time peer address with it. The address was subsequently obtained through a separate `getpeername()` query.

Node initially performed that query eagerly. In 2011, it was made lazy, avoiding an unconditional syscall for
applications that never used the remote address and improving the connection-heavy `http_simple` benchmark by about 1%.

In 2012, libuv also stopped requesting the sockaddr from `accept()`, since it was not being retained anyway.

Each of these decisions makes sense in isolation. Together, however, they mean that a successfully accepted connection does not necessarily retain the peer information that was available at accept time.

The same underlying race appears to have been identified in [nodejs/node-v0.x-archive#7566](https://github.com/nodejs/node-v0.x-archive/issues/7566) in 2014, where retaining the
address returned by `accept()` was already discussed as a possible solution.

The 2018 report in #23858 is particularly relevant because the remote properties were accessed directly inside the
server's connection handler: the information could already be unavailable at the first application-visible opportunity to read it.

Later Node.js changes improved caching after a successful peer-address lookup. That helps preserve information already obtained, but does not address the case where the socket state changes before the first lookup succeeds.

## Performance

I built a proof-of-concept libuv patch that retrieves and preserves the accept-time sockaddr, and benchmarked it against the same unmodified libuv revision: https://github.com/bobnil/libuv-accept-peer-address-poc/blob/main/BENCHMARK.md

The benchmark deliberately favors upstream: the server accepts and immediately closes each connection without querying the peer address. Upstream therefore performs neither accept-time address retrieval nor a later `getpeername()`, while the patched build retrieves and retains an address that the application never uses.

Tests included local loopback and two-machine runs, ranging from 500,000 to 50 million connections.

Across the datasets, the direction of the measured difference changed: some favored upstream and some favored the patched build, with run-to-run variation larger than the observed differences.

I therefore could not identify a reproducible connection-throughput regression from retrieving and preserving the accept-time sockaddr in this Linux environment.

This does not establish zero cost on every platform or workload. It does suggest that this approach merits evaluation separately from the historical cost of an unconditional `getpeername()` call: asking `accept()` to return the peer address does not add that extra syscall.

## Where to go from here

The implementation question belongs primarily in libuv, which is why I opened the issue there.

A production-quality solution needs somewhere to retain the peer sockaddr together with the pending accepted connection while respecting libuv's API/ABI compatibility requirements. My patch changes internal storage and is intended as a proof of concept, rather than a proposed final implementation.

I'm raising it here because the behavior is directly visible to Node.js applications. A server can successfully accept a TCP connection yet be unable to determine its remote endpoint even in the connection callback.

That can matter for connection logging, auditing, diagnostics, and IP-based abuse mitigation.

I'd be interested in the Node.js networking/libuv maintainers' thoughts on two questions:

1. Should an accepted TCP connection ideally retain the peer address that was available when it was accepted, rather than depending entirely on a later socket-state query?
2. If so, what would be the best way for Node.js and libuv to coordinate on preserving that information without disrupting libuv 1.x ABI compatibility?

The [libuv issue](https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/5308) contains the reproducer, proof of concept, kernel references, and more detailed analysis.

Thanks for taking a look.

### Disclaimer

_I used AI tools alongside other search tools to help investigate the history, organize the source material, and draft this report in technical English, which is not my native language._

_I personally checked the cited sources, reviewed and edited the text. I also ran the reproducer and benchmarks myself. I stand behind the findings and take responsibility for the contents of this report._

{"repository": "nodejs/node", "task_candidate_id": 17860, "repository_id": 183, "issue_number": 66422, "github_issue_id": 5652533557, "html_url": "https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/66422", "created_at": "2026-09-30T20:22:25+00:00", "author_association": null, "title": "Discussion: preserving TCP peer addresses at accept time", "body_text": "I'd like to revisit a long-standing `net.Socket` behavior, following an investigation and proof of concept in libuv: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/5308

This is closely related to [nodejs/node#23858](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/23858), opened in 2018,  where `socket.remoteAddress`, `remotePort`, and `remoteFamily` could already be `undefined` inside the server's connection handler.

That discussion ended without a fix, but a maintainer comment also left room for reconsideration if a stronger technical case could be made.

I've tried to approach this follow-up in that spirit: I traced the behavior through the Node.js and libuv history, examined the relevant Linux kernel semantics, built a libuv proof of concept that preserves the accept-time peer address, and benchmarked its connection-throughput cost.

The findings point to an information-lifetime issue at the libuv layer. Preserving the accept-time address also has a different performance profile from restoring the old unconditional `getpeername()` call.

## What happens

On Unix, libuv accepts incoming TCP connections without requesting the peer sockaddr from `accept()` / `accept4()`. When Node.js later needs the remote address, libuv calls `getpeername()` on the accepted socket.

Normally that works. However, a connection can complete successfully and then be reset before the application processes it. The distinction between obtaining the peer address as part of `accept()` and querying it later with `getpeername()` is part of the original BSD sockets API design, introduced with 4.2BSD in 1983; it is not specific to Linux. The Linux reproducer demonstrates why this distinction matters: `accept()` can still return the peer address even when a subsequent `getpeername()` fails with `ENOTCONN`.

Once the accept-time sockaddr has been discarded, the later query cannot recover it.

A reproducer in the libuv issue demonstrates this using a normal TCP `connect()` followed by an abortive close with `SO_LINGER`.

In one 100,000-connection run using Node.js v26.10.0 / libuv v1.52.1:

```text
upstream:
  Address:    3,268
  Undefined: 96,732

patched:
  Address:   100,000
  Undefined:      0
```

The exact percentage is timing-dependent. The relevant observation is that the connections completed and were accepted, but their peer addresses could become unavailable before the later query. Preserving the sockaddr returned at accept time eliminated that failure mode in this test.

## Historical context

I documented the relevant Node.js and libuv history here: https://github.com/bobnil/libuv-accept-peer-address-poc/blob/main/HISTORICAL_CONTEXT.md

Before the libuv backend, Node's networking code retained the peer address returned by the accept operation.

The first public Node.js/libuv backend retained the accepted fd but did not propagate the accept-time peer address with it. The address was subsequently obtained through a separate `getpeername()` query.

Node initially performed that query eagerly. In 2011, it was made lazy, avoiding an unconditional syscall for
applications that never used the remote address and improving the connection-heavy `http_simple` benchmark by about 1%.

In 2012, libuv also stopped requesting the sockaddr from `accept()`, since it was not being retained anyway.

Each of these decisions makes sense in isolation. Together, however, they mean that a successfully accepted connection does not necessarily retain the peer information that was available at accept time.

The same underlying race appears to have been identified in [nodejs/node-v0.x-archive#7566](https://github.com/nodejs/node-v0.x-archive/issues/7566) in 2014, where retaining the
address returned by `accept()` was already discussed as a possible solution.

The 2018 report in #23858 is particularly relevant because the remote properties were accessed directly inside the
server's connection handler: the information could already be unavailable at the first application-visible opportunity to read it.

Later Node.js changes improved caching after a successful peer-address lookup. That helps preserve information already obtained, but does not address the case where the socket state changes before the first lookup succeeds.

## Performance

I built a proof-of-concept libuv patch that retrieves and preserves the accept-time sockaddr, and benchmarked it against the same unmodified libuv revision: https://github.com/bobnil/libuv-accept-peer-address-poc/blob/main/BENCHMARK.md

The benchmark deliberately favors upstream: the server accepts and immediately closes each connection without querying the peer address. Upstream therefore performs neither accept-time address retrieval nor a later `getpeername()`, while the patched build retrieves and retains an address that the application never uses.

Tests included local loopback and two-machine runs, ranging from 500,000 to 50 million connections.

Across the datasets, the direction of the measured difference changed: some favored upstream and some favored the patched build, with run-to-run variation larger than the observed differences.

I therefore could not identify a reproducible connection-throughput regression from retrieving and preserving the accept-time sockaddr in this Linux environment.

This does not establish zero cost on every platform or workload. It does suggest that this approach merits evaluation separately from the historical cost of an unconditional `getpeername()` call: asking `accept()` to return the peer address does not add that extra syscall.

## Where to go from here

The implementation question belongs primarily in libuv, which is why I opened the issue there.

A production-quality solution needs somewhere to retain the peer sockaddr together with the pending accepted connection while respecting libuv's API/ABI compatibility requirements. My patch changes internal storage and is intended as a proof of concept, rather than a proposed final implementation.

I'm raising it here because the behavior is directly visible to Node.js applications. A server can successfully accept a TCP connection yet be unable to determine its remote endpoint even in the connection callback.

That can matter for connection logging, auditing, diagnostics, and IP-based abuse mitigation.

I'd be interested in the Node.js networking/libuv maintainers' thoughts on two questions:

1. Should an accepted TCP connection ideally retain the peer address that was available when it was accepted, rather than depending entirely on a later socket-state query?
2. If so, what would be the best way for Node.js and libuv to coordinate on preserving that information without disrupting libuv 1.x ABI compatibility?

The [libuv issue](https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/5308) contains the reproducer, proof of concept, kernel references, and more detailed analysis.

Thanks for taking a look.

_I personally checked the cited sources, reviewed and edited the text. I also ran the reproducer and benchmarks myself. I stand behind the findings and take responsibility for the contents of this report._

This issue is just informative, feel free to close it if you think there is no action needed.

### Version

v27.0.0-pre (main @ 4486dce7097)

### Platform

```text
Darwin 25.6.0 arm64
```

### Subsystem

sqlite

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
db.exec('CREATE TABLE r(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE o(x)');
db.prepare('INSERT INTO r VALUES (?)').run(2n ** 53n + 1n); // ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE, row is inserted
db.prepare('DELETE FROM o').run();                          // ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, when `readBigInts` is off and the connection's last insert rowid exceeds 2^53.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

`run()` shouldn't throw after the write has committed. Proposal: return a `BigInt` for out-of-range values regardless of `readBigInts`. Is that acceptable, or should we only document it?

### What do you see instead?

`run()` converts `lastInsertRowid` and `changes` only after stepping (`src/node_sqlite.cc:4153`). If a value is outside the safe-integer range, it throws, but the write has already committed. The last insert rowid belongs to the connection, so every later `run()` on that connection also throws. Not documented.

### Version

v24.21.0 (also seen on 24.16.0)

### Platform

darwin arm64 (the logic is platform-independent)

### Subsystem

esm, modules

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

No dependencies are needed. Create one package with 200 chained modules and a large `exports` map:

```js
// make.mjs: one package, 200 chained modules, an exports map of about 130 KB
import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
const N = 200, EXPORTS = +process.argv[2];
mkdirSync('node_modules/big/lib', { recursive: true });
const exp = { '.': './lib/m0.js' };
for (let i = 0; i < EXPORTS; i++) exp[`./sub/feature-${i}/deep/path`] = { types: `./lib/s${i}.d.ts`, import: `./lib/s${i}.js`, require: `./lib/s${i}.cjs`, default: `./lib/s${i}.js` };
writeFileSync('node_modules/big/package.json', JSON.stringify({ name: 'big', type: 'module', exports: exp }, null, 2));
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) writeFileSync(`node_modules/big/lib/m${i}.js`, (i + 1 < N ? `import './m${i + 1}.js';\n` : '') + `export const v${i} = ${i};\n`);
```

```
$ node make.mjs 700 && node --input-type=module -e "const t=performance.now(); await import('big'); console.log(Math.round(performance.now()-t)+'ms', Math.round(process.resourceUsage().maxRSS/1024)+'MB')"
90ms 140MB
$ node make.mjs 0   && node --input-type=module -e "...same..."
18ms 55MB
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Every time. The cost grows with (import edges inside a package) × (size of that package's `exports` map).

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Resolving a module's format should not depend on the size of its package's `exports` map. `getFileProtocolModuleFormat` only reads `type`, `pjsonPath` and `exists`.

### What do you see instead?

For every resolved `.js` URL, `getFileProtocolModuleFormat` (lib/internal/modules/esm/get_format.js) calls `getPackageScopeConfig(url)` to read the package `type`. `getPackageScopeConfig` returns `{ ...data, exists, pjsonPath }`. The `...data` spread fires the lazy `exports` (and `imports`) getters from `deserializePackageJSON`, and those getters JSON-parse the raw string on every access. So the whole `exports` map is parsed again for every import edge inside the package, although format detection needs only `type`.

Real-world case: drizzle-orm 1.0.0-rc.4 ships a 290 KB package.json with 718 exports. `await import('drizzle-orm/sqlite-core')` peaks at 301 MB RSS and takes 181 ms. The same code loaded through drizzle's CJS build, which never takes this path, peaks at 60 MB. A heap-sampling profile that includes collected objects attributes about 137 MB of allocations to `package_json_reader` `get` / `getPackageScopeConfig`, under `defaultResolve -> defaultGetFormatWithoutErrors`.

### Additional information

Possible fixes, any one of which would do:
- call `getPackageType()`, which already exists and returns only the type;
- read the three fields without spreading `data`;
- cache the parsed `exports`/`imports` per package.json instead of re-parsing on each getter access.

We work around it in our CLI with a `module.registerHooks` resolve hook that caches the package-scope `type` per directory. That takes the drizzle case from 301 MB to 63 MB. Today every ESM consumer of a package with a large `exports` map pays this cost.

### Version

v26.10.0 (all repros below). The `expandedSQL` blob repro also aborts on v24.21.0 and v22.23.2.

### Platform

```text
Linux hostname 7.0.0-34-generic #34-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Sep  2 14:29:37 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

### Subsystem

sqlite

### What steps will reproduce the bug?


`statement.expandedSQL`:

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
const stmt = db.prepare('SELECT ?');
stmt.run(Buffer.alloc((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH >>> 1) + 1));
stmt.expandedSQL; // aborts
```

`sqlite.db.query` diagnostics channel (v26.8.0 and later):

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const dc = require('node:diagnostics_channel');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

dc.subscribe('sqlite.db.query', () => {});
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
db.prepare('SELECT length(?)').get(
  Buffer.alloc((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH >>> 1) + 1)); // aborts
```

`statement.sourceSQL`:

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

const n = Math.ceil((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH + 1) / 3);
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
const stmt = db.prepare(`SELECT '${'€'.repeat(n)}'`);
stmt.sourceSQL; // aborts
```

In the first two, the blob is 268,435,445 bytes. `sqlite3_expanded_sql()` renders a bound blob as `x'<hex>'`, so the expanded SQL is 536,870,900 bytes, which is more than `String::kMaxLength` (536,870,888 on 64-bit).

In the third, the SQL string has 178,956,972 characters, which is under `String::kMaxLength`, but its UTF-8 encoding is 536,870,898 bytes, which is over it.


### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Every run. The condition is SQL text whose UTF-8 encoding is longer than `String::kMaxLength` bytes:

- `expandedSQL` and the trace callback: a bound parameter makes the expanded SQL that long. A blob does it at about 256 MiB. On v26.10.0, a text parameter of multi-byte characters also does it: `stmt.run('€'.repeat(178956963))` followed by `stmt.expandedSQL` aborts.
- `sourceSQL`: the SQL passed to `prepare()` is that long in UTF-8.

The two blob repros take about 8 s and reach about 830 MB peak RSS. The `sourceSQL` repro takes 7.4 s and reaches 3.0 GB. All were measured with `/usr/bin/time`.


### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?


The process should not abort.

- `statement.expandedSQL` should throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`. Since c5b7a06d9b (#66209), column values and user-defined function arguments longer than `String::kMaxLength` throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`, and `buffer.toString()` throws the same code for the same limit.
- A statement traced through `sqlite.db.query` should complete as it does without a subscriber. If the SQL text cannot be represented as a string, the event can be skipped.
- `statement.sourceSQL` should return the string or throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`. On v24.21.0 the `sourceSQL` repro and the text-parameter `expandedSQL` variant both return the string.


### What do you see instead?


`expandedSQL` on v26.10.0 (exit code 133, SIGTRAP):

```text
#
# Fatal error in , line 0
# Check failed: String::kMaxLength >= len.
#
#
#
#FailureMessage Object: 0x7ffdf8743130
----- Native stack trace -----
 1: 0xaa1c41  [node]
 2: 0x28ff6b1 V8_Fatal(char const*, ...) [node]
 3: 0xcf20be  [node]
 4: 0xbb1ff5 node::sqlite::StatementSync::ExpandedSQLGetter(v8::FunctionCallbackInfo<v8::Value> const&) [node]
 5: 0x73297fdcfae9
Trace/breakpoint trap (core dumped)
```

`sqlite.db.query` on v26.10.0 (exit code 133):

```text
#
# Fatal error in , line 0
# Check failed: String::kMaxLength >= len.
#
#
#
#FailureMessage Object: 0x7ffd1b3ad090
----- Native stack trace -----
 1: 0xaa1c41  [node]
 2: 0x28ff6b1 V8_Fatal(char const*, ...) [node]
 3: 0xcf20be  [node]
 4: 0xba679c node::sqlite::DatabaseSync::TraceCallback(unsigned int, void*, void*, void*) [node]
 5: 0x22f1a46  [node]
 6: 0x22eda9d  [node]
 7: 0xbb07ac node::sqlite::StatementExecutionHelper::Get(node::Environment*, node::sqlite::StatementSync*) [node]
 8: 0xbb1368 node::sqlite::StatementSync::Get(v8::FunctionCallbackInfo<v8::Value> const&) [node]
 9: 0x746b6f58fae9
Trace/breakpoint trap (core dumped)
```

`sourceSQL` on v26.10.0 (exit code 133):

```text
#
# Fatal error in , line 0
# Check failed: String::kMaxLength >= len.
#
#
#
#FailureMessage Object: 0x7ffe08b2f620
----- Native stack trace -----
 1: 0xaa1c41  [node]
 2: 0x28ff6b1 V8_Fatal(char const*, ...) [node]
 3: 0xcf20be  [node]
 4: 0xbb1ea6 node::sqlite::StatementSync::SourceSQLGetter(v8::FunctionCallbackInfo<v8::Value> const&) [node]
Trace/breakpoint trap (core dumped)
```

On v24.21.0 and v22.23.2 the blob `expandedSQL` repro fails a different check, `Check failed: (location_) != nullptr.`, with the same `ExpandedSQLGetter` frame. The reason is below.


### Additional information

This was discovered and repro'ed by claude opus 5.5.

These call sites pass SQLite's text to `String::NewFromUtf8()` without a length:

- `Statement::ExpandedSQLGetter`: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L4437](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4437)
- `Statement::SourceSQLGetter`: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L4417](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4417)
- `Database::TraceCallback`, for the expanded SQL: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L3716](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L3716) (added in c7b962c222b, #62241)
- `Database::TraceCallback`, for the source SQL fallback: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L3725](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L3725)

Each one then checks `ToLocal()`, but that code is not reached. In V8's `NEW_STRING` macro ([deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7524-L7543](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7524-L7543)), the check that returns an empty handle for `length > String::kMaxLength` runs only when `length > 0`. With the default length of -1, V8 measures the string itself:

- V8 in v26.x and main (14.6): `StringLength()` runs `CHECK_GE(String::kMaxLength, len)` on the `strlen()` byte count ([api.cc#L7470-L7475](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7470-L7475)) and aborts. This CHECK is present from v26.0.0. v25.9.0 (V8 14.1) checks only against `kMaxInt`.
- V8 in v24.x (13.6) and v22.x (12.4): `StringLength()` checks only against `kMaxInt`. `Factory::NewStringFromUtf8()` then sizes the string by its UTF-16 length. If that is over `String::kMaxLength`, `NewRawStringWithMap()` throws `InvalidStringLength`, returns an empty `MaybeHandle`, and the `.ToHandleChecked()` in `NEW_STRING` ([v24.21.0 api.cc#L7624](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/955266bfdd854cd280dffd47548673914484e4c0/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7624)) aborts. If it is under, as in the `sourceSQL` repro, the string is created.

So the blob `expandedSQL` repro aborts on v22.23.2, v24.21.0, and v26.10.0. The `sourceSQL` repro and the text-parameter `expandedSQL` variant abort on v26.10.0 and return the string on v24.21.0.

With an explicit length greater than `String::kMaxLength`, `NEW_STRING` returns an empty `MaybeLocal` without throwing and without aborting.

`TraceCallback` uses the source SQL fallback when `sqlite3_expanded_sql()` returns NULL. That happens when the expansion would exceed `SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` (1,000,000,000 bytes by default). This aborts v26.10.0 in `TraceCallback` (14.5 s, 2.7 GB peak RSS):

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const dc = require('node:diagnostics_channel');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

dc.subscribe('sqlite.db.query', () => {});
const n = Math.ceil((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH + 1) / 3);
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
const stmt = db.prepare(
  `SELECT length('${'€'.repeat(n)}') AS a, length(?) AS b`);
stmt.get(Buffer.alloc(240_000_000)); // aborts
```

Column names take the same path. `Statement::ColumnNameToName` ([src/node_sqlite.cc#L4007](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4007)) creates row object keys with `NewFromUtf8(..., NewStringType::kInternalized)` and no length, and SQLite names an unaliased result column after its expression text. This aborts v26.10.0 in `StatementSync::GetCachedColumnNames` (8.4 s, 3.5 GB peak RSS). On v24.21.0 it returns a row whose key has 178,956,973 characters:

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

const n = Math.ceil((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH + 1) / 3);
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
db.prepare(`SELECT length('${'€'.repeat(n)}')`).get(); // aborts
```

These calls also pass no length. I have not tested whether SQLite can produce text that long for them:

- `NullableSQLiteStringToValue()`, used by `statement.columns()` and the authorizer callback: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L402](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L402)
- `CreateSQLiteErrorImpl()`, for the error message and `errstr`: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L287](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L287) and [#L296](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L296)

c5b7a06d9b added the `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` check in `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte()` ([src/node_sqlite.cc#L74-L93](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L74-L93)) for column values and function arguments. It did not change these call sites.

Suggested fix (not built or tested against Node.js core):

- `ExpandedSQLGetter` and `SourceSQLGetter`: pass the length, and throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` when V8 returns an empty handle. `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte(env->isolate(), std::string_view(...))` already does both.
- `ColumnNameToName`: same, but it needs `kInternalized`, so it would pass the length to `NewFromUtf8()` directly and throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` itself. `GetCachedColumnNames()` already returns `false` when it gets an empty handle.
- `TraceCallback`, both calls: pass `strlen()` as the length. The existing `return 0` on an empty handle then skips publishing and the traced statement completes, so subscribing to the channel does not change whether a statement succeeds. SQLite calls this callback from inside `sqlite3_step()`, `sqlite3_reset()`, or `sqlite3_finalize()`. Both strings are capped at 1,000,000,000 bytes by default (`SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` and `SQLITE_LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH`), so the length fits in an `int`.

V8 compares an explicit length against `String::kMaxLength` in bytes, not UTF-16 code units. With this fix, the `sourceSQL` repro, the text-parameter `expandedSQL` variant, and the column-name repro would throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`, where v24.21.0 returns the string or row. `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte()` already rejects column values by byte length the same way. Returning those strings would require computing the UTF-16 length and transcoding before creating the string.

@photostructure/sqlite, a Node-API port of `node:sqlite`, hit the same abort through `napi_create_string_utf8(..., NAPI_AUTO_LENGTH, ...)`, which takes the same `length = -1` path. Its fix, [photostructure/node-sqlite@095efcd](https://github.com/photostructure/node-sqlite/commit/095efcdc38957c7d09da98634ab248e317c21c7a), takes the approach above for `expandedSQL` and the trace callback: pass `strlen()`, throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` from `expandedSQL`, and skip the trace event.

- `Database::TraceCallback`, for the expanded SQL: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L3716](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L3716) (added in c7b962c222b, #62241)
- `Database::TraceCallback`, for the source SQL fallback: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L3725](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L3725)

Each one then checks `ToLocal()`, but that code is not reached. In V8's `NEW_STRING` macro ([deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7524-L7543](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7524-L7543)), the check that returns an empty handle for `length > String::kMaxLength` runs only when `length > 0`. With the default length of -1, V8 measures the string itself:

- V8 in v26.x and main (14.6): `StringLength()` runs `CHECK_GE(String::kMaxLength, len)` on the `strlen()` byte count ([api.cc#L7470-L7475](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7470-L7475)) and aborts. This CHECK is present from v26.0.0. v25.9.0 (V8 14.1) checks only against `kMaxInt`.
- V8 in v24.x (13.6) and v22.x (12.4): `StringLength()` checks only against `kMaxInt`. `Factory::NewStringFromUtf8()` then sizes the string by its UTF-16 length. If that is over `String::kMaxLength`, `NewRawStringWithMap()` throws `InvalidStringLength`, returns an empty `MaybeHandle`, and the `.ToHandleChecked()` in `NEW_STRING` ([v24.21.0 api.cc#L7624](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/955266bfdd854cd280dffd47548673914484e4c0/deps/v8/src/api/api.cc#L7624)) aborts. If it is under, as in the `sourceSQL` repro, the string is created.

So the blob `expandedSQL` repro aborts on v22.23.2, v24.21.0, and v26.10.0. The `sourceSQL` repro and the text-parameter `expandedSQL` variant abort on v26.10.0 and return the string on v24.21.0.

With an explicit length greater than `String::kMaxLength`, `NEW_STRING` returns an empty `MaybeLocal` without throwing and without aborting.

`TraceCallback` uses the source SQL fallback when `sqlite3_expanded_sql()` returns NULL. That happens when the expansion would exceed `SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` (1,000,000,000 bytes by default). This aborts v26.10.0 in `TraceCallback` (14.5 s, 2.7 GB peak RSS):

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const dc = require('node:diagnostics_channel');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

dc.subscribe('sqlite.db.query', () => {});
const n = Math.ceil((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH + 1) / 3);
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
const stmt = db.prepare(
  `SELECT length('${'€'.repeat(n)}') AS a, length(?) AS b`);
stmt.get(Buffer.alloc(240_000_000)); // aborts
```

Column names take the same path. `Statement::ColumnNameToName` ([src/node_sqlite.cc#L4007](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4007)) creates row object keys with `NewFromUtf8(..., NewStringType::kInternalized)` and no length, and SQLite names an unaliased result column after its expression text. This aborts v26.10.0 in `StatementSync::GetCachedColumnNames` (8.4 s, 3.5 GB peak RSS). On v24.21.0 it returns a row whose key has 178,956,973 characters:

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
const { constants } = require('node:buffer');

const n = Math.ceil((constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH + 1) / 3);
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:');
db.prepare(`SELECT length('${'€'.repeat(n)}')`).get(); // aborts
```

These calls also pass no length. I have not tested whether SQLite can produce text that long for them:

- `NullableSQLiteStringToValue()`, used by `statement.columns()` and the authorizer callback: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L402](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L402)
- `CreateSQLiteErrorImpl()`, for the error message and `errstr`: [src/node_sqlite.cc#L287](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L287) and [#L296](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L296)

c5b7a06d9b added the `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` check in `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte()` ([src/node_sqlite.cc#L74-L93](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/2152942d52f9f841f7de79c7219742ed61e82b90/src/node_sqlite.cc#L74-L93)) for column values and function arguments. It did not change these call sites.

Suggested fix (not built or tested against Node.js core):

- `ExpandedSQLGetter` and `SourceSQLGetter`: pass the length, and throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` when V8 returns an empty handle. `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte(env->isolate(), std::string_view(...))` already does both.
- `ColumnNameToName`: same, but it needs `kInternalized`, so it would pass the length to `NewFromUtf8()` directly and throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` itself. `GetCachedColumnNames()` already returns `false` when it gets an empty handle.
- `TraceCallback`, both calls: pass `strlen()` as the length. The existing `return 0` on an empty handle then skips publishing and the traced statement completes, so subscribing to the channel does not change whether a statement succeeds. SQLite calls this callback from inside `sqlite3_step()`, `sqlite3_reset()`, or `sqlite3_finalize()`. Both strings are capped at 1,000,000,000 bytes by default (`SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` and `SQLITE_LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH`), so the length fits in an `int`.

V8 compares an explicit length against `String::kMaxLength` in bytes, not UTF-16 code units. With this fix, the `sourceSQL` repro, the text-parameter `expandedSQL` variant, and the column-name repro would throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG`, where v24.21.0 returns the string or row. `Utf8StringMaybeOneByte()` already rejects column values by byte length the same way. Returning those strings would require computing the UTF-16 length and transcoding before creating the string.

@photostructure/sqlite, a Node-API port of `node:sqlite`, hit the same abort through `napi_create_string_utf8(..., NAPI_AUTO_LENGTH, ...)`, which takes the same `length = -1` path. Its fix, [photostructure/node-sqlite@095efcd](https://github.com/photostructure/node-sqlite/commit/095efcdc38957c7d09da98634ab248e317c21c7a), takes the approach above for `expandedSQL` and the trace callback: pass `strlen()`, throw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` from `expandedSQL`, and skip the trace event.

### Version

v27.0.0-v8-canary202610014c9d7d7153 (V8 15.7.19), v27.0.0-nightly20261002a7a978415c (V8 14.6.202.34), v26.10.0 (V8 14.6.202.34), v25.9.0 (V8 14.1.146.11, end of life). v24.18.0 (V8 13.6.233.17) only with `--json-stringify-fast-path`.

### Platform

```text
Linux 6.12 x86_64
```

### Subsystem

v8 (`JSON.stringify` fast path)

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
const s = JSON.stringify('\u20ac' + 'a'.repeat(134217723));
console.log(JSON.stringify(s).length);
```

The inner `JSON.stringify` returns a flat two-byte string of 134,217,726 characters. A bare `'a'.repeat(n)` does not reproduce (tested to 330,000,000 characters), because it is a cons string and the fast path hands cons strings to the slow path. The same abort happens through `child_process.fork()` and `child.send(s)` with the default JSON serialization, because `writeChannelMessage` calls `JSONStringify(message)` ([serialization.js:122](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/151845ab90d3926ceb36eedf1eade09619c3adc9/lib/internal/child_process/serialization.js#L122)).

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Every run. The condition is a flat (sequential, external or thin) string of at least 134,217,726 two-byte characters or 268,435,451 one-byte characters, passed to `JSON.stringify` with no replacer and no gap, with the fast path on. Both thresholds are exact: one character fewer passes. Length alone sets them, so plain ASCII with nothing to escape aborts, and `{ type: 'x', payload: s }` aborts at the same length as `s`. It is not memory pressure: `--max-old-space-size=8192` changes nothing, and the thresholds come from a fixed size check in V8.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

`134217730`, which every build listed above prints with `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`. When the result is longer than `String::kMaxLength`, a catchable `RangeError: Invalid string length`. Both are what the slow path returns for the same input, and the fast path is an optimization of the same operation.

### What do you see instead?

```text
FATAL ERROR: Zone Allocation failed - process out of memory
```

The process exits with SIGABRT. The symbolized frames in microsoft/vscode#325814 (Electron 42.6.0, V8 14.8.178.38) show the same abort as `Zone::Expand` called from `FastJsonStringifier::SerializeObject`. A result over `String::kMaxLength` also aborts instead of throwing: `JSON.stringify(JSON.stringify('"'.repeat(149999999)))` has a result of about 600,000,000 characters and gets the `RangeError` only with `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`.

### Additional information

I hit this on Node 26 in a [Stryker](https://stryker-mutator.io) mutation-testing run, where the string being serialized had 329,208,089 two-byte characters. The workaround is `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`; Node refuses it in `NODE_OPTIONS`, so it must go on the command line.

## Technical details (V8 14.6.202.34, byte-identical in v26.10.0 `deps/v8`)

1. `SerializeString` reserves the worst case for the whole string before writing anything, `EnsureCapacity(MaxEscapedStringLength(length) + 2)` ([json-stringifier.cc:2551](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2551)), where `MaxEscapedStringLength(length)` is `length << 3` ([:2476](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2476)). Nothing compares that size with `String::kMaxLength` or with a zone limit.
2. `OutBuffer::Extend` sizes the new segment as `std::max(min_size, SegmentCapacity(...))` and allocates it with `zone_->AllocateVector<Char>(new_segment_size)` ([:1914-1916](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L1914-L1916)), so the whole reservation is one zone allocation. `kMaxSegmentSize` caps only the growth schedule, and `Extend` returns `void`.
3. `Zone::Expand` adds the 32-byte `kSegmentOverhead` ([zone.cc:158](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/zone/zone.cc#L158)) and calls `V8::FatalProcessOutOfMemory(nullptr, "Zone")` when the total exceeds `INT_MAX` ([zone.cc:175](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/zone/zone.cc#L175)).

For 134,217,726 two-byte characters the request is (8 × 134,217,726 + 2) × 2 bytes, rounded up to 8, plus 32, which is 2,147,483,656 and over `INT_MAX`. One character fewer gives 2,147,483,640. The one-byte pair, 268,435,451 and 268,435,450, gives 2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,640. Both match the measured thresholds. The `String::kMaxLength` checks that throw the `RangeError` ([:3547](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3547), [:3564](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3564)) run after serialization, so they are never reached. The reservation came in with [2a7e338c75f1](https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/2a7e338c75f1eaa2d99917d4a43b3e9e10c2c38d) "Stringify: Reserve buffer capacity upfront", and the fast path became the default in [109a22dfaf1e](https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/109a22dfaf1e080fd4c86e71e0b4a213a8ea1d9d), which is after V8 13.6. V8 main at [fd2fd94f](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/fd2fd94f4cce38c88bd78c57c83344927f76eb9d/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2557) (2026-10-02) has the same code.

## Related existing reports

- superset-sh/superset#7327 and hakkisagdic/keyflip#1 show the same abort under `JSON.stringify` in Electron and Node apps. Neither was traced to V8.

## Suggested fix

This needs a V8 change, and I found no fix on V8 main, in Gerrit or on issues.chromium.org. I am asking for this to be forwarded to V8, or I can file it on issues.chromium.org and link it here. One direction: return `SLOW_PATH` from `SerializeString` when `MaxEscapedStringLength(length) + 2` exceeds what one zone segment can hold. `FastJsonStringify` already restarts on the slow stringifier after `SLOW_PATH` ([:3581](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3581)), which returns the correct result or the `RangeError`. The other direction is to append the string in bounded chunks. `SerializeObjectKey` reserves the same way ([:2508-2511](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2508-L2511)), so an equally long key presumably aborts too; I have not tested it. A check of the reservation against `String::kMaxLength`, as in the unmerged [CL 6520234](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/v8/v8/+/6520234), would throw a `RangeError` for any flat string over about 67 million characters, valid results included.

Both thresholds are exact: one character fewer passes. Length alone sets them, so plain ASCII with nothing to escape aborts, and `{ type: 'x', payload: s }` aborts at the same length as `s`. It is not memory pressure: `--max-old-space-size=8192` changes nothing, and the thresholds come from a fixed size check in V8.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

`134217730`, which every build listed above prints with `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`. When the result is longer than `String::kMaxLength`, a catchable `RangeError: Invalid string length`. Both are what the slow path returns for the same input, and the fast path is an optimization of the same operation.

### What do you see instead?

```text
FATAL ERROR: Zone Allocation failed - process out of memory
```

The process exits with SIGABRT. The symbolized frames in microsoft/vscode#325814 (Electron 42.6.0, V8 14.8.178.38) show the same abort as `Zone::Expand` called from `FastJsonStringifier::SerializeObject`. A result over `String::kMaxLength` also aborts instead of throwing: `JSON.stringify(JSON.stringify('"'.repeat(149999999)))` has a result of about 600,000,000 characters and gets the `RangeError` only with `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`.

### Additional information

I hit this on Node 26 in a [Stryker](https://stryker-mutator.io) mutation-testing run, where the string being serialized had 329,208,089 two-byte characters. The workaround is `--no-json-stringify-fast-path`; Node refuses it in `NODE_OPTIONS`, so it must go on the command line.

## Technical details (V8 14.6.202.34, byte-identical in v26.10.0 `deps/v8`)

1. `SerializeString` reserves the worst case for the whole string before writing anything, `EnsureCapacity(MaxEscapedStringLength(length) + 2)` ([json-stringifier.cc:2551](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2551)), where `MaxEscapedStringLength(length)` is `length << 3` ([:2476](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2476)). Nothing compares that size with `String::kMaxLength` or with a zone limit.
2. `OutBuffer::Extend` sizes the new segment as `std::max(min_size, SegmentCapacity(...))` and allocates it with `zone_->AllocateVector<Char>(new_segment_size)` ([:1914-1916](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L1914-L1916)), so the whole reservation is one zone allocation. `kMaxSegmentSize` caps only the growth schedule, and `Extend` returns `void`.
3. `Zone::Expand` adds the 32-byte `kSegmentOverhead` ([zone.cc:158](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/zone/zone.cc#L158)) and calls `V8::FatalProcessOutOfMemory(nullptr, "Zone")` when the total exceeds `INT_MAX` ([zone.cc:175](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/zone/zone.cc#L175)).

For 134,217,726 two-byte characters the request is (8 × 134,217,726 + 2) × 2 bytes, rounded up to 8, plus 32, which is 2,147,483,656 and over `INT_MAX`. One character fewer gives 2,147,483,640. The one-byte pair, 268,435,451 and 268,435,450, gives 2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,640. Both match the measured thresholds. The `String::kMaxLength` checks that throw the `RangeError` ([:3547](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3547), [:3564](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3564)) run after serialization, so they are never reached. The reservation came in with [2a7e338c75f1](https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/2a7e338c75f1eaa2d99917d4a43b3e9e10c2c38d) "Stringify: Reserve buffer capacity upfront", and the fast path became the default in [109a22dfaf1e](https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/109a22dfaf1e080fd4c86e71e0b4a213a8ea1d9d), which is after V8 13.6. V8 main at [fd2fd94f](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/fd2fd94f4cce38c88bd78c57c83344927f76eb9d/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2557) (2026-10-02) has the same code.

## Related existing reports

- superset-sh/superset#7327 and hakkisagdic/keyflip#1 show the same abort under `JSON.stringify` in Electron and Node apps. Neither was traced to V8.

## Suggested fix

This needs a V8 change, and I found no fix on V8 main, in Gerrit or on issues.chromium.org. I am asking for this to be forwarded to V8, or I can file it on issues.chromium.org and link it here. One direction: return `SLOW_PATH` from `SerializeString` when `MaxEscapedStringLength(length) + 2` exceeds what one zone segment can hold. `FastJsonStringify` already restarts on the slow stringifier after `SLOW_PATH` ([:3581](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L3581)), which returns the correct result or the `RangeError`. The other direction is to append the string in bounded chunks. `SerializeObjectKey` reserves the same way ([:2508-2511](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/json/json-stringifier.cc#L2508-L2511)), so an equally long key presumably aborts too; I have not tested it. A check of the reservation against `String::kMaxLength`, as in the unmerged [CL 6520234](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/v8/v8/+/6520234), would throw a `RangeError` for any flat string over about 67 million characters, valid results included.

### Version

v24.21.0 (also v24.8.0, v24.15.0, v26.10.0; not v22.14.0 or v22.18.0)

### Platform

```text
Darwin <host> 25.6.0 Darwin Kernel Version 25.6.0: Fri Jul 31 19:17:26 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.161.14~5/RELEASE_ARM64_T6041 arm64
```

### Subsystem

vm

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

I put a small repro here: https://github.com/markmssd/nodejs-repro/tree/vm-context-retained-maps

```sh
git clone -b vm-context-retained-maps https://github.com/markmssd/nodejs-repro.git
cd nodejs-repro
npm install
npm run repro        # "still in memory" goes up to 8
npm run repro:fixed  # same thing with --retain-maps-for-n-gc=0, stays at 1
```

Jest runs each test file in its own `vm` context. `many.test.js` has 3000 trivial tests, which is enough to get Jest's per-test code optimized, and then there are seven files with a single test each. `counting-environment.js` is Jest's node environment plus a small counter: after each test file it runs a GC and prints how many test-file globals are still around.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Every time on Node 24 and 26. You just need one test file that does enough per-test work for Jest's code to get optimized. 3000 empty tests does it. In our real project, about 120 tests is enough, because our setup files register around 12 beforeEach hooks.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Once a test file is done, its context should be garbage collected, so only the file that's currently running should still be in memory:

```
test files finished: 1, still in memory: 1
test files finished: 2, still in memory: 1
...
test files finished: 8, still in memory: 1
```

That's what I get on Node 22, and on Node 24/26 with `--retain-maps-for-n-gc=0` (`npm run repro:fixed`).

### What do you see instead?

On Node 24 and 26, none of the test files after `many.test.js` ever get freed:

```
test files finished: 1, still in memory: 1
test files finished: 2, still in memory: 2
...
test files finished: 8, still in memory: 8
```

This is how I found it: in our real test suite, one Jest worker running 180 test files ended up holding 44 old contexts and about 1.1 GB of heap. With `--retain-maps-for-n-gc=0` it's 2 contexts and around 330 MB. In CI our workers peak at 1.4–1.9 GB of retained heap, and 670–820 MB with the flag.

### Additional information

- The old contexts aren't strongly reachable. A heap snapshot (`v8.writeHeapSnapshot()`, whose GC tries to reduce memory) frees them, and afterwards the snapshot only shows the current one. Plain `global.gc()` calls never do, which is why I think it's the retained maps. `--retain-maps-for-n-gc=0` makes it go away completely.
- `--no-maglev` mostly hides it (2 stay alive instead of all of them), I assume because less code gets optimized.
- I did find one strong path, but it only keeps a single previous test file alive: from Jest's runtime, through the `FeedbackVector` / `AllocationSite` of `createInitialModule`, the boilerplate object's `Map` → `DescriptorArray` → `AccessorPair` (a `module.parent` getter Jest defines on every module with `Object.defineProperty`), and from that getter's closure to the test file's environment.
- I couldn't reproduce it with a plain `node:vm` loop (new context each iteration with a hot function inside), so it probably depends on how Jest's code is shared between the outer realm and the contexts.

### Version

v26.10.0

### Platform

```text
Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19045.0 x64
```

### Subsystem

vfs

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

`test.cjs`:
```javascript
const vfs = require('node:vfs')
const path = require('node:path')
const fs = require('node:fs')

const myVfs = vfs.create()
myVfs.mount() // Cause VFS to install its fs handler

const outputPath = path.resolve('test.txt') // File on the real filesystem, not VFS
console.log('outputPath:', outputPath)

const fd = fs.openSync(outputPath, 'w')

fs.writev(
  fd,
  [Buffer.from('hello'), Buffer.from('world')],
  null,
  (err, bytesWritten) => {
    console.log(err, bytesWritten)
  },
)
```
Run command:
```
PS D:\code\node-vfs-writev-bug> node --experimental-vfs test.cjs
outputPath: D:\code\node-vfs-writev-bug\test.txt
node:fs:1270
    const promise = h.writev(fd, buffers, position);
                      ^

TypeError: h.writev is not a function
    at Object.writev (node:fs:1270:23)
    at Object.<anonymous> (D:\code\node-vfs-writev-bug\test.cjs:13:4)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1956:14)
    at Object..js (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:2096:10)
    at Module.load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1678:32)
    at Module._load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1470:12)
    at wrapModuleLoad (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:261:19)
    at Module.executeUserEntryPoint [as runMain] (node:internal/modules/run_main:171:5)
    at node:internal/main/run_main_module:33:47

Node.js v26.10.0
````

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Reproduces 100% of the time when a VFS is mounted and `fs.writev()` is called.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

`fs.writev()` should write to `test.txt` successfully.

The VFS handler should implement `writev()`, consistent with the other filesystem handlers.

### What do you see instead?

```
outputPath: D:\code\node-vfs-writev-bug\test.txt
node:fs:1270
    const promise = h.writev(fd, buffers, position);
                      ^

TypeError: h.writev is not a function
    at Object.writev (node:fs:1270:23)
    at Object.<anonymous> (D:\code\node-vfs-writev-bug\test.cjs:13:4)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1956:14)
    at Object..js (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:2096:10)
    at Module.load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1678:32)
    at Module._load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1470:12)
    at wrapModuleLoad (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:261:19)
    at Module.executeUserEntryPoint [as runMain] (node:internal/modules/run_main:171:5)
    at node:internal/main/run_main_module:33:47

Node.js v26.10.0
```

### Additional information

The issue reproduces simply by mounting any VFS, even though the file being written is outside the VFS mount.

In Node.js v26.10.0, the VFS handler installed for node:fs provides an async `write()` handler and a synchronous `writevSync()` handler, but does not provide an async `writev()` handler. See:
https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/9224b248492af09694dc68c6187713dd1c0ddfba/lib/internal/vfs/setup.js#L359


`fs.writev()` calls the installed VFS handler unconditionally when VFS handlers are present. See:
https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/9224b248492af09694dc68c6187713dd1c0ddfba/lib/fs.js#L1268-L1270

This also affects `fs.createWriteStream()` when its `_writev()` path is used. See:
https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/9224b248492af09694dc68c6187713dd1c0ddfba/lib/internal/fs/streams.js#L475-L476

This also affects SEA applications built with `node --build-sea sea-config.json` with `useVfs: true`, since enabling `useVfs` implicitly mounts a VFS at startup. As a result, `fs.writev()` fails even without explicitly mounting a VFS.

### Version

v24.15.0 (also reproduced on v18.15.0, v20.17.0, v22.17.0, v23.11.0)

### Platform

```text
Darwin 27.0.0 arm64
```

### Subsystem

source maps

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

`index.js`:

```js
function fail() {
  throw new Error('boom');
}
fail();
//# sourceMappingURL=index.js.map
```

`index.js.map`, an [index map](https://tc39.es/ecma426/#sec-index-source-map) with a single section:

```json
{
  "version": 3,
  "sections": [
    {
      "offset": {"line": 0, "column": 0},
      "map": {
        "version": 3,
        "sources": ["original.js"],
        "names": [],
        "mappings": "AAAA;AACA;AACA;AACA"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

```console
$ node --enable-source-maps index.js
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, for any index map. The same mappings as a regular map (`flat.js.map` below) work.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

The stack trace is source mapped, as it is when the same mappings are in a regular map:

```console
$ cat flat.js.map
{"version":3,"sources":["original.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA;AACA;AACA;AACA"}
$ node --enable-source-maps flat.js
...
    at fail (/tmp/node-index-map-repro/original.js:2:1)
```

Index maps are part of the source map spec, and `module.SourceMap` already supports them: `new SourceMap(payload).findEntry(1, 2)` on the map above returns `originalSource: 'original.js'`.

### What do you see instead?

The stack trace is not mapped:

```console
$ node --enable-source-maps index.js
...
    at fail (/tmp/node-index-map-repro/index.js:2:9)
```

`module.findSourceMap()` also returns `undefined` for `index.js`. With `NODE_DEBUG=source_map`, the map fails to load:

```console
$ NODE_DEBUG=source_map node --enable-source-maps index.js
SOURCE_MAP 12345: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
```

### Additional information

The error comes from `sourcesToAbsolute()` in `lib/internal/source_map/source_map_cache.js`, which runs `data.sources.map(...)` on the top-level map. Index maps have no top-level `sources`, so it throws, and the map isn't cached.

A possible fix is to resolve the `sources` of each section's map (with that map's `sourceRoot`) when the map has `sections`. Index maps appear to be tested only by constructing `SourceMap` directly (`test/parallel/test-source-map-api.js` with `fixtures/source-map/disk-index.map`), not through `--enable-source-maps`.

As a workaround, adding `"sources": []` to the top level of the index map makes Node apply the sections. However, the sections' `sources` are then not resolved to absolute URLs, and `sourceRoot` is ignored, so stack traces show them verbatim (e.g. `original.js:2:1` rather than an absolute path).

I ran into this in Parcel, which writes bundle source maps as index maps.

### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Many Node.js users need to process CSV files partially — for example, reading only specific rows or columns without loading the entire file into the V8 heap.

However, most existing CSV libraries convert the entire CSV into strings or objects, which:

-increases heap usage
-triggers unnecessary garbage collection
-slows down partial data extraction
-wastes resources when only a small portion of the CSV is needed

**Why this matters**
For large CSV files (hundreds of MB or several GB), loading the entire file into memory is inefficient.
A buffer‑based approach allows users to extract only the required segments without converting the whole file into strings.



### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

**Example solution**
I created an npm module called getdatafromcsvbuffer, which manipulates CSV data directly from raw Buffer operations.

Key characteristics:

operates directly on Buffer
-avoids string conversion and split()
-significantly reduces heap usage
-minimizes GC pressure
-ideal for partial CSV extraction

This approach demonstrates that CSV processing can be much faster when using Buffer‑only operations.

**Reference**
Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/getdatafromcsvbuffer

**Proposal**
I would like to propose discussing whether Node.js could:

1.Provide official utilities for partial CSV processing using Buffer

2.Offer APIs that help developers manipulate structured text formats without converting entire files into strings

3.Consider exposing lower‑level primitives that make buffer‑based parsing easier and more ergonomic

This could benefit workloads involving:

-machine learning data preprocessing
-ETL pipelines
-log processing
-large CSV datasets
-streaming analytics


I would appreciate feedback from the Node.js team on whether such functionality aligns with Node’s direction or could be considered for future enhancements.
I will not hesitate to give you the benchmark if you need, so please ask me .

### What alternatives have you considered?

### Version
v24.13.0 (OpenSSL 3.5.4)

### Platform
Windows 11 x64 (10.0.22631). Not yet checked on Linux/macOS.

### Subsystem
crypto

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
import crypto from "node:crypto";

const { privateKey } = crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", {
  modulusLength: 2048,
  privateKeyEncoding: { type: "pkcs8", format: "pem" },
  publicKeyEncoding: { type: "spki", format: "pem" },
});

crypto.createPrivateKey(privateKey); // ok

try {
  // 128 * r * (N + 2) > maxmem → ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS (expected)
  crypto.scryptSync("pw", crypto.randomBytes(16), 32, { N: 131072, r: 32, p: 1, maxmem: 256 * 1024 * 1024 });
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.code); // ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS
}

crypto.createPrivateKey(privateKey);
// throws: ERR_OSSL_EVP_MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
//   error:030000AC:digital envelope routines::memory limit exceeded

crypto.createPrivateKey(privateKey); // ok again
```

The asynchronous `crypto.scrypt(..., cb)` behaves the same way: its parameter check throws synchronously and leaves the
same error queued.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?
Always, when the scrypt parameters exceed `maxmem` (the memory check). A non-power-of-two `N` (also
`ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS`) does not leave an error behind.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?
The failed scrypt parameter check should not affect unrelated later crypto calls: `createPrivateKey` of a valid key
should succeed. The OpenSSL error queue should be cleared when the parameter check fails, as Node does elsewhere.

### What do you see instead?
The first `createPrivateKey` (or other key-parsing call) after the failed scrypt throws the scrypt's
`EVP_R_MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. Through jsonwebtoken this surfaced as «secretOrPrivateKey must be an asymmetric key when
using RS256» (jsonwebtoken retries a key that fails `createPrivateKey` as an HMAC secret), which made it look like a
random signing failure under load.

### Additional information
The likely source is the fix for #53291 (PR #53300): when `ncrypto::checkScryptParams` fails, `src/crypto/crypto_scrypt.cc`
(line ~92 on `main`) reads the OpenSSL error with `ERR_peek_last_error()` to build the message, but never pops or
clears it, so it stays queued for the next OpenSSL consumer on the thread. A `ClearErrorOnReturn` (or
`ERR_get_error()` / `ERR_clear_error()` after formatting) on that path should fix it. Same class as #45485
(`X509Certificate.checkPrivateKey()` with a non-matching key makes the next `createPrivateKey()` fail), #21281 and
#42793.

### Version

Reproduced on **v24.18.0** and **v26.11.1**, with 20/20 failures on each. v26.11.1 was the `node` npm package's latest version when tested.

### Platform

Linux 6.12.95+deb13-amd64, x86_64 GNU/Linux.

The installed v24.18.0 reports nghttp2 1.69.0 and OpenSSL 3.5.7. v26.11.1 was tested using `npm exec --yes --package=node@26.11.1 -- node ...`.

### Subsystem

`http2`, `stream` (`ClientHttp2Stream` readable async iteration / end-of-stream handling).

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

A standalone, dependency-free reproduction gist:

https://gist.github.com/jbeda/cb47933e03eb33febf937c159b780b9b

Pinned script: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/jbeda/cb47933e03eb33febf937c159b780b9b/raw/6502872f0d06b6c3b93ee1c83ab17b4c19dbe7e2/repro.mjs

Save the gist's `repro.mjs` locally and run:

```sh
node repro.mjs
```

No package installation, proxy, Go server, or gRPC library is required. It uses `node:http2` as the client and a small `node:net` peer bound to a loopback ephemeral port. The peer writes explicit HTTP/2 frames with a static-table `:status: 200` HPACK entry and a literal `grpc-status: 0` trailer. The body is synthetic plain bytes, not protobuf or gRPC framing.

The script synchronizes on events, without scheduling sleeps or retries:

1. Client starts a POST, writes some request bytes, and deliberately does **not** call `request.end()`.
2. Peer sends response HEADERS and initial DATA.
3. Client creates the built-in async iterator, consumes the initial DATA, verifies `writableEnded === false`, then pauses iteration.
4. Peer sends final DATA, trailers with `END_STREAM`, and `RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR)` in that order in one socket write. The reset does not overtake the response bytes on the wire.
5. Client waits for trailers and the reset-induced `aborted` event. It verifies `grpc-status === '0'`, `rstCode === 0`, and that all 17 final response bytes remain buffered.
6. Client resumes the **existing** iterator. It receives and verifies the exact final bytes.
7. The following `next()` throws `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` instead of returning EOF.

The five-second timeout only catches a hung reproduction. Session/socket destruction is in `finally`, after the EOF read; it does not cause the failure.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Deterministic with the event-gated sequence above. I tested the failing case and both controls 20 times each on both runtimes, checking the failing exit status, specific error code, and complete-byte receipt:

| Version | Buffered final DATA + NO_ERROR reset | Same exchange without reset | Final DATA consumed before trailers/reset |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v24.18.0 | 20/20 `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` | 20/20 clean EOF | 20/20 clean EOF |
| v26.11.1 | 20/20 `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` | 20/20 clean EOF | 20/20 clean EOF |

Controls:

```sh
node repro.mjs no-reset
node repro.mjs drained
```

The relevant conditions are an open request side, an already-created readable async iterator, and response DATA still buffered when a post-response `NO_ERROR` reset arrives. Without event gating, this manifests intermittently in application traffic.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

The request side is closed by the reset, but the complete response remains consumable and the readable iterator finishes normally. Successful response END_STREAM has already arrived and every response byte can still be read.

RFC 9113 section 8.1 explicitly permits `RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR)` after a complete response while a request remains in progress and says clients must not discard responses because of such a reset. Both control cases demonstrate clean EOF on the same response content.

### What do you see instead?

On v24.18.0:

```text
{"node":"v24.18.0","mode":"reset","status":"0","rstCode":0,"readableLength":17,"writableEnded":true}
Complete response bytes received.
node:internal/streams/end-of-stream:166
                             new ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE());
                             ^

Error [ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE]: Premature close
    at ClientHttp2Stream.onclose (node:internal/streams/end-of-stream:166:30)
    at ClientHttp2Stream.emit (node:events:521:24)
    at closeStream (node:internal/http2/core:2033:14)
    at Http2Stream.onStreamClose (node:internal/http2/core:605:5) {
  code: 'ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE'
}

Node.js v24.18.0
```

`writableEnded` becomes true upon reset; it was explicitly checked as false before sending completion, and the script never calls `request.end()`.

v26.11.1 also yields all response bytes and then throws, with `getEosOnCloseError` at `end-of-stream:98`, `onclose` at `end-of-stream:265`, and `closeStream` at `http2/core:2088`.

### Additional information

**Related, but a different reproducer from #65677 / #65689:** that issue ends the request and begins iteration after normal stream closure. It lists v24.18.0 as passing. This case leaves the request open and starts/consumes the iterator before closure; it fails on v24.18.0 as well. I have not tested #65689's proposed patch against this case and am not claiming it fixes or fails to fix it.

The observed sequence suggests readable end-of-stream handling interprets the reset-induced duplex `aborted` event as premature response termination while completed-response bytes are buffered. Those bytes can subsequently be yielded, but the iterator retains a premature-close error for its next read. This is a mechanism hypothesis for maintainers to validate, not a proposed production monkeypatch.

This was observed in the wild with gRPC, but it is a more general HTTP/2 response-consumption issue. The standalone reproduction uses only Node core and synthetic response bytes; it does not depend on gRPC or an application framework.

Filing this to determine whether the open-request/active-iterator case belongs with #65677 or requires separate handling.

### Version

v24.18.1 and v24.19.0: the official darwin-arm64 builds, signed by the Node.js Foundation (V8 13.6.233.17-node.50 and 13.6.233.17-node.51)

### Platform

```text
Darwin 25.6.0 Darwin Kernel Version 25.6.0: Fri Jul 31 19:18:48 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.161.14~5/RELEASE_ARM64_T6020 arm64
```

macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple silicon (Mac14,6). The host name is left out of the `uname -a` line.

### Subsystem

worker_threads; V8 (garbage collection, WebAssembly code GC); child_process (`spawnSync` on a worker thread)

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

We have no minimal reproduction. Every crash below came from Vitest 4.1.11 running one of two test suites in its `threads` pool (`worker_threads`), with Vite 8.2.0 and rolldown 1.2.1, and with `maxWorkers` 5 except where noted:

- a suite of TypeScript tests for AWS CDK constructs (aws-cdk-lib 2.265.0), many of which build CDK apps inside the worker. Its size varied from 342 to 697 test files across the commits involved; the table under "How often" gives it at each crash;
- a CLI's test suite (824 and 854 test files at its two crashes), some of which render Ink 7.1.1 components. Ink calls terminal-size 4.0.1, which runs `execFileSync('tput', …)` on the worker thread.

Both suites leave `isolate` at its default, so Vitest 4.1.11 runs each test file in a new worker and starts terminating the previous one without waiting for it: worker threads are created and torn down throughout a run.

We have not run these suites with `--no-sparkplug` (see #62393 under Additional information) or with `--no-wasm-code-gc` (see D).

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Rarely: 12 crashes in the 883 runs that started at least one whole suite on one machine, about 1 in 74.

Our test wrapper logs every run it starts: the command, the Node version, how the run ended, and the machine's average idle CPU over the run. From 2026-09-25 12:10 UTC, when that log begins, to the end of 2026-10-12 UTC, it records 5,545 runs of these two suites' tests. 14 of them ended in a native crash: 13 with SIGSEGV and 1 with the abort in C.

- 12 came from the 883 runs that started a whole suite: 210 runs of every workspace's tests (`npm run test:all`, which includes both suites), 348 runs of the CDK suite alone and 306 of the CLI suite alone (`npm test`), 11 bare `vitest run`, and 8 runs of a suite started from a wrapper script or a multi-workspace command. 11 of the 883 stopped at a build-freshness check before any test ran, and 29 were stopped before they finished; on the runs that ran any test, the rate is 12 in 864. Ten of the 12 were in the CDK suite and two in the CLI suite.
- 2 came from the 32 runs of the CDK suite's `deploy-tests` directory alone (222 test files at both crashes, which were consecutive runs of the same code).
- None came from the other 4,587 runs, which ran part of a suite or used another Vitest config (206 did): 3,664 of them ran a single test file, and 4,375 ran ten or fewer. 43 more runs were cancelled before they started. Another 3,058 runs of 20 test files or fewer ran outside the wrapper, which logs them without their outcome, so they are not counted.
- By version: 4 of the 87 whole-suite runs on v24.18.1 crashed, and 8 of the 796 on v24.19.0. Both `deploy-tests` crashes were on v24.19.0.
- 10 of the 13 crashed runs with a CPU reading averaged under 5% idle over the run. So did 685 of the 870 whole-suite runs with a reading (79%), so load does not set the crashed runs apart.

Which signature each crash was:

- **#62393.** The third crash report, `node-2026-10-12-051041.ips.txt` (crash 13 in the table: v24.19.0, the CDK suite at 697 test files), shows the stack reported in #62393: the same frames from `ClearStaleLeftTrimmedPointerVisitor::VisitRootPointers` down to `Builtins_BaselineOutOfLinePrologue + 116`, at `0xe`, on a `WorkerThread`. It is in the gist only for comparison with A. We do not know whether A or C shares its cause. We will add here whether either recurs on v24.22.0, whose release proposal (#66667) includes #65753, the backport of the V8 fix for #62393.
- **vitest-dev/vitest#11291** (Vitest 4.1.10, Vite 8.1.4, `pool: 'threads'`, macOS 15 arm64) lists two signatures from "~15 crash reports on this machine alone", each with `WorkerThread` as the faulting thread. One is A: `IncrementalMarkingJob::Task::RunInternal` → `MarkCompactCollector::StartMarking` → `MarkingWorklists::Local::~Local`, a near-null dereference at `0x89`. The other is at worker teardown: `Isolate::Deinit` → `Heap::StartTearDown` → `CppHeap::StartDetachingIsolate` → `Heap::CollectGarbage` → `GlobalHandles::InvokeFirstPassWeakCallbacks`. It names the same two `.node` addons and 18 `rolldown-worker` threads. It says that Node 24.19.0 and 26.8.1 both reproduce, and that the crash was also seen on GitHub Actions' arm64 macOS runners, without saying which signature each version or machine gave. Its author later wrote that their machine was "under really high load" when they hit it, and that they could not get their reproduction to work. It was closed on 2026-09-24 without one.
- **Native modules.** In each of the three crash reports, the only `.node` images on any thread's stack are rolldown 1.2.1's binding (whose own pool had 18 to 21 threads named `rolldown-worker`) and fsevents. A report's `usedImages` lists only the images that some thread's frames reference (none of the three lists libc++ or libsystem_c, both of which the node binary loads), so these processes may also have loaded other native modules.
- **Crash reports** (https://gist.github.com/peoram/cd10c877f515c51f2476ce6015363ef7). The three crash reports as macOS wrote them, except that every file path and the identifiers of the machine and of the crash (the incident id, the crash-reporter key, and the boot and sleep/wake session ids) read `<removed>`. The binary images' UUIDs are kept: `55FD9EB9-D7D1-3FB3-829D-EE7233BE3116` is the official v24.18.1 build and `5CF2F254-9668-37EE-9BAE-7B6F0ECE16F6` the official v24.19.0 build.
- We are moving these suites to Vitest's `forks` pool (one child process per worker), with a reporter that names each test file whose worker was lost, and the worker's pid where the worker recorded one.
