### Version

v26.11.1

### Platform

```text
Darwin L1845 25.6.0 Darwin Kernel Version 25.6.0: Tue Aug 18 17:49:13 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.161.15.700.19~2/RELEASE_ARM64_T6000 arm64
```

### Subsystem

v8 engine

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```bash
mkdir repro && cd repro
npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install big.js@7.0.1
```

`repro.mjs`:

```js
import Big from 'big.js'

// Deterministic PRNG (mulberry32)
let seed = Number(process.argv[2] ?? 1) >>> 0
const random = () => {
  seed = (seed + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0
  let t = seed
  t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1)
  t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61)
  return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296
}

let sink = 0
const start = performance.now()
for (let i = 0; i < 300000; i++) {
  const a = Big((random() * 30).toFixed(2))
  const b = Big((random() * 5 + 0.5).toFixed(i % 3))
  sink += Number(a.times(b).div(i % 2 ? Big(1.255) : b.plus(1)).round(2))
}
console.log(`${process.version} took ${Math.round(performance.now() - start)} ms (${sink > 0})`)
```

```bash
node repro.mjs 2
node --trace-deopt repro.mjs 2 2>&1 | grep -c "JSFunction P.div"
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Deterministic with seed 2 (6/6 runs on both v26.7.0 and v26.11.1). Whether the loop starts depends on
the input sequence: with seeds 1..12, seeds 2, 3, 7 and 9 trigger it on v26 and none trigger it on v24.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

P.div should deoptimize a few times, after which V8 should reoptimize it with updated feedback.
This is what happens on v24.21.0: 1-3 deopts of P.div for every seed, and every run takes ~1.0-1.1 s.

### What do you see instead?

On v26, `P.div` is deoptimized thousands of times at the same bytecode offset with the same reason,
and the run is ~6x slower:

| | v24.21.0 | v26.7.0 | v26.11.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node repro.mjs 1` | ~1,040 ms | ~1,030 ms | ~1,010 ms |
| `node repro.mjs 2` | ~1,075 ms | **6,620–8,640 ms** | **~6,600 ms** |
| `P.div` deopts, seed 2 | 2 | **~5,150** | **~5,600** |

Every deopt has the same signature (v26.11.1):

```
[bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: wrong map): begin. deoptimizing 0x3e332d0efef9 <JSFunction P.div (sfi = 0x3e332d0ee969)>, 0x2cf238c84509 <Code MAGLEV>, opt id 2, bytecode offset 447, deopt exit 39, FP to SP delta 240, caller SP 0x00016fb98c20, pc 0x000115b8ba88]
```

Bytecode offset 447 is a `Dec` bytecode (`--rl`) in `r[--rl] < bt[rl]` in big.js `div`
(https://github.com/MikeMcl/big.js/blob/v7.0.1/big.mjs#L410):

```
10242 S> @  445 : 0b ea             Ldar r15
         @  447 : 5a 4f             Dec FBV[79]
         @  449 : c3                Star15
10247 E> @  450 : 35 eb 50          GetKeyedProperty r14, FBV[80]
```

The loop is not specific to Maglev. With `--no-maglev`, TurboFan code loops at the same offset with the same reason:

| Flags (v26.11.1, seed 2) | `P.div` deopts | Deoptimized code | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| (default) | 5,649 | Maglev | 6,614 ms |
| `--no-maglev` | 855 | TurboFan, offset 447, `wrong map` | 6,850 ms |
| `--no-maglev-osr` | 5,709 | Maglev | 6,621 ms |
| `--no-turbofan` | 5,713 | Maglev | 6,640 ms |

### Additional information

We noticed this through a performance smoke test in a calculation library that uses big.js
for all arithmetic. On v26 the test became ~30% slower and flaky in CI (GitHub Actions
ubuntu-latest, x64), while v22 and v24 were stable. In that test suite the same signature appears:
~1,250 "wrong map" deopts of P.div at bytecode offset 447.

The repro above was measured only on macOS arm64; the CI symptom suggests Linux x64 is also affected,
but I did not verify the deopt trace there.

Possibly related, but a different symptom: #66457 (Maglev OSR correctness bug, also v24.11/v26,
also repeated eager deopts of the same code). --no-maglev-osr does not help here.

```js
  sink += Number(a.times(b).div(i % 2 ? Big(1.255) : b.plus(1)).round(2))
}
console.log(`${process.version} took ${Math.round(performance.now() - start)} ms (${sink > 0})`)
```

```bash
node repro.mjs 2
node --trace-deopt repro.mjs 2 2>&1 | grep -c "JSFunction P.div"
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Deterministic with seed 2 (6/6 runs on both v26.7.0 and v26.11.1). Whether the loop starts depends on
the input sequence: with seeds 1..12, seeds 2, 3, 7 and 9 trigger it on v26 and none trigger it on v24.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

P.div should deoptimize a few times, after which V8 should reoptimize it with updated feedback.
This is what happens on v24.21.0: 1-3 deopts of P.div for every seed, and every run takes ~1.0-1.1 s.

### What do you see instead?

On v26, `P.div` is deoptimized thousands of times at the same bytecode offset with the same reason,
and the run is ~6x slower:

| | v24.21.0 | v26.7.0 | v26.11.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node repro.mjs 1` | ~1,040 ms | ~1,030 ms | ~1,010 ms |
| `node repro.mjs 2` | ~1,075 ms | **6,620–8,640 ms** | **~6,600 ms** |
| `P.div` deopts, seed 2 | 2 | **~5,150** | **~5,600** |

Every deopt has the same signature (v26.11.1):

```
[bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: wrong map): begin. deoptimizing 0x3e332d0efef9 <JSFunction P.div (sfi = 0x3e332d0ee969)>, 0x2cf238c84509 <Code MAGLEV>, opt id 2, bytecode offset 447, deopt exit 39, FP to SP delta 240, caller SP 0x00016fb98c20, pc 0x000115b8ba88]
```

Bytecode offset 447 is a `Dec` bytecode (`--rl`) in `r[--rl] < bt[rl]` in big.js `div`
(https://github.com/MikeMcl/big.js/blob/v7.0.1/big.mjs#L410):

```
10242 S> @  445 : 0b ea             Ldar r15
         @  447 : 5a 4f             Dec FBV[79]
         @  449 : c3                Star15
10247 E> @  450 : 35 eb 50          GetKeyedProperty r14, FBV[80]
```

The loop is not specific to Maglev. With `--no-maglev`, TurboFan code loops at the same offset with the same reason:

| Flags (v26.11.1, seed 2) | `P.div` deopts | Deoptimized code | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| (default) | 5,649 | Maglev | 6,614 ms |
| `--no-maglev` | 855 | TurboFan, offset 447, `wrong map` | 6,850 ms |
| `--no-maglev-osr` | 5,709 | Maglev | 6,621 ms |
| `--no-turbofan` | 5,713 | Maglev | 6,640 ms |

### Additional information

We noticed this through a performance smoke test in a calculation library that uses big.js
for all arithmetic. On v26 the test became ~30% slower and flaky in CI (GitHub Actions
ubuntu-latest, x64), while v22 and v24 were stable. In that test suite the same signature appears:
~1,250 "wrong map" deopts of P.div at bytecode offset 447.

The repro above was measured only on macOS arm64; the CI symptom suggests Linux x64 is also affected,
but I did not verify the deopt trace there.

Possibly related, but a different symptom: #66457 (Maglev OSR correctness bug, also v24.11/v26,

body_text:
### Version

v26.12.0

### Platform

Linux 6.17 aarch64 (also expected on other platforms; the cause is not platform specific)

### Subsystem

sqlite

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
import { Database } from 'node:sqlite';
const db = new Database(':memory:');
db.exec('create table t (id integer primary key, h text); create table p (id integer primary key, a integer)');
const insT = db.prepare('insert into t values (?, ?)');
const insP = db.prepare('insert into p values (?, ?)');
for (let i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) { insT.run(i, 'x'); insP.run(i, i); }
for (const sql of ['select h from t where id = ?', 'select t.h from p join t on t.id = p.a where p.id = ?']) {
  const st = db.prepare(sql);
  const t0 = performance.now();
  for (let i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) st.get(1 + (i % 1000));
  console.log(sql, ((performance.now() - t0) * 1000 / 100_000).toFixed(2), 'us/op, reprepare =', st.stat('reprepare'));
}
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, for statements where SQLite 3.54's planner marks a bound parameter for
re-optimization (e.g. a JOIN filtered by `rowid = ?`).

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

The statement is prepared once and reused, as on v24.21.0 (SQLite 3.53.4).

### What do you see instead?

```
v24.21.0 (SQLite 3.53.4)  join: 2.14 us/op   (same script with DatabaseSync; no stat() on v24)
v26.12.0 (SQLite 3.54.0)  join: 8.44 us/op, reprepare = 100000
                          single table: 1.53 us/op, reprepare = 0 (unchanged)
```

### Additional information

`Statement::BindParams()` and `SQLTagStore::ResetAndBindStatement()` call `sqlite3_clear_bindings()`
before every execution. In SQLite 3.54, `sqlite3_clear_bindings()` expires any
statement whose `expmask` is non-zero, without honouring the new `smimask`
"only re-prepare on change to/from 0 or 1" rule that `sqlite3_bind_*()` honours.
3.54 sets `expmask` for ordinary JOIN statements, so they are re-prepared on every
`sqlite3_step()`. A plain C repro (no Node involved) shows the same thing:
3.54.1 with `clear_bindings` re-prepares 200000/200000 runs; without it, 8.

This is also being reported on the SQLite forum; I'll link the thread in a comment.

Independently of an upstream fix, node:sqlite could avoid the unconditional
`sqlite3_clear_bindings()` call, e.g. only clear when fewer parameters are bound
than `sqlite3_bind_parameter_count()`, or bind NULL explicitly to the remaining
ones. This also matters for LTS lines once SQLite 3.54 is backported (deps update
was #66663).

### Version

v26.12.0 (V8 14.6.202.34-node.39). It works in v24.22.0 (V8 13.6) and v25.9.0 (V8 14.1.146.11). Deno 2.9.7 (V8 15.0.245.2) fails the same way, so the bug looks like it is in V8.

### Platform

```text
Linux 6.8.0-147-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

### Subsystem

esm / V8 module evaluation (top-level await + dynamic `import()`)

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```sh
mkdir tla-tdz && cd tla-tdz
cat > main.mjs <<'JS'
import { a } from './a.mjs';
import { x } from './b.mjs';
console.log('ok', a(), x);
JS
cat > a.mjs <<'JS'
await import('./d.mjs');
const { x } = await import('./b.mjs'); // b is evaluating-async here
export const a = () => x;
JS
cat > b.mjs <<'JS'
import { c } from './c.mjs';
export const x = c + 1;
JS
cat > c.mjs <<'JS'
await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
export const c = 1;
JS
echo 'export const d = 0;' > d.mjs
node main.mjs
```

Here is what happens. `main` evaluates `a` first. `a` suspends on its first `await import()`, so `main` goes on to evaluate `b`. `b` depends on `c`, and `c` has a top-level `await`, so `b` becomes *evaluating-async*. Then `a` resumes and runs `await import('./b.mjs')` while `b` has not executed yet.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

It fails every time. It needs a top-level `await import()` of a module that another branch of the same graph has already started evaluating, so that the module is *evaluating-async*. The module also must not be the cycle root of a capability that already exists.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

```text
ok 2 2
```

Node 24.22.0, Node 25.9.0 and Bun 1.4.3 all print this. In ECMA-262 [Evaluate()](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-moduleevaluation), `b` is *evaluating-async*, so `module` is set to `b.[[CycleRoot]]`, which is `b`. Its `[[TopLevelCapability]]` is empty, so a new capability is created. `InnerModuleEvaluation` then returns immediately, and because the status is not *evaluated* the promise is left pending. The promise is resolved only by [AsyncModuleExecutionFulfilled](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-async-module-execution-fulfilled) or its `GatherAvailableAncestors` loop, after `b` has executed. `ContinueDynamicImport` resolves `import()` with the namespace only once that promise fulfils.

### What do you see instead?

```text
file:///…/a.mjs:2
const { x } = await import('./b.mjs'); // b is evaluating-async here
        ^

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization
    at file:///…/a.mjs:2:9

Node.js v26.12.0
```

The `import()` promise resolves with the namespace of a module whose body has not run yet.

### Additional information

We hit this in a real application: [link-assistant/hive-mind#3469](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/3469). 43 top-level `await import()` calls in its `src/` threw TDZ errors once a host moved to Node 26, while CI on Node 24 stayed green. The reproduction is also in [`experiments/node26-tla-tdz`](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/tree/issue-3469-80e8383bb928/experiments/node26-tla-tdz).

**Workaround:** replace the top-level `await import('./b.mjs')` with a static `import * as b from './b.mjs'`. A static import is part of the graph, so it is evaluated before the importer's body on every runtime.

**Suggested fix:** in V8's `SourceTextModule::Evaluate` / `Module::Evaluate` path, when the module (or its cycle root) is *evaluating-async* and has no top-level capability yet, store a new capability on the cycle root and leave it pending until async evaluation fulfils, as the spec does. Do not resolve it right away. A regression test would be the five files above, expecting `ok 2 2`. The behaviour changed between V8 14.1 and 14.6. One candidate is the module-evaluation refactoring for `import defer`, but I have not bisected it.

### Version

v26.12.0 (also v24.21.0 and v20.20.2)

### Platform

```text
Linux 7.0.0-38-generic x86_64 (Ubuntu)
```

### Subsystem

permission

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

Grant read access to a directory and to a sibling whose name starts with the
first directory's name (`/x/app` and `/x/appx`, or `/x/app` and `/x/app_data`):

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/pm/app /tmp/pm/appx
echo hi > /tmp/pm/app/f.txt

node --permission --allow-fs-read=/tmp/pm/app --allow-fs-read=/tmp/pm/appx -e "
  const fs = require('fs');
  console.log('has(app)      ', process.permission.has('fs.read', '/tmp/pm/app'));
  console.log('has(app/f.txt)', process.permission.has('fs.read', '/tmp/pm/app/f.txt'));
  console.log('has(appx)     ', process.permission.has('fs.read', '/tmp/pm/appx'));
  for (const call of ['statSync', 'readdirSync', 'existsSync']) {
    try { const r = fs[call]('/tmp/pm/app'); console.log(call, typeof r === 'boolean' ? r : 'ok'); } catch (e) { console.log(call, e.code); }
  }
"
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, when another granted path extends the granted directory's name
character by character. The order of the flags does not matter, and a
trailing slash on the grant (`--allow-fs-read=/tmp/pm/app/`) does not help.
With only `--allow-fs-read=/tmp/pm/app` everything works.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

```text
has(app)       true
has(app/f.txt) true
has(appx)      true
statSync ok
readdirSync ok
existsSync true
```

`/tmp/pm/app` is explicitly granted, so the directory itself should be
readable (stat, readdir, access), as it is when it is the only grant. Adding
an unrelated sibling grant should not take access away.

### What do you see instead?

```text
has(app)       false
has(app/f.txt) true
has(appx)      true
statSync ERR_ACCESS_DENIED
readdirSync ERR_ACCESS_DENIED
existsSync ERR_ACCESS_DENIED
```

The granted directory itself is denied: `permission.has` returns `false`, and
`fs.stat`, `fs.readdir`, `fs.access` and `fs.existsSync` (sync, callback and
promise forms) fail with `ERR_ACCESS_DENIED`. Files inside it, and the sibling, stay readable.
`fs.realpathSync` of the directory still succeeds.

### Additional information

The same happens with `--allow-fs-write`. It looks like the
character-prefix radix tree behind `--allow-fs-read` / `--allow-fs-write`
(`src/permission/fs_permission.h`): when the second grant splits the node
holding the first, the exact directory path no longer ends at a granted
node, while `<dir>/*` still does. This is the opposite direction of
CVE-2026-58043 (fixed in ad99d075b1, "permission: avoid granting radix split
nodes"); Node 20.20.2, which does not have that fix, behaves the same way, so
it does not seem to be a regression from it.

It fails closed, so it is not a security issue, but it breaks a common
layout: an application directory next to a data directory named after it
(`/srv/myapp` and `/srv/myapp_data`). We found it running a server under
`--permission` with grants for its install directory and a
`<install>_module_data` directory; we work around it by creating the
directories before launch and avoiding operations on the directory itself.

Covered in part by https://github.com/nodejs/build/issues/4099#issuecomment-4038743335 but raising as a separate issue because:
- The crash is still occurring in `main` on my SpacemiT-K1 board and fixes for othrt crashes have not resolved this

```text
Darwin 27.0.0 arm64
```

### Subsystem

intl (V8 Temporal formatting)

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
const opts = { year: "numeric", month: "long", day: "numeric" };
for (const iso of ["1500-03-31", "1582-10-14", "1582-10-15", "1000-01-01"]) {
  const zdt = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(`${iso}T12:00[UTC]`);
  console.log(iso,
    "| Date:", new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { ...opts, timeZone: "UTC" }).format(zdt.epochMilliseconds),
    "| ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString:", zdt.toLocaleString("en-US", opts),
    "| PlainDate#toLocaleString:", Temporal.PlainDate.from(iso).toLocaleString("en-US", opts),
    "| format(PlainDate):", new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", opts).format(Temporal.PlainDate.from(iso)));
}
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, for Temporal values before 1582-10-15 in the ISO 8601 or Gregorian calendar.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Each line shows the date it was given, for example `1500-03-31 | Date: March 31, 1500 | ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString: March 31, 1500 | ...`. The ISO 8601 calendar is proleptic Gregorian, and Node already formats the same instant that way as a Date. V8 15.8 (d8), JavaScriptCore and Bun print the ISO date for Temporal values too.

### What do you see instead?

```text
1500-03-31 | Date: March 31, 1500 | ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString: March 21, 1500 | PlainDate#toLocaleString: March 21, 1500 | format(PlainDate): March 21, 1500
1582-10-14 | Date: October 14, 1582 | ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString: October 4, 1582 | PlainDate#toLocaleString: October 4, 1582 | format(PlainDate): October 4, 1582
1582-10-15 | Date: October 15, 1582 | ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString: October 15, 1582 | PlainDate#toLocaleString: October 15, 1582 | format(PlainDate): October 15, 1582
1000-01-01 | Date: January 1, 1000 | ZonedDateTime#toLocaleString: December 27, 999 | PlainDate#toLocaleString: December 27, 999 | format(PlainDate): December 27, 999
```

Temporal values before the Gregorian reform come out as Julian dates (10 days off in 1500). `formatToParts`, `PlainDateTime#toLocaleString` and `Instant#toLocaleString` do the same; `formatRange` is right.

### Additional information

In V8 14.6.202.34, which Node 26 ships, `CallICUFormat` formats Temporal values with a second formatter built by `GetSimpleDateTimeForTemporal`, which has ICU's default Gregorian calendar (cutover 1582-10-15) and never calls `setGregorianChange`, unlike the Date path ([js-date-time-format.cc#L1675-L1738](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/objects/js-date-time-format.cc#L1675-L1738), Date path [#L2138-L2155](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f9116f3bf9a50b0f7925daacfdc6fed503a9dbe2/src/objects/js-date-time-format.cc#L2138-L2155)).

V8 fixed it as a side effect of [3102739ec1d8](https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/3102739ec1d85b94e9f314ecb4e89e31c196ae20) ("[temporal] Use get_epoch_ms_for_utc and track isPlain"), first in V8 14.8.98: `CallICUFormat` now formats with a clone of the DateTimeFormat's calendar. Could that commit, or its `CallICUFormat` part, be backported to v26.x? The rest of the commit implements a spec change in the temporal_rs bindings.

## Summary
`ProxyConfig#shouldUseProxy()` (`lib/internal/http.js`) compares the request host against `NO_PROXY`. Three forms of loopback are **not** recognised and are routed to the configured proxy anyway:

- `http://localhost./` - trailing dot (`new URL(u).hostname === 'localhost.'`)
- `http://[::1]/` - IPv6 loopback as `new URL(u).hostname` returns it (`'[::1]'`)
- `http://[::ffff:7f00:1]/` - IPv4-mapped loopback

with `NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`.

## Expected
The request goes **direct**, like `http://localhost/`.

## Actual
It is sent through the proxy, including any `Authorization` header the operator explicitly excluded.

## Repro
```js
process.env.HTTP_PROXY = 'http://127.0.0.1:8080';
process.env.NO_PROXY   = 'localhost,127.0.0.1,::1';
require('http').get('http://localhost./', r => r.resume());  // observed at the proxy
```
Control: `http://localhost/` is not sent to the proxy.

## Suggested fix
Normalise before comparing: strip a single trailing dot, unwrap `[`/`]`, lowercase, and canonicalise IPv4-mapped forms - compare the canonical host, not the raw `URL.hostname`. Add tests for all three.

Note: filed as a **parity/correctness** issue, not a security report - `SECURITY.md` places proxy/deployment network policy out of scope. `undici` fixed the identical mismatch as a non-security parity bug (undici#5637 / #5623).

body_text:
### Version

v22.22.3, v22.23.3 and v26.12.0 (all reproduce, with different windows of affected values)

### Platform

```text
Linux x64 (`Linux 7.0.0-1014-aws`, overlayfs; also ext4 on `Linux 6.18`)
```

### Subsystem

fs

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
// repro.mjs — run with: node repro.mjs
import fs from 'node:fs';
import os from 'node:os';
import path from 'node:path';
import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';

const base = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'cp-ts-'));
fs.mkdirSync(path.join(base, 'src'));
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(base, 'src', 'index.js'), 'x');

// v22: 1792178171.684500000, v26: 1792178171.684499870
const value = process.argv[2] ?? '1792178171.684500000';
execFileSync('touch', ['-m', '-d', `@${value}`, path.join(base, 'src', 'index.js')]);

fs.cpSync(path.join(base, 'src'), path.join(base, 'dest'), { recursive: true, preserveTimestamps: true });

const src = fs.statSync(path.join(base, 'src', 'index.js'));
const dest = fs.statSync(path.join(base, 'dest', 'index.js'));
console.log(src.mtime.getTime(), dest.mtime.getTime());
```

Node's own test shows the same: setting the mtime of `test/fixtures/copy/kitchen-sink/index.js` to one of these values makes `test/parallel/test-fs-cp-sync-preserve-timestamps.mjs` fail.

```
$ touch -m -d @1792178171.684500000 test/fixtures/copy/kitchen-sink/index.js
$ node-v22.22.3 test/parallel/test-fs-cp-sync-preserve-timestamps.mjs
AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly equal:
+ 1792178171685
- 1792178171684

$ touch -m -d @1792178171.684499870 test/fixtures/copy/kitchen-sink/index.js
$ node-v26.12.0 test/parallel/test-fs-cp-sync-preserve-timestamps.mjs
AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly equal:
+ 1792178171684
- 1792178171685
```

In practice the fixture gets its mtime from the checkout, so the test fails for a checkout whose mtime lands in the
window, and keeps failing on every retry of that checkout.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Deterministically for source mtimes in a window of about 220 ns per millisecond on v22 (sub-millisecond offsets
499878–500098 ns) and about 18 ns per millisecond on v26 (499860–499877 ns). For a file written at a random time that is roughly 2 in 10,000 on v22.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

`preserveTimestamps` should give the copy the same timestamps as the source, so at least `mtime` (millisecond
precision) should be equal. The async `fs.cp` doesn't have this problem (0 mismatches over the same 25,000 values), because it sets the times from the `Date` values of the source's stats.

### What do you see instead?

`strace` of `cpSync` for a source with mtime `1792178171.684500000` on v22.22.3:

```
utimensat(AT_FDCWD, ".../dest/index.js", [{tv_sec=1792408731, tv_nsec=623148000}, {tv_sec=1792178171, tv_nsec=684499000}], 0) = 0
```

`stat -c %.9Y`: source `1792178171.684500000`, copy `1792178171.684499000`; `mtimeMs` `1792178171684.5` vs `1792178171684.499`, so `mtime` rounds to `...685` vs `...684`.

### Version

`v26.10.0` (`node-26.10.0-linux-x64` from `actions/setup-node@v5`).

The same abort also occurred on 2026-08-28 in a second CI run on the then-current 26.x build, so it is not a one-off.

### Platform

```text
Linux 6.x x64 (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner)
```

All local attempts to reproduce on Windows 11 x64 with `v26.10.0` and `v26.12.0` failed (details below).

### Subsystem

`http` / `buffer` (V8 fast API call inside `Buffer.byteLength`, reached from `_http_outgoing`).

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

There is no standalone minimal repro yet - this is the report of a real production abort with a complete V8 stack. The reproducing workload is a Vite dev server under sustained browser traffic:

1. Run `vite` (8.3.4) on Linux with Node 26.10.0.
2. Load a page that pulls a large pre-bundled dependency chunk. In this case `node_modules/.vite/deps/lib-*.js` is 17,416,067 bytes; Vite's `send` helper appends an inline source map, producing a `String[43640789]`.
3. Drive continuous Playwright traffic for roughly ten minutes (261 browser tests hitting the dev server).
4. The dev-server process aborts and every later connection fails with `net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`.

The abort itself:

```text
abort: Lazy deopt after a fast API call with return value is unsupported

==== JS stack trace =========================================

    0: ExitFrame [pc: 0x7f49dce3ea76]
    1: byteLength [0x3fc66a4d8b91] [node:buffer:923] [bytecode=0xe4e3e6b3dc1 offset=88](this=0x3fc66a4d72e1 <JSFunction Buffer (sfi = 0x385470d41a39)>#0#,0x3ba819d309a1 <String[43640789]: uc"...<truncated>>">#1#,0x36331f5c0011 <undefined>)
    2: maybePrepareFinalChunk(aka maybePrepareFinalChunk) [0x67fc7c1ba61] [node:_http_outgoing:1069] [bytecode=0x1de7ebdcd5d1 offset=58](this=0x36331f5c0011 <undefined>,0x3ba819d357d9 <ServerResponse map = 0x25850d03f771>#2#,0x3ba819d309a1 <String[43640789]: uc"...<truncated>>">#1#,0x36331f5c0011 <undefined>)
    3: end [0x67fc7c1e8b9] [node:_http_outgoing:1197] [bytecode=0x1de7ebdcd0b1 offset=117](this=0x3ba819d357d9 <ServerResponse map = 0x25850d03f771>#2#,0x3ba819d309a1 <String[43640789]: uc"...<truncated>>">#1#,0x36331f5c0011 <undefined>,0x36331f5c0011 <undefined>)
    4: send$1(aka send$1) [0x1b9f12a631e9] [file:///home/runner/work/<repo>/node_modules/vite/dist/node/chunks/node.js:~17519] [pc=0x7f49bd3567a7](...)
    5: viteTransformMiddleware [file:///home/runner/work/<repo>/node_modules/vite/dist/node/chunks/node.js:~20159]
```

Frame 1 is Node's own `Buffer.byteLength` (`node:buffer:923`) and frame 2 is Node's `maybePrepareFinalChunk` (`node:_http_outgoing:1069`), whose source is captured in the report:

```js
function maybePrepareFinalChunk(msg, chunk, encoding) {
  if (typeof chunk !== 'string' && !isUint8Array(chunk))
    return false;

  if (msg.destroyed || msg.strictContentLength)
    return false;

  if (!msg._header) {
    msg._contentLength = typeof chunk === 'string' ?
      Buffer.byteLength(chunk, encoding) : chunk.byteLength
```

So the aborting path is `res.end(string)` with `msg._header` unset, which calls `Buffer.byteLength(hugeString, undefined)`.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Twice in two CI runs on Linux x64, roughly ten minutes into sustained dev-server traffic. It did not reproduce in short bursts.

I could not reproduce it locally on Windows 11 x64, with either `v26.10.0` or `v26.12.0`, using:

- 300 sequential `res.end()` responses of a 43.6 MB string;
- 3,000 responses of a 1 MB string alternating with a `Buffer` and with `res.end(string, 'utf8')` to vary the call site;
- 2,800 requests for the real 43.8 MB Vite dev-server chunk (the same `send` path as the crash) over keep-alive sockets;
- the same runs with `--deopt-every-n-times=3` to force deopts at deopt points.

So the trigger appears to need more than "a large string through `res.end`" - possibly the specific optimized-code state of the Vite middleware chain on the CI runner, or a longer warm-up than a few thousand requests.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Serving a large string with `res.end()` should never abort the process. Payload size and repetition may cost memory and CPU, but a correct runtime either deoptimizes or keeps the optimized code; it does not terminate.

### What do you see instead?

The process aborts with `Lazy deopt after a fast API call with return value is unsupported`, killing the server mid-suite.

### Additional information

The fatal string is a V8 bailout reason, `v8/src/codegen/bailout-reason.h`:

```text
"Lazy deopt after a fast API call with return value is unsupported"
```

and `Buffer.byteLength` is exactly a fast API call with a return value, per `src/node_buffer.cc`:

```cpp
uint32_t FastByteLengthUtf8(...) {
TRACK_V8_FAST_API_CALL("Buffer::FastByteLengthUtf8");
static CFunction fast_byte_length_utf8(CFunction::Make(FastByteLengthUtf8));
```

The corresponding V8 work item is "Add deopt support after fast api calls with return values" (https://issues.chromium.org/issues/418936518), so this may be a V8 limitation that Node surfaces. Filing here because the aborting frame is Node's `_http_outgoing` code and the call is Node's own `Buffer.byteLength`, and because the practical fix may be on the Node side.

Our workaround, in case it is useful for triage, is to make the caller hand Node bytes so the fast API is not on the path (`res.end(Buffer.from(content))` instead of `res.end(content)`); with that in place the dev server survives the same workload.

If a standalone reproduction is required before this is actionable, I am happy to run a loop on a Linux runner against a candidate commit - please say which shape you want (for example a `node:test` server plus a client loop, or a V8 `d8` snippet) and I will provide it.

- the same runs with `--deopt-every-n-times=3` to force deopts at deopt points.

So the trigger appears to need more than "a large string through `res.end`" - possibly the specific optimized-code state of the Vite middleware chain on the CI runner, or a longer warm-up than a few thousand requests.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Serving a large string with `res.end()` should never abort the process. Payload size and repetition may cost memory and CPU, but a correct runtime either deoptimizes or keeps the optimized code; it does not terminate.

### What do you see instead?

The process aborts with `Lazy deopt after a fast API call with return value is unsupported`, killing the server mid-suite.

### Additional information

The fatal string is a V8 bailout reason, `v8/src/codegen/bailout-reason.h`:

```text
"Lazy deopt after a fast API call with return value is unsupported"
```

and `Buffer.byteLength` is exactly a fast API call with a return value, per `src/node_buffer.cc`:

```cpp
uint32_t FastByteLengthUtf8(...) {
TRACK_V8_FAST_API_CALL("Buffer::FastByteLengthUtf8");
static CFunction fast_byte_length_utf8(CFunction::Make(FastByteLengthUtf8));
```

The corresponding V8 work item is "Add deopt support after fast api calls with return values" (https://issues.chromium.org/issues/418936518), so this may be a V8 limitation that Node surfaces. Filing here because the aborting frame is Node's `_http_outgoing` code and the call is Node's own `Buffer.byteLength`, and because the practical fix may be on the Node side.

Our workaround, in case it is useful for triage, is to make the caller hand Node bytes so the fast API is not on the path (`res.end(Buffer.from(content))` instead of `res.end(content)`); with that in place the dev server survives the same workload.

If a standalone reproduction is required before this is actionable, I am happy to run a loop on a Linux runner against a candidate commit - please say which shape you want (for example a `node:test` server plus a client loop, or a V8 `d8` snippet) and I will provide it.

### Affected URL(s)

https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#cryptorandombytessize-callback (also `crypto.randomInt`, `crypto.randomFill`, `crypto.randomUUID`, and `crypto.getRandomValues` of the Web Crypto API)

### Description of the problem

We measure how userspace random generators behave when a process or a machine is duplicated.
For Node 24.18.0 linked against the system OpenSSL 3.5.9 (Fedora 44, Linux 7.2.11) the picture is
this; the harness and every log are available.

One guest or process saved and restored twice from the same image, the two continuations'
outputs compared block by block at equal sequence numbers: `Math.random`, `crypto.randomBytes`,
`crypto.randomInt` and `crypto.getRandomValues` are 32 of 32 blocks identical under QEMU with and
without a vmgenid device and under Firecracker with VMGenID and VMClock attached, and 14 of 14
under CRIU; a read of `/dev/urandom` beside them is distinct from the first block wherever the
guest kernel's vmgenid driver is present. The three `crypto` calls repeat because OpenSSL's
DRBG does; `Math.random` repeats because V8's generator is seeded once per isolate. We asked
the OpenSSL project where it places the case; its answer (2026-10-20) is that reseeding after a
restore "is currently a non-goal", not yet documented, that a documentation pull request will
be accepted and backported, and that a check-and-reseed on the VMClock generation counter would
be considered as a new feature for a future release.

What we would like to know is whether the `crypto` documentation should say that these calls
inherit OpenSSL's behaviour across a snapshot or checkpoint restore, so that applications
resumed from one image (SnapStart-style platforms, CRIU) know to arrange a reseed, and whether
Node would want to call `RAND_poll` itself on a restore signal (its own startup snapshot
feature, `--build-snapshot`, resumes an isolate from an image in the same way, and
`crypto.randomUUID` serves identifiers from a cache of 128 filled in one draw,
lib/internal/crypto/random.js).

The repeated blocks are the generators' own output; we have not looked at anything downstream.

Concretely, a sentence in the `crypto` documentation of the kind "these functions draw from OpenSSL's DRBG inside the process; after a snapshot or checkpoint restore the DRBG continues from the saved state until its next scheduled reseed, so an application resumed from a saved image should reseed after its own restore signal" would tell such applications what to do, and `crypto.randomUUID` could note its cache of 128 identifiers (`lib/internal/crypto/random.js`, `disableEntropyCache` turns it off). We can send a documentation pull request if that is welcome. The harness, the logs and the OpenSSL exchange are available on request.

### Version

v26.11.0 and later (tested v26.11.1, v26.12.0). v26.10.0, v24.14.1, and v22.23.3 are not affected.

### Platform

```text
Linux x86_64 (official linux-x64 binaries)
```

### Subsystem

child_process

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
// repro.js
const { spawnSync } = require('node:child_process');

process.env = { ...process.env, FOO: 'set' };

const args = ['-p', 'process.env.FOO'];
spawnSync(process.execPath, args, { stdio: 'inherit' });                    // no options.env
spawnSync(process.execPath, args, { stdio: 'inherit', env: process.env });  // explicit env
```

```console
$ node-v26.10.0 repro.js
set
set

$ node-v26.12.0 repro.js
undefined
set

$ node-v26.12.0 --permission --allow-child-process --allow-fs-read='*' repro.js 2>/dev/null
set
set
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, when `process.env` has been reassigned and a child is spawned without `options.env` while the permission model is off. This affects every `child_process` API (`spawn`, `exec`, `execFile`, `fork`, and the sync variants).

Mutating `process.env` in place (`process.env.FOO = 'set'`) is not affected.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

A child spawned without `options.env` should get the same environment as one spawned with `{ env: process.env }`.

The `child_process` docs list the `env` default as `process.env` for every spawning API, and say "Use `env` to specify environment variables that will be visible to the new process, the default is `process.env`" ([L177](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.0/doc/api/child_process.md?plain=1#L177), [L751](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.0/doc/api/child_process.md?plain=1#L751)). Command lookup is documented as using `options.env.PATH`, falling back to `process.env.PATH` ([L55](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.0/doc/api/child_process.md?plain=1#L55)).

`process.env` is writable, and nothing deprecates or warns about reassigning it. `{ env: process.env }` still sees the reassigned object, so the actual default and the documented default now disagree.

`Worker`, `TZ`, and `os.homedir()` read the OS environment, so reassigning `process.env` never affected them. `child_process` is different: its default is documented as `process.env`, and until v26.10.0 it was implemented by copying `process.env`.

### What do you see instead?

The child gets the OS environment and ignores the reassigned `process.env`. `FOO` is unset, and a reassigned `PATH` is ignored for command lookup.

The result also depends on `--permission`. With the permission model on, the old code path runs and the child sees `FOO=set`.

### Additional information

Caused by #65325 ("child_process: build the default env block in one native pass", first released in v26.11.0). When `!options.env && !permission.isEnabled()`, `normalizeSpawnArguments()` builds `envPairs` with `getEnvPairs()`, which reads the OS environment block, instead of copying `process.env` ([lib/child_process.js L706](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.0/lib/child_process.js#L706)). Its test (`test-child-process-default-env.js`) only mutates `process.env` in place and never reassigns it.

Reassigning `process.env` with a spread copy is a common pattern. [GitHub code search](https://github.com/search?q=%22process.env+%3D+%7B+...process.env%22&type=code) finds a few thousand files containing `process.env = { ...process.env`, for example in build scripts, test setup, and Vite configs. Tools that override `PATH` or `npm_config_*` this way and then spawn without `env` lose the overrides on v26.11+ without any error. We hit this with an npm wrapper that sets `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY` and `PATH` this way: its npm child fell back to registry.npmjs.org.

Possible fixes:
- keep the fast path, but only take it while `process.env` is still the native env proxy. For example, pass `process.env` to `getEnvPairs()` and fall back to the copy path unless `env_proxy_ctor_template()->HasInstance()` is true (the check `node_messaging.cc` already uses). Spreading a reassigned plain object is cheap, so the speedup is kept where it matters;
- or revert #65325 on v26.x before v26 enters LTS on 2026-10-28. If the new behavior is intended, label it semver-major after the fact so it ships only in v27, and update the `options.env` default and the PATH lookup docs.

### Version

v24.18.0 and v22.22.2 (both reproduce)

### Platform

Linux 7.0.0-38-generic x86_64, Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS; libuv 1.52.1

### Subsystem

fs

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```sh
# sync: never returns, main thread at 100 % CPU
node -e "require('fs').mkdirSync('/proc/nope/deeper', { recursive: true })"

# async: the promise never settles, process never exits, CPU busy
node -e "require('fs/promises').mkdir('/proc/nope/deeper', { recursive: true }).then(() => console.log('ok'), (e) => console.log('err', e.code))"
```

Both hang until killed (`timeout 20 node ...` exits 124).

The precondition is a filesystem where `mkdir` of a child fails with `ENOENT` while the parent exists and is a directory. procfs does exactly that:

```
$ mkdir /proc/nope
mkdir: cannot create directory '/proc/nope': No such file or directory
```

sysfs answers `EACCES` instead and the call fails fast, as expected. A plain `fs.mkdirSync('/proc/nope')` (non-recursive) also fails fast with `ENOENT`.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Always, on any path whose intermediate component cannot be created and whose filesystem reports `ENOENT` for that `mkdir` (procfs; presumably some FUSE / network filesystems too).

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Reject / throw with the `mkdir` error (`ENOENT` here, as the non-recursive call does), the same way `EACCES`, `EPERM`, `ENOSPC` and `ENOTDIR` are already returned by the recursive implementation.

### What do you see instead?

The call never completes. Sync: the main thread spins. Async: the request bounces between the event loop and the libuv threadpool forever — on a hung process we measured ~24.5 M voluntary context switches in 18 minutes (~22 k/s), RSS flat at ~40 MB, `wchan` `ep_poll`.

### Additional information

Looking at `src/node_file.cc` (v24.18.0):

- `MKDirpSync` (L1759): in `case UV_ENOENT` (L1792) the failed path and its `dirname` are pushed back onto the continuation stack. The outer loop pops the parent (`/proc`), `uv_fs_mkdir` returns `EEXIST`, the `default:` branch `stat`s it, sees a directory and `break`s. The loop then pops `/proc/nope` again, `mkdir` returns `ENOENT` again, the same two paths are pushed again, and so on. Nothing records that the parent was just verified to exist, so the state machine cycles forever.
- `MKDirpAsync` (L1827, `case UV_ENOENT` at L1873) has the same structure, so the async variant spins as well.

A possible fix: when `mkdir(child)` returns `ENOENT` right after its parent was created or confirmed to be an existing directory, stop and return `ENOENT` instead of pushing the pair again (e.g. remember the last confirmed parent in the continuation data, or bound the number of `ENOENT` retries per path).

How we hit it: a test used `/proc/…/file.json` as an "unwritable path" for a fail-open on-disk store. The store's debounced write called `mkdir(dirname, { recursive: true })`; under host load the write fired before the `node --test` child exited, and the child spun for 2.3 hours in three separate CI runs before anyone noticed. Related earlier report about recursive mkdir error mapping: #47098.

body_text:
### Version

main at 697ecce05e7

### Platform

```text
Host: Ubuntu 24.04, Linux x86_64
Target: Linux AArch64
Rust: 1.88.0
```

### Subsystem

build, Temporal

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

Install an AArch64 C/C++ cross toolchain and the Rust `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` target, then run from a clean checkout:

```sh
export CC=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc
export CXX=aarch64-linux-gnu-g++
export CC_host=gcc
export CXX_host=g++
export CARGO_BUILD_TARGET=aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc

./configure --cross-compiling --dest-os=linux --dest-cpu=arm64 \
  --v8-enable-temporal-support

make -C out BUILDTYPE=Release V=1 \
  "$PWD/out/Release/obj/gen//release/libnode_crates.a"

ls out/Release/obj/gen/release/libnode_crates.a
ls out/Release/obj/gen/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/libnode_crates.a
```

The double slash in the Make target matches the generated rule.

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Reproduced consistently with bundled Temporal enabled when cross-compiling from Linux x86_64 to AArch64.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Separate Rust archives should be generated for host and target, at the paths used by their respective link steps.

### What do you see instead?

Both host and target toolsets declare the same Rust archive path, but Cargo writes the target archive to a different path. No x86_64 archive is generated for host executables.

### Additional information

Also observed when targeting RISC-V.

Refs: #66803

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Reproduced consistently with bundled Temporal enabled when cross-compiling from Linux x86_64 to AArch64.

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Separate Rust archives should be generated for host and target, at the paths used by their respective link steps.

### What do you see instead?

Both host and target toolsets declare the same Rust archive path, but Cargo writes the target archive to a different path. No x86_64 archive is generated for host executables.

### Additional information

Also observed when targeting RISC-V.

## This would solve...

`maxRequestsPerClient` currently limits the number of requests sent over an HTTP/1.1 connection, but it does not appear to apply after HTTP/2 is negotiated.

The option is documented as:

> The maximum number of requests to send over a single connection before the socket is reset.

In Undici 8.10.0, the request counter is enforced in [`client-h1.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v8.10.0/lib/dispatcher/client-h1.js#L1296-L1298). The [HTTP/2 implementation](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v8.10.0/lib/dispatcher/client-h2.js#L12-L42) does not import or use `kMaxRequests`.

This means applications using `allowH2` cannot place a request-count lifetime on an HTTP/2 session. We encountered a case where an HTTP/2 session remained logically reusable after its transport stopped making progress. Subsequent requests continued selecting that session. Periodically retiring a session after a bounded number of requests would provide useful defense in depth and limit how long unhealthy or stale sessions can be reused.

## The implementation should look like...

When HTTP/2 is negotiated and `maxRequestsPerClient` is a positive number:

- Count requests/streams opened on the current HTTP/2 session.
- Once the limit is reached, stop assigning new requests to that session.
- Allow existing streams to complete, then gracefully retire the session.
- Establish a new session for queued or subsequent requests.
- Preserve the existing `null`/`0` behavior that disables the limit.

The exact behavior around concurrent streams could follow maintainer guidance—for example, whether the limit is strict or may be exceeded by streams already opened concurrently.

## I have also considered...

- Rotating the dispatcher in application code after request timeouts. This works as a reactive mitigation, but requires applications to own dispatcher lifecycle and duplicate session-health logic.
- HTTP/2 PING frames. These help with liveness detection but do not provide a bounded session lifetime.
- A separate HTTP/2-specific option. That would be workable, but extending `maxRequestsPerClient` seems consistent with its documented connection-level semantics.

## Additional context

Environment where this was observed:

- Node.js 24
- Undici 8.10.0
- HTTP/2 enabled with `allowH2`

I would be happy to help test the behavior or contribute a change with guidance on the preferred HTTP/2 retirement semantics.

body_text:
I understand that Undici doesn't support the HTTP/1.1 `Expect: 100-continue` handshake. However, [RFC 9110 §15.2.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.100) explicitly permits discarding a `100 Continue` response when no expectation was sent.

In my own Playwright tests, Chromium, Firefox and WebKit continued to the final response, while Undici closed the connection. The [README](https://github.com/nodejs/undici#expect) also says these responses are ignored.

body_text:
## Bug Description

With `fetch` from undici 7.15.0 through 7.30.0, once a server closes a keep-alive connection with `Connection: close`, subsequent connections are used for a single request each. `undici.request` is not affected, and neither is `fetch` in 7.14.0 or 8.11.0.

Node.js v24 bundles an affected version (v24.18.0 ships undici 7.28.0), so global `fetch` on Node 24 LTS is affected.

Real-world impact: a test suite talking to a local Supabase stack (Kong/nginx closes each keep-alive socket after `keepalive_requests` = 100) opened 16,331 TCP connections for 17,920 requests and failed on macOS with `EADDRNOTAVAIL` / `UND_ERR_SOCKET` once ephemeral ports ran out. The same suite on Node 22 (undici 6.x) reuses sockets normally.

## Reproducible By

`server.mjs`: closes each socket after 100 requests and reports how many requests each socket served:

```js
import http from "node:http";
let ids = 0; const per = {};
http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const s = req.socket; s.n = (s.n ?? 0) + 1; s.id ??= ++ids; per[s.id] = s.n;
  if (req.url === "/stats") return res.end(JSON.stringify(Object.values(per).slice(0, 8)));
  if (s.n >= 100) res.setHeader("connection", "close");
  res.end("ok");
}).listen(Number(process.argv[2]));
```

`client.mjs`: 400 sequential fetches with the body fully consumed:

```js
import { fetch } from "undici";
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${process.argv[2]}/`;
for (let i = 0; i < 400; i++) await (await fetch(url)).text();
console.log(await (await fetch(url + "stats", { headers: { connection: "close" } })).text());
```

```sh
node server.mjs 47000 &
node client.mjs 47000
```

Server and client run in separate processes. The server's Node version does not matter (same result on 22 and 24).

## Expected Behavior

Each connection serves 100 requests: `[100,100,100,100,1]` (the final `1` is the `/stats` request).

## Actual Behavior

After the second close, each new connection serves one request: `[100,100,1,1,1,1,1,1]` (400 requests → ~202 connections).

| client | `[requests per socket]` |
|---|---|
| undici 6.29.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,100,100,1]` |
| undici 7.14.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,100,100,1]` |
| undici 7.15.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,1,1,1,1,1,1]` |
| undici 7.30.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,1,1,1,1,1,1]` |
| undici 8.0.0 – 8.1.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,1,1,1,1,1,1]` |
| undici 8.2.0 – 8.10.0 `fetch` | `[100,100,1,100,100]` |
| undici 8.11.0 / 8.11.2 `fetch` | `[100,100,100,100,1]` |
| undici 7.30.0 / 8.11.2 `request` | `[100,100,100,100,1]` |
| `node:http` Agent `keepAlive` (Node 24) | `[100,100,100,100,1,…]` |
| Node 24.18.0 global `fetch` (undici 7.28.0) | `[100,100,1,1,1,1,1,1]` |

Bisected: last good 7.14.0, first bad 7.15.0. Results are identical on Node 22.22.3 and 24.18.0 for the npm package.

## Environment

macOS 26 (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64), Node.js v22.22.3 and v24.18.0.

## Additional context

It looks fixed on `main` as of 8.11.0 (8.2.0 fixed it partially). Could the fix be backported to v7.x so it reaches Node.js 24?

body_text:
Hi, and thanks for restoring trusted publishing on the 6.x line in 6.23.0 (#4666).

An FYI with data, since the restoration doesn't quite reach the affected users:

- `@types/node` **20.x and 22.x pin `undici-types ~6.21.0`**, up to the latest 22.20.4 (2026-09-19) and 20.19.43. Older ones pin `~6.19.2`, `~6.19.8` or `~6.20.0`.
- The only versions inside those ranges (6.19.3–6.19.8, 6.20.0, 6.21.0) were published without provenance after 6.19.1/6.19.2 had it.
- So pnpm's `trustPolicy: no-downgrade` still rejects them. The 6.23+ trusted releases fall outside the ranges.
- In a random sample of 200 stable npm releases replayed with pnpm 10.29.3, 16 of the 18 that failed did so because of `undici-types` 6.21.0 or 6.19.8, almost all through `@types/node`.
- For reach: `@types/node` versions with those pins account for roughly 175M of its 499M weekly downloads (all clients).

Reproduce (lockfile-only, read-only):

```bash
mkdir t && cd t
echo '{"name":"t","version":"0.0.0","private":true,"dependencies":{"@types/node":"22.20.4"}}' > package.json
printf 'trustPolicy: no-downgrade\n' > pnpm-workspace.yaml
npx pnpm@10.29.3 install --lockfile-only --ignore-scripts
# ERR_PNPM_TRUST_DOWNGRADE  High-risk trust downgrade for "undici-types@6.21.0"
```

**Suggestion, only if it's cheap for you:** publish `undici-types@6.21.1` (same content as 6.21.0, or matching undici 6.21.x) through the current trusted-publisher workflow. `~6.21.0` would then resolve to a trusted release with no change needed in DefinitelyTyped.

We know the root issue is the policy's date-based design, and we have raised that with pnpm separately. Feel free to close this if it isn't worth a release.

Igor Santos-Grueiro

## Bug Description

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->

## Reproduction

<!-- 
IMPORTANT: Provide a standalone reproduction script.

See the Reproduction guide in CONTRIBUTING.md for detailed instructions:
https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#reproduction

Guidelines:
- The script must be self-contained (uses only undici and Node.js built-in modules).
- Use createServer from node:http to run a local server inside the script.
- Run `node --test test/repro-XXXX.js` locally to confirm the bug is reproducible.
- Attach the script inline or as a GitHub Gist link below.
-->

**Standalone reproduction script:**

```javascript
'use strict'

import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks'
import { subscribe } from 'node:diagnostics_channel'

const storage = new AsyncLocalStorage()

subscribe('undici:request:create', ({ request }) => {
  console.log(request.path, '→', storage.getStore())
})

await Promise.all(
  ['a', 'b', 'c'].map((name) =>
    storage.run(name, () => fetch(`https://example.com/${name}`)),
  ),
)
```

**Steps to reproduce (if not using the script above):**

<!-- A step by step list on how the bug can be reproduced for examination. -->

## Expected Behavior

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen. -->

```
/a → a
/b → b
/c → c
```

Every request dispatches in the async context of its own fetch() / request() caller, whether it was sent immediately or queued behind the connection probe.

## Actual Behavior

<!-- What actually happens instead. Include any error messages. -->

```
/a → a
/b → a
/c → a
```

Same with request() from the undici package. Only https: origins are affected. http://example.com prints a, b, c correctly on the same version. Cause: Pool defers /b and /c until /a's connection finishes ALPN negotiation, then dispatches them from /a's connect callback, so they inherit /a's async context.

## Logs & Screenshots

<!-- If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem, or
alternatively add your console logs here. -->

## Environment

- OS: <!-- e.g. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS -->
- Node.js version: <!-- e.g. v22.14.0 -->
- undici version: <!-- e.g. 7.x.x (run `node -e 'require("undici/package.json").version'`) -->

### Additional context

<!-- Add any other context about the problem here. -->

Discovered in a test failure in MSW (see [job](https://github.com/mswjs/msw/actions/runs/37751445963/job/113225391936)) after Undici introduced changes in Node.js v26 (passes in v22 and v24).

used in [`interceptors.cache`](https://undici.nodejs.org/api/Interceptors#interceptorscacheopts) is a "404: NOT_FOUND" page.

Also, the text below the link says:

## Bug Description

After `mockPool.cleanMocks()`, requests from Node.js' global `fetch` still match the interceptors from before the call, and never match interceptors added after it. Requests through undici's own `fetch`/`request` aren't affected.

Cause: since #5648 (v8.10.1), `MockAgent.dispatch` mirrors a pool's interceptors into a separate `${origin}#http1-only` dispatcher for legacy global dispatcher consumers like Node.js' bundled `fetch` (which goes through `Dispatcher1Wrapper` with `allowH2: false`). It does so by sharing the `kDispatches` array once:

```js
http1OnlyDispatcher[kDispatches] = mockDispatcher[kDispatches]
```

`cleanMocks()` on `MockPool` and `MockClient` replaces that array instead of emptying it:

```js
cleanMocks () {
  this[kDispatches] = []
}
```

So the `#http1-only` dispatcher keeps the old array: its interceptors stay active, and new ones never reach it.

## Reproduction

**Standalone reproduction script:**

```javascript
'use strict'

const { test } = require('node:test')
const assert = require('node:assert')
const { MockAgent, setGlobalDispatcher } = require('undici')

test('cleanMocks() also clears the interceptors that global fetch uses', async (t) => {
  const agent = new MockAgent()
  agent.disableNetConnect()
  setGlobalDispatcher(agent)
  t.after(() => agent.close())

  const mockPool = agent.get('https://example.com')
  mockPool.intercept({ path: '/' }).reply(200, 'first').persist()
  assert.strictEqual(await (await fetch('https://example.com/')).text(), 'first')

  mockPool.cleanMocks()
  mockPool.intercept({ path: '/' }).reply(200, 'second').persist()
  assert.strictEqual(await (await fetch('https://example.com/')).text(), 'second')
})
```

## Expected Behavior

The second `fetch` gets `'second'`: after `cleanMocks()`, only the interceptors added after it apply.

## Actual Behavior

The second `fetch` gets `'first'`:

```
actual: 'first',
expected: 'second',
```

Without `.persist()`, the first interceptor is used up, and the second `fetch` fails with `MockNotMatchedError` instead.

## Environment

- OS: Linux
- Node.js version: v24.15.0
- undici version: 8.12.1 (current `main`), also 8.11.2

### Additional context

This breaks the common test setup of one `MockAgent` as the global dispatcher with `cleanMocks()` between tests, for code that uses Node.js' global `fetch`. I'll open a PR that empties the array in place.

## Bug Description

When I compose `interceptors.dns()` into an `Agent`, any response that is preceded by an interim `1xx` response (in my case `103 Early Hints`) fails with `TypeError: fetch failed`. The cause is an `AssertionError` from `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart`:

```
assert(!this.#onResponseStartCalled)
```

Both the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 clients deliver interim responses through `onResponseStart` before the final one, so the final `200` is the second `onResponseStart` call on `DNSDispatchHandler` (which extends `DecoratorHandler`) and trips the once-only assertion.

I hit this in production fetching Cloudflare-hosted pages (for example usafacts.org and Substack posts): Cloudflare sends `103 Early Hints` over HTTP/2, and every such page failed through my DNS-pinning dispatcher. The same requests without the dns interceptor succeed.

## Reproduction

**Standalone reproduction script:**

```javascript
'use strict'

const { test } = require('node:test')
const { createServer } = require('node:http')
const { once } = require('node:events')
const { Agent, fetch, interceptors } = require('undici')

async function earlyHintsServer (t) {
  const server = createServer((req, res) => {
    res.writeEarlyHints({ link: '</style.css>; rel=preload; as=style' })
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'text/plain' })
    res.end('ok')
  })
  t.after(() => { server.closeAllConnections?.(); server.close() })
  server.listen(0)
  await once(server, 'listening')
  return `http://localhost:${server.address().port}/`
}

test('103 Early Hints without the dns interceptor', { timeout: 60000 }, async (t) => {
  t.plan(1)
  const url = await earlyHintsServer(t)
  const dispatcher = new Agent()
  t.after(() => dispatcher.close())

  const res = await fetch(url, { dispatcher })
  t.assert.strictEqual(await res.text(), 'ok')
})

test('103 Early Hints with the dns interceptor', { timeout: 60000 }, async (t) => {
  t.plan(1)
  const url = await earlyHintsServer(t)
  const dispatcher = new Agent().compose(interceptors.dns())
  t.after(() => dispatcher.close())

  const res = await fetch(url, { dispatcher })
  t.assert.strictEqual(await res.text(), 'ok')
})
```

On undici 8.12.2 the first test passes and the second fails.

Versions I tested:

| undici | HTTP/1.1 + 103 | HTTP/2 + 103 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7.29.1 | fails | not tested |
| 8.9.0 | fails | works |
| 8.10.0 | fails | works |
| 8.10.1 | fails | fails |
| 8.11.2 | fails | fails |
| 8.12.2 | fails | fails |

For HTTP/2 I used a `node:http2` `createSecureServer` that calls `stream.additionalHeaders({ ':status': 103, link: '...' })` before `stream.respond({ ':status': 200 })`, fetched with `new Agent({ allowH2: true, connect: { rejectUnauthorized: false } }).compose(interceptors.dns())`. It works in 8.10.0 and fails from 8.10.1, which is the release containing #5712 (forwarding 1xx responses on HTTP/2). A plain `Agent` works on both protocols in every version above.

## Expected Behavior

Interim `1xx` responses don't count as the response start, and the request resolves with the final `200` and body `ok`. `fetch` itself already ignores `status < 200` in its `onResponseStart`.

## Actual Behavior

`fetch` rejects with `TypeError: fetch failed` whose `cause` is `AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]`.

## Logs & Screenshots

```
TypeError: fetch failed
  [cause]: AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: The expression evaluated to a falsy value:

    assert(!this.#onResponseStartCalled)

      at DNSDispatchHandler.onResponseStart (undici/lib/handler/decorator-handler.js:35:5)
      at Request.onResponseStart (undici/lib/core/request.js:345:39)
      at ClientHttp2Stream.onResponse (undici/lib/dispatcher/client-h2.js:1449:15)
```

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu, Linux 6.8.0
- Node.js version: v24.19.0
- undici version: 8.12.2 (also 7.29.1 through 8.11.2, see the table above)

### Additional context

A fix might be for `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart` to skip the once-only check (and not set the flag) when `statusCode < 200`. As a workaround I compose an innermost interceptor that drops `onResponseStart` calls with `statusCode < 200` before they reach the dns interceptor's handler.

## Summary

undici already publishes 20+ diagnostics channels for client / request / websocket lifecycle (`lib/core/diagnostics.js:12-27`). One interceptor — `deduplicate` — follows that pattern (`lib/interceptor/deduplicate.js:103, 112`). The other seven built-in interceptors and `Dispatcher.compose()` itself emit nothing. The result: when you compose a chain, the behaviour between the dispatcher's socket-level channels and the user-visible outcome is a black box.

This RFC proposes a pure-additive set of channels so observability tools (OpenTelemetry, Datadog, Sentry — and the application developer at 2 a.m.) can see where retries happen, which hop added latency, and which interceptor errored.

Not a PR yet — looking for direction on channel names + payload shape first.

## Proposed channels

Three channels, named following the existing `undici:X:Y` convention (`lib/core/diagnostics.js:12`):

* `undici:interceptor:enter` — published when dispatch enters an interceptor
* `undici:interceptor:exit`  — published when the interceptor's returned dispatch call resolves
* `undici:interceptor:error` — published when the interceptor's dispatch call rejects

## Proposed payload

```ts
interface InterceptorHopPayload {
  interceptor: string          // interceptor function name or 'anonymous'
  requestId: symbol            // stable across enter / exit / error for one request
  method: string               // from opts.method
  origin: string               // from opts.origin
  path: string                 // from opts.path
  startTime?: number           // enter: when hop started
  duration?: number            // exit / error: ms elapsed in this hop
  error?: Error                // error channel only
}
```

Minimum surface, every field verifiable at publish time, no leakage of headers or auth material by default.

## Where it ships

Pure additive change inside `lib/dispatcher/dispatcher.js:18-55` — the body of `compose()`. User-registered interceptor functions do not change their signature; the instrumentation lives in the composition wrapper. Expected diff: ~30-50 LOC in `dispatcher.js`, 0 LOC in interceptor files, ~5 LOC in `lib/core/diagnostics.js` to add the channels.

Zero existing listener → zero behaviour change. Node's `diagnostics_channel` already fast-paths unlistened channels, so the per-hop cost when nobody subscribes is negligible — this is why `deduplicate.js:103` can publish per-request without regressing throughput.

## Testing

Follow the convention in `test/node-test/diagnostics-channel/` (`get.js`, `error.js`, `post.js`): subscribe → send request → assert payload shape. Expected: `test/node-test/diagnostics-channel/interceptor-hop.js`, 5-6 scenarios, ~150 LOC:

1. subscribe to `enter` + `exit` → receive matched pair on successful request
2. subscribe to `error` → receive it on interceptor-raised rejection
3. multiple subscribers receive same payload instance (reference, not mutated)
4. `requestId` symbol matches across enter / exit / error for one request
5. `duration` is monotonic (`exit.duration >= 0`)

## Why this, why now

The gap is real: it costs third-party observability tools the ability to instrument the interceptor chain. The existing fetch-level RFC (#2701, open since Feb 2024) covers fetch lifecycle, not interceptor hops — the two are complementary. The `deduplicate.js` precedent shows the pattern is accepted in principle. A thin addition on top of `compose()` closes the biggest black-box gap in undici's observability story without touching the WHATWG fetch surface.

## Not in scope

* No change to `fetch()` surface
* No sanitization layer (payload is minimal by design — if downstream wants auth masking, that's a subscriber concern)
* No TypeScript types churn beyond adding the three channel entries to `types/diagnostic-channel.d.ts`
* No new API — subscribers use `diagnostics_channel.subscribe()` exactly as they do for existing undici channels

## Open questions for the maintainers

1. Three channels vs one (`undici:interceptor:hop` with `phase: 'enter'|'exit'|'error'`)? The three-channel shape mirrors `undici:client:connectError` as a sibling of `connected`, but one channel reduces subscription boilerplate.
2. `requestId` as a symbol (per-process stable) vs a UUID string (cross-process traceable)? Symbol is cheaper, UUID is what tracing libraries want.
3. Should `enter` carry the full `opts` object (easier for subscribers) or only the whitelisted fields above (safer by default)?
4. Should `compose()` also emit a `chain` event listing the interceptor names once per composition, so subscribers can lazily enable per-chain tracing?

Happy to open the PR as soon as the shape is settled, with the test suite and docs ready.

---

Research notes: discovered this gap after the discoverability pass in #6042. Verified: `deduplicate.js` publishes on `undici:request:pending-requests`; the other seven interceptors + compose() publish nothing. Not duplicating #2701 — that's fetch-level, this is interceptor-level.

This RFC proposes a pure-additive set of channels so observability tools (OpenTelemetry, Datadog, Sentry — and the application developer at 2 a.m.) can see where retries happen, which hop added latency, and which interceptor errored.

Not a PR yet — looking for direction on channel names + payload shape first.

## Proposed channels

Three channels, named following the existing `undici:X:Y` convention (`lib/core/diagnostics.js:12`):

* `undici:interceptor:enter` — published when dispatch enters an interceptor
* `undici:interceptor:exit`  — published when the interceptor's returned dispatch call resolves
* `undici:interceptor:error` — published when the interceptor's dispatch call rejects

## Proposed payload

```ts
interface InterceptorHopPayload {
  interceptor: string          // interceptor function name or 'anonymous'
  requestId: symbol            // stable across enter / exit / error for one request
  method: string               // from opts.method
  origin: string               // from opts.origin
  path: string                 // from opts.path
  startTime?: number           // enter: when hop started
  duration?: number            // exit / error: ms elapsed in this hop
  error?: Error                // error channel only
}
```

Minimum surface, every field verifiable at publish time, no leakage of headers or auth material by default.

## Where it ships

Pure additive change inside `lib/dispatcher/dispatcher.js:18-55` — the body of `compose()`. User-registered interceptor functions do not change their signature; the instrumentation lives in the composition wrapper. Expected diff: ~30-50 LOC in `dispatcher.js`, 0 LOC in interceptor files, ~5 LOC in `lib/core/diagnostics.js` to add the channels.

Zero existing listener → zero behaviour change. Node's `diagnostics_channel` already fast-paths unlistened channels, so the per-hop cost when nobody subscribes is negligible — this is why `deduplicate.js:103` can publish per-request without regressing throughput.

## Testing

Follow the convention in `test/node-test/diagnostics-channel/` (`get.js`, `error.js`, `post.js`): subscribe → send request → assert payload shape. Expected: `test/node-test/diagnostics-channel/interceptor-hop.js`, 5-6 scenarios, ~150 LOC:

1. subscribe to `enter` + `exit` → receive matched pair on successful request
2. subscribe to `error` → receive it on interceptor-raised rejection
3. multiple subscribers receive same payload instance (reference, not mutated)
4. `requestId` symbol matches across enter / exit / error for one request
5. `duration` is monotonic (`exit.duration >= 0`)

## Why this, why now

The gap is real: it costs third-party observability tools the ability to instrument the interceptor chain. The existing fetch-level RFC (#2701, open since Feb 2024) covers fetch lifecycle, not interceptor hops — the two are complementary. The `deduplicate.js` precedent shows the pattern is accepted in principle. A thin addition on top of `compose()` closes the biggest black-box gap in undici's observability story without touching the WHATWG fetch surface.

## Not in scope

* No change to `fetch()` surface
* No sanitization layer (payload is minimal by design — if downstream wants auth masking, that's a subscriber concern)
* No TypeScript types churn beyond adding the three channel entries to `types/diagnostic-channel.d.ts`
* No new API — subscribers use `diagnostics_channel.subscribe()` exactly as they do for existing undici channels

## Open questions for the maintainers

1. Three channels vs one (`undici:interceptor:hop` with `phase: 'enter'|'exit'|'error'`)? The three-channel shape mirrors `undici:client:connectError` as a sibling of `connected`, but one channel reduces subscription boilerplate.
2. `requestId` as a symbol (per-process stable) vs a UUID string (cross-process traceable)? Symbol is cheaper, UUID is what tracing libraries want.
3. Should `enter` carry the full `opts` object (easier for subscribers) or only the whitelisted fields above (safer by default)?
4. Should `compose()` also emit a `chain` event listing the interceptor names once per composition, so subscribers can lazily enable per-chain tracing?

Happy to open the PR as soon as the shape is settled, with the test suite and docs ready.

body_text:
## Bug Description

A synchronous request validation failure can leave a free `Client` permanently marked as needing drain inside a `Pool`. Subsequent valid requests stay queued even though no request is running.

With `connections: 1`, one rejected header value is enough to reproduce this. With a larger finite limit, repeated validation failures can exhaust the available client slots. This reproduces with the stock `Pool` and `request()` APIs; no custom dispatcher, interceptors, or diagnostics subscribers are involved.

## Reproduction

Install `undici@7.30.1`, save the following as `repro.cjs`, and run:

```sh
npm install --save-exact undici@7.30.1
node --test repro.cjs
```

The test asserts the expected behavior and currently fails.

```javascript
'use strict'

const { test } = require('node:test')
const assert = require('node:assert/strict')
const { createServer } = require('node:http')
const { once } = require('node:events')
const { setImmediate: nextTurn } = require('node:timers/promises')
const { Pool } = require('undici')

test('Pool remains usable after a request validation error', { timeout: 5000 }, async (t) => {
  let received = 0
  const server = createServer((req, res) => {
    received++
    res.end('ok')
  })
  server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')
  await once(server, 'listening')

  const pool = new Pool(`http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`, { connections: 1 })
  t.after(async () => {
    await pool.destroy()
    server.closeAllConnections()
    await new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve))
  })

  // Warm the only connection and fully consume its response.
  const warm = await pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET' })
  assert.equal(await warm.body.text(), 'ok')
  await nextTurn()
  assert.equal(pool.stats.free, 1)

  await assert.rejects(
    pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET', headers: { 'x-invalid': '\n' } }),
    { code: 'UND_ERR_INVALID_ARG' }
  )

  const next = pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET' })
    .then(async ({ body }) => body.text())
  let timer
  const outcome = await Promise.race([
    next,
    new Promise(resolve => { timer = setTimeout(() => resolve('TIMEOUT'), 500) })
  ]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer))

  const { connected, free, running, pending, queued, size } = pool.stats
  console.log({ outcome, received, connected, free, running, pending, queued, size })
  assert.equal(outcome, 'ok')
  assert.equal(received, 2)
})
```

## Expected Behavior

The invalid request rejects with `UND_ERR_INVALID_ARG`, is not sent to the server, and does not consume a pool slot. The following valid request completes with `ok`.

## Actual Behavior

The invalid request rejects as expected, but the following valid request never reaches the server. The reproduction prints:

```text
{
  outcome: 'TIMEOUT',
  received: 1,
  connected: 1,
  free: 0,
  running: 0,
  pending: 1,
  queued: 1,
  size: 1
}
```

Only the warm-up request reaches the server. Removing the `assert.rejects(...)` block makes the same test pass.

## Environment

- OS: Windows, x64
- Node.js: v24.18.0
- Undici: 7.30.1, installed from npm

### Additional context

The apparent sequence in the v7.30.1 source is:

1. [Client dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/client.js#L340-L343) constructs `Request` before adding it to the client queue.
2. An invalid header causes the constructor to throw. [DispatcherBase.dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/dispatcher-base.js#L172-L180) calls `handler.onError(err)` and returns `false`.
3. [PoolBase dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/pool-base.js#L147-L158) treats that `false` as backpressure and sets the pool's per-client `kNeedDrain` flag.
4. No request was enqueued, so there is no corresponding drain to make that slot available again.

It looks like a validation failure before enqueueing should be distinguished from actual backpressure, or the pool should otherwise restore the slot's readiness.

Could a fix also be backported to the 7.x branch?

A synchronous request validation failure can leave a free `Client` permanently marked as needing drain inside a `Pool`. Subsequent valid requests stay queued even though no request is running.

With `connections: 1`, one rejected header value is enough to reproduce this. With a larger finite limit, repeated validation failures can exhaust the available client slots. This reproduces with the stock `Pool` and `request()` APIs; no custom dispatcher, interceptors, or diagnostics subscribers are involved.

## Reproduction

Install `undici@7.30.1`, save the following as `repro.cjs`, and run:

```sh
npm install --save-exact undici@7.30.1
node --test repro.cjs
```

The test asserts the expected behavior and currently fails.

```javascript
'use strict'

const { test } = require('node:test')
const assert = require('node:assert/strict')
const { createServer } = require('node:http')
const { once } = require('node:events')
const { setImmediate: nextTurn } = require('node:timers/promises')
const { Pool } = require('undici')

test('Pool remains usable after a request validation error', { timeout: 5000 }, async (t) => {
  let received = 0
  const server = createServer((req, res) => {
    received++
    res.end('ok')
  })
  server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')
  await once(server, 'listening')

  const pool = new Pool(`http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`, { connections: 1 })
  t.after(async () => {
    await pool.destroy()
    server.closeAllConnections()
    await new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve))
  })

  // Warm the only connection and fully consume its response.
  const warm = await pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET' })
  assert.equal(await warm.body.text(), 'ok')
  await nextTurn()
  assert.equal(pool.stats.free, 1)

  await assert.rejects(
    pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET', headers: { 'x-invalid': '\n' } }),
    { code: 'UND_ERR_INVALID_ARG' }
  )

  const next = pool.request({ path: '/', method: 'GET' })
    .then(async ({ body }) => body.text())
  let timer
  const outcome = await Promise.race([
    next,
    new Promise(resolve => { timer = setTimeout(() => resolve('TIMEOUT'), 500) })
  ]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer))

  const { connected, free, running, pending, queued, size } = pool.stats
  console.log({ outcome, received, connected, free, running, pending, queued, size })
  assert.equal(outcome, 'ok')
  assert.equal(received, 2)
})
```

## Expected Behavior

The invalid request rejects with `UND_ERR_INVALID_ARG`, is not sent to the server, and does not consume a pool slot. The following valid request completes with `ok`.

## Actual Behavior

The invalid request rejects as expected, but the following valid request never reaches the server. The reproduction prints:

```text
{
  outcome: 'TIMEOUT',
  received: 1,
  connected: 1,
  free: 0,
  running: 0,
  pending: 1,
  queued: 1,
  size: 1
}
```

Only the warm-up request reaches the server. Removing the `assert.rejects(...)` block makes the same test pass.

## Environment

- OS: Windows, x64
- Node.js: v24.18.0
- Undici: 7.30.1, installed from npm

### Additional context

The apparent sequence in the v7.30.1 source is:

1. [Client dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/client.js#L340-L343) constructs `Request` before adding it to the client queue.
2. An invalid header causes the constructor to throw. [DispatcherBase.dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/dispatcher-base.js#L172-L180) calls `handler.onError(err)` and returns `false`.
3. [PoolBase dispatch](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v7.30.1/lib/dispatcher/pool-base.js#L147-L158) treats that `false` as backpressure and sets the pool's per-client `kNeedDrain` flag.
4. No request was enqueued, so there is no corresponding drain to make that slot available again.

It looks like a validation failure before enqueueing should be distinguished from actual backpressure, or the pool should otherwise restore the slot's readiness.

Could a fix also be backported to the 7.x branch?
