## This would solve...

This would solve issues with extracting author information automatically for legal purposes., Currently this is the only package we use that does not have the author information set. Instead, only contributors are set. This means that `npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --omit dev --gather-license-texts`  will not be able to extract author information and leading to manual setting for each new version on our side.

## The implementation should look like...

```
{
  "name": "undici",
  "version": "8.12.3",
  "description": "An HTTP/1.1 client, written from scratch for Node.js",
  "author": {
    "name": "Jane Doe",
    "email": "jane.doe@example.com",
    "url": "https://github.com/janedoe"
  },
  "homepage": "https://undici.nodejs.org",
  "bugs": {
    "url": "https://github.com/nodejs/undici/issues"
  },
  "repository": {
    "type": "git",
    "url": "git+https://github.com/nodejs/undici.git"
  },
  "license": "MIT"
}
```

## I have also considered...

...requesting this from CycloneDX but I think an author would be more generalized as almost everyone is using it.

## Bug Description

Since undici 8 negotiates HTTP/2 by default (`allowH2` defaults to `true`), a long-lived h2 session that dies silently (the peer or a middlebox drops it, no GOAWAY, no RST, no FIN reaching the client) is not detected. undici keeps dispatching new requests onto that session; each one hangs until `headersTimeout`/the application timeout fires, and new requests are routed to the same dead session. The pool never recovers on its own; we had to restart the affected processes.

With HTTP/1.1 (undici 7 default / `allowH2: false`) the same network event only affects the in-flight request on that socket; subsequent requests open new connections and succeed.

## Reproducible By

Production observation (not yet reduced to a minimal repro):

- Node.js 26 (bundled undici 8.10.2), global `fetch` to an internal service behind a Traefik ingress that offers h2 via ALPN.

- One long-lived h2 connection per client process.

- At a network event between the client and the ingress, the ingress saw one stream stay open for 600 s before it closed it. On the client side, 4 of ~18 processes kept sending requests into the dead session: most of them never reached the ingress, and they all failed on our client timeout. After ~10 min the error changed to `TypeError: fetch failed`, but the processes did not recover until restarted.

Setting a global dispatcher with `new Agent({ allowH2: false })` removed the issue; a later network blip of the same kind recovered within ~1 min without any stuck connections.

A minimal repro would probably be: an h2 server behind a TCP proxy that, after a few requests, stops forwarding packets in both directions without closing the sockets. Then keep sending `fetch` requests from the client.

## Expected Behavior

One of:

- Dead h2 sessions are detected (for example with periodic HTTP/2 PING frames and a ping timeout, as other h2 clients do) and evicted from the pool, so new requests open a new session.

- After a request on a session times out (`headersTimeout`/`bodyTimeout`), the session is marked unhealthy and not reused for new requests.

At the least, the change in default and its failure mode for long-lived service-to-service connections could be documented, with `allowH2: false` as the mitigation.

## Logs & Screenshots

Ingress (Traefik) access logs showed `RequestProtocol: HTTP/2.0` for all traffic from the clients, one long-lived connection per client process. Client-side errors were timeouts, then `fetch failed`. No GOAWAY was observed.

## Environment

- Node.js v26.8.2 (official `node:26.8.2-alpine` image), bundled undici 8.10.2 (also the `undici` 8.10.2 package for `setGlobalDispatcher`)

- Linux containers on Kubernetes (Alpine/musl), Traefik ingress in front of the server

### Additional context

Possibly related: #6064 (stall around a graceful GOAWAY), #5381 (h2 sessions never idle-reaped, closed). This report is about a session that dies *without* GOAWAY.

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### This is a CLI Docs Enhancement, not another kind of Docs Enhancement.

- [x] This is a CLI Docs Enhancement.

### Description of Problem

The `package.json` docs are internally inconsistent about the type of the `os`, `cpu`, and `libc` fields, and the ecosystem has diverged as a result.

The `os` section documents an array:

```json
{
  "os": ["darwin", "linux"]
}
```

The `cpu` section likewise documents an array. But the `libc` section, a few paragraphs below, documents both fields as plain strings:

```json
{
  "os": "linux",
  "libc": "glibc"
}
```

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### This issue exists in the latest npm version

- [x] I am using the latest npm

### This is not just a request to bump a dependency for a CVE

- [x] This is not solely a request to bump a dependency for a CVE

### Current Behavior

In a workspaces project, if the root `node_modules` and `package-lock.json` are deleted but a workspace's own `node_modules` is left in place, `npm install` reuses the packages it finds under the workspace without installing their dependencies. Dependencies that were previously hoisted to the root are silently dropped: npm exits 0, prints no warning, and the regenerated `package-lock.json` omits them too, so committing it carries the gap to every `npm ci`.

Related but not the same: #9977 (lockfile present) and its fix #9985, which does not change this case. #4471 may be this bug with an unidentified trigger.

### Expected Behavior

Every declared dependency is installed and recorded in the new lockfile, as it is when every `node_modules` folder is deleted first.

### Steps To Reproduce

```bash
mkdir x && cd x && mkdir -p packages/a
echo '{"name":"r","workspaces":["packages/*"],"dependencies":{"chalk":"5.3.0"}}' > package.json
echo '{"name":"a","version":"1.0.0","dependencies":{"chalk":"4.1.2"}}' > packages/a/package.json
npm install        # chalk@4.1.2 lands in packages/a/node_modules; its deps are hoisted to the root
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install        # exit 0, no warning
npm ls --all       # npm error missing: ansi-styles@^4.1.0, required by chalk@4.1.2
                   # npm error missing: supports-color@^7.1.0, required by chalk@4.1.2
grep -c '"node_modules/ansi-styles"' package-lock.json    # 0
node -e 'require("./packages/a/node_modules/chalk")'      # Error: Cannot find module 'ansi-styles'
```

Control: also deleting `packages/a/node_modules` before the second install gives a complete tree.

Reproduces every time on npm 12.0.2, 11.19.1 and 10.9.9, with `npm_config_userconfig=/dev/null` and an empty cache.

With no lockfile, `#initTree` in `build-ideal-tree.js` loads the actual tree and then scans it for missing or invalid edges. Tracing that scan on the reproduction shows it visits only the project root, whose edges are `a -> null` and `chalk -> null`: with the root `node_modules` gone, the workspace has no `Link` yet, so nothing under `packages/a/node_modules` is examined. Applying #9985's change to 12.0.2 gives the same result, because there is no link for it to follow.

### Environment

- npm: 12.0.2 (also 11.19.1, 10.9.9)
- Node.js: v24.19.0
- OS Name: macOS (Darwin 25.6.0)
- System Model Name: MacBook Air
- npm config: defaults (`npm_config_userconfig=/dev/null`)

## Summary

The Node.js nightly leg of the npm 12.1.0 release integration failed before Node.js could be built or npm could be tested.

## Failing workflow

Workflow run: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486

Failing job: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486/job/106921944687

Branch: `latest`

Commit: `c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a`

Job: `Release Integration / publish (nightly) / build nodejs@nightly npm@12.1.0`

## Failure

The workflow selected Node.js nightly `v27.0.0-nightly20260922dd9f4dac32` and attempted to extract:

```text
https://nodejs.org/download/nightly/v27.0.0-nightly20260922dd9f4dac32/node-v27.0.0-nightly20260922dd9f4dac32.tar.gz
```

The downloaded response was not a gzip archive:

```text
gzip: stdin: not in gzip format
tar: Child returned status 1
tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now
Process completed with exit code 2
```

The failure occurs in `.github/workflows/node-integration.yml` while streaming the nightly source response directly into `tar`:

```sh
curl -sSL \"$nodeUrl\" | tar xz -C \"$sourceDir\" --strip=1
```

This appears consistent with the newest nightly being listed in `index.json` before its source archive was available, or the archive request otherwise returning a non-success response. Because `curl` does not fail on HTTP error responses here, the response body is passed to `tar`, which reports only that it is not gzip data.

Node.js compilation, npm injection, and the Node.js and npm test jobs never ran, so this failure does not indicate an npm 12.1.0 compatibility problem with Node.js nightly.

body_text:
### Current behaviour

When a registry does not publish signing keys, `audit signatures` skips the packages installed
from it. That part is intended — #5479 asked for `E400` to be treated like `E404` for exactly
this reason, and the summary counts only what was checked, through `auditedWithKeysCount`.

What the summary does not say is how much was skipped. In a tree where some dependencies resolve
from a registry with keys and some from a registry without, the output and the exit code are
indistinguishable from a tree that was fully verified.

Reproduced on npm 10.9.8 with a local registry that answers `404` on `/-/npm/v1/keys`:

```
$ cat package.json
{ "name":"mixed-test","version":"1.0.0",
  "dependencies":{ "@nl/nokeys-dep":"1.0.0", "lodash":"4.17.21" } }
$ cat .npmrc
@nl:registry=http://127.0.0.1:8899

$ npm audit signatures
audited 1 package in 0s

1 package has a verified registry signature
$ echo $?
0
```

`@nl/nokeys-dep` is in the tree and carries no signature. It is not in the audited count, not
under `missing`, not under `invalid`. Nothing in the output indicates it exists.

When *nothing* can be audited the command already does the right thing:

```
$ npm audit signatures
npm error found no dependencies to audit that were installed from a supported registry
$ echo $?
1
```

### Why it matters

A pipeline that runs `npm audit signatures` and branches on the exit code is asking "is this tree
verified". In the mixed case it is told yes, when the honest answer is "the part of it that could
be checked". The configuration where this arises — part of the tree resolving through an internal
mirror, a proxy or a third-party registry that does not publish keys — is a common one, and
arguably the one where the gate matters most.

The tree's total is not printed next to the audited count, so the two cannot be compared without
counting the lockfile separately.

### Suggested change

Report the skipped count. Something like:

```
audited 1 package in 0s
1 package skipped: no signing keys published by http://127.0.0.1:8899

1 package has a verified registry signature
```

The information is already in hand at that point — the edges walked, the registries resolved and
`auditedWithKeysCount` — so this is a reporting change rather than a behavioural one. Whether a
skipped package should also affect the exit code is a separate decision, and a flag along the
lines of `--require-signatures` would leave the current default alone.

I am not suggesting the skip itself should change.

`auditedWithKeysCount` — so this is a reporting change rather than a behavioural one. Whether a

## Summary

The npm 11.20.0 release integration failed in the Node.js 22 and Node.js 23 CITGM jobs before `binary-split@1.0.5` could be tested.

## Failing workflow

Workflow run: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787155620

Failing jobs:

* Node.js 22: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787155620/job/106973411919
* Node.js 23: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787155620/job/106974673276

## Failure

Both jobs attempted to download the source archive from:

```text
https://codeload.github.com/maxogden/binary-split/tar.gz/47044d430f5973380bfd4ef3d179f9d5f3eb54b4
```

The response was not a gzip archive:

```text
gzip: stdin: not in gzip format
tar: Child returned status 1
tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now
Process completed with exit code 2.
```

The referenced commit still exists, but GitHub resolves it under the transferred repository:

```text
https://github.com/max-mapper/binary-split/commit/47044d430f5973380bfd4ef3d179f9d5f3eb54b4
```

The CITGM source URL still uses the former `maxogden` owner. The old codeload URL returns non archive content, which is streamed directly into `tar` by `.github/workflows/node-integration.yml`:

```sh
curl -sSL "${{ matrix.url }}" | tar xz -C "$TARGET_DIR" --strip=1
```

## Expected behavior

The integration matrix should use a working source URL for `binary-split`, and HTTP download failures should be reported as HTTP errors rather than gzip extraction errors.

## Suggested changes

1. Update the `binary-split` source URL to use the current `max-mapper` repository owner.
2. Use `curl --fail --show-error --location` for archive downloads so non successful HTTP responses are not passed to `tar`.

The download handling is the same underlying workflow weakness discussed in #10016, although the unavailable Node.js nightly archive and this stale GitHub repository URL are separate upstream conditions.

## Summary

The ordinary CI Smoke Tests job on `latest` fails when the live-registry, low-memory installation scenario receives a socket reset. The smoke harness disables fetch retries, so the reset immediately fails the job.

This issue tracks one network-sensitive test incident and its missing root-cause evidence. The logs do not establish whether the socket reset originated in npm's client, the runner/network, or the registry.

## Affected run

Branch: `latest`, commit `c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a`, npm `12.1.0`, Node `v26.10.0`.

Workflow: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779327465

Failing job: [Smoke Tests](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779327465/job/106920468035)

Failing scenario: `smoke-tests/test/large-install.js`, `large install, no lock and low memory`.

The other 22 jobs in this CI run passed.

## Failure

```text
npm error code ECONNRESET
npm error errno ECONNRESET
npm error network request to {REGISTRY}/@popperjs/core/-/core-2.11.8.tgz failed, reason: socket hang up
```

The logged command explicitly contains:

```text
--fetch-retries=0
```

The process exits with code 1 and no signal. This is not an out-of-memory diagnostic despite the scenario's low-memory setting.

## Confirmed mechanism and uncertainty

[The scenario](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a/smoke-tests/test/large-install.js) deliberately uses the production registry, omits the lockfile, and constrains the V8 heap to 500 MB. [The shared harness](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a/smoke-tests/test/fixtures/setup.js) adds `--fetch-retries=0`, including for this non-mocked test.

The immediate failure is a tarball-request connection reset with no retry. The initiating cause of that reset is unresolved. Do not label it a confirmed registry outage, an npm regression, or a harmless transient without additional evidence.

The test's own comments link #6763 and #7072 and explain that earlier flakes might reveal a `maxSockets` bug. That context must be preserved when deciding whether to change retry behavior.

## Investigation and resolution

* Correlate repetitions with runtime, runner, concurrency, socket limits, and fetch timing to distinguish an infrastructure interruption from a client regression.
* Decide whether zero retries is intentional for this real-network scenario. If bounded retries are appropriate, scope them to the live-registry case and retain useful diagnostics rather than weakening all mocked smoke tests.
* Preserve coverage for large installs and constrained memory.

## Acceptance criteria

* The issue records the best-supported cause or explicitly retains the remaining uncertainty.
* Any retry or concurrency change has a documented rationale that accounts for #6763 and #7072.
* The scenario completes on supported runtimes without concealing a reproducible socket-management regression.

## Scope boundary

This is ordinary CI, not the Release Integration nightly download in #10016 or the stale archive URL in #10020. It is also different from the npm 12 Node 23 engine failures: this run uses supported Node 26.

## Summary

CITGM supplies `--build-from-source` to `npm install` for `thread-sleep`. npm 12 rejects that option with `EUNKNOWNCONFIG` before installation or testing. Both Node 22 and Node 23 failures share this cause.

This is a compatibility break in historical native-tool option forwarding, not evidence that source builds were removed from Node.js or that `--build-from-source` never worked.

## Affected run

Branch: `latest`, commit `c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a`, npm `12.1.0`.

Workflow: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486

* [Node 22: thread-sleep@2.2.0](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486/job/106953430654)
* [Node 23: thread-sleep@2.2.0](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486/job/106949101714)

These are the workflow's displayed package versions; the downloaded source is selected separately from package metadata. The corresponding v11 integration jobs passed.

## Failure

```sh
npm install --no-audit --no-fund --build-from-source
```

```text
npm error code EUNKNOWNCONFIG
npm error Unknown cli flag:
npm error   - --build-from-source
npm error Run `npm help config` for supported options.
```

The CITGM lookup contains:

```json
"install": ["install", "--build-from-source"]
```

npm/cli's matrix generator appends those arguments to `npm install`. The `(flaky)` label does not explain or excuse this deterministic configuration rejection.

## Historical context: how this worked

`--build-from-source` is a documented `node-pre-gyp` option, not a Node.js runtime flag and not a source-build operation implemented by npm itself.

In [mapbox/node-pre-gyp#58](https://github.com/mapbox/node-pre-gyp/issues/58#issuecomment-39261084), the maintainer recommended `npm install --build-from-source` in 2014. That invocation worked through npm's permissive configuration forwarding:

1. npm accepted the otherwise unknown CLI configuration key.
2. npm exported `npm_config_build_from_source=true` to lifecycle scripts.
3. A package's installer using `node-pre-gyp` read that environment variable.
4. `node-pre-gyp` selected compilation instead of a prebuilt binary download.

npm 11 still accepts the CLI option with an unknown-config warning. npm 12 changed unknown CLI flags from warnings to errors in #9276, as documented in the [npm 12.0.0 breaking changes](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a/CHANGELOG.md#1200-2026-07-08).

The [node-pre-gyp README](https://github.com/mapbox/node-pre-gyp/blob/e35bbcfceb59ced246ba3692f2a03286d543ed1f/README.md#options) still documents the option and the old npm invocation. Its [option parser](https://github.com/mapbox/node-pre-gyp/blob/e35bbcfceb59ced246ba3692f2a03286d543ed1f/lib/node-pre-gyp.js) still reads `npm_config_` environment variables, and its [installer](https://github.com/mapbox/node-pre-gyp/blob/e35bbcfceb59ced246ba3692f2a03286d543ed1f/lib/install.js) still honors `build-from-source` or `build_from_source`. The tool capability remains; the npm CLI transport is what now rejects this invocation.

## Proposed resolution

Inspect the exact `thread-sleep` source and installer selected by CITGM before choosing a replacement. Do not assume that its current source still needs this legacy flag merely because other native packages use it.

If forcing compilation is still required, use the actual installer's supported configuration mechanism rather than passing an unknown flag to npm. For `node-pre-gyp`, the existing environment-variable mechanism avoids this particular npm CLI rejection, but support must be verified for the tool and version used by the fixture. `node-gyp` and `node-pre-gyp` are different tools and must not be treated as having interchangeable configuration.

If the selected source no longer has a native build path, retire the stale metadata instead. Preserve genuine source-build coverage where applicable. npm 12's separate lifecycle-script approval policy must also be handled; successful argument parsing alone does not prove a native build happened.

## Acceptance criteria

* The CITGM invocation no longer supplies an unknown npm CLI flag.
* The selected fixture's actual installer and source-build requirement are documented.
* Where a native build is required, the job demonstrates that it ran rather than silently skipping scripts or using a prebuilt binary.
* The relevant jobs pass on supported npm 12 runtimes and remain compatible with v11.
* The fix reaches the CITGM metadata consumed by npm/cli, or the npm/cli workflow and its source template as appropriate.

## Scope boundary

This also fails on supported Node 22, so it is independent of the Node 23 engine mismatch. It is separate from Git-dependency policy failures, #10016, and #10020.

## Summary

The release integration matrix selects Node.js 23 for npm 12.1.0 even though that runtime is outside npm's declared supported engines. This causes multiple failures in two jobs. They belong in one issue because they share the same unsupported-runtime selection, not in separate issues for each assertion.

## Affected run

Branch: `latest`, commit `c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a`, npm `12.1.0`.

Workflow: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486

| Job | Evidence |
|---|---|
| [Node 23: test nodejs](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486/job/106949095962) | `parallel/test-release-npm` rejects npm's unsupported-engine warning. |
| [Node 23: test npm](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35779328486/job/106949096225) | Engine-dependent coverage and smoke assertions fail; self-install rejects the unsupported runtime. |

## Root cause

[The release integration matrix](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/c039090578a5b21a1aa3aba9c96e199feaf1823a/.github/workflows/release-integration.yml) contains `22`, `23`, and `nightly`. The Node 23 leg resolves to `v23.11.1`, while npm 12.1.0 declares:

```text
^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0
```

The failure is a mismatch between the integration matrix and the supported runtime contract. It is not evidence that npm must support Node 23. The corresponding v11 jobs passed, consistent with that branch's different engine range.

## Failures explained by this cause

* Node's `test-release-npm` asserts that invoking bundled npm must not print warnings. It fails on `npm v12.1.0 does not support Node.js v23.11.1`.
* The npm smoke test `basic / npm (no args)` expects empty stderr but receives that same warning.
* `publish and replace global self` fails with `EBADENGINE`, explicitly showing required versus actual engines.
* The subsequently unsatisfied mock-registry requests are consequences of the self-install stopping early, not evidence of another registry failure.
* npm's root tests report 99.97% branch coverage instead of 100%, with the uncovered branch at `lib/cli/entry.js:29`, the supported-engine conditional. The suite's normal runtime is unsupported in this job.

The expected lockfile-mismatch error printed by the `npm ci` negative test is not another failure.

## Proposed resolution

Align the stable release integration targets with each release branch's supported engines, while preserving nightly as an intentional forward-compatibility target. Update the source template as well as generated workflows. Do not suppress engine warnings or broaden npm's supported engines merely to make this stale matrix green.

## Acceptance criteria

* Stable integration targets satisfy the npm release's declared engines on both branches.
* Node and npm integration jobs pass on the intended supported targets without weakening their assertions.
* Supported Node 24 and 26 coverage is considered when replacing the stale Node 23 leg for npm 12.

## Scope boundary

This is separate from #10016 and #10020. The CITGM `EALLOWGIT` and `EUNKNOWNCONFIG` failures also occur on supported Node 22, so correcting this matrix will not resolve them.

## Summary

The `release/v11` Windows Shims Tests job fails during Cygwin provisioning, before the shim tests execute. The setup action attempts a Chocolatey downgrade that conflicts with an installed runner package, continues, and then receives exit code 1 from the Cygwin installer.

This issue tracks the provisioning incident, including both observed failures. The available logs do not prove that the failed downgrade caused the Cygwin installer failure. Keep that causal uncertainty explicit rather than treating adjacent errors as a proven chain.

## Affected run

Branch: `release/v11`, commit `d12b9434dd010b5fb7044c3cc149cdda317813f8`, npm `11.20.0`.

Workflow: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787154762

Failing job: [Windows Shims Tests](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787154762/job/106946629063)

Failing step: `Setup Cygwin`, using `egor-tensin/setup-cygwin@v4.0.1`.

The other 16 jobs in this CI run passed.

## Evidence

The action attempts to downgrade Chocolatey 2.7.4 to 1.1.0:

```text
Unable to resolve dependency 'chocolatey': Unable to resolve dependencies.
'chocolatey 1.1.0' is not compatible with
'apache-httpd 2.4.55 constraint: chocolatey (>= 1.2.0)'.
```

The action continues using Chocolatey 2.7.4, installs the Cygwin 3.6.10 package files, and runs its setup executable. That operation fails:

```text
Installing 64-bit Cygwin...
ERROR: Running [...] was not successful. Exit code was '1'.
See log for possible error messages.
The upgrade of Cygwin was NOT successful.
```

The installer invocation selects `http://mirrors.kernel.org/sourceware/cygwin/`. The workflow log names the mirror but does not establish that it was unavailable.

The action's downgrade workaround references chocolatey/choco#2953. The recorded [action source](https://github.com/egor-tensin/setup-cygwin/blob/d2c752bab416d4b0662591bd366fc2686297c82d/action.yml) and the [v11 workflow](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/d12b9434dd010b5fb7044c3cc149cdda317813f8/.github/workflows/ci.yml) identify the provisioning path.

## Root-cause status

Confirmed: the bootstrap's requested Chocolatey downgrade is incompatible with an installed runner dependency, and the subsequent Cygwin installation fails. The Windows shim assertions never execute.

Unresolved: why `setup-x86_64.exe` exits 1 and whether the downgrade failure contributes. The referenced Chocolatey and Cygwin setup logs are not included in the captured job output. Cache-service warnings elsewhere in the job are not sufficient evidence of the cause.

## Proposed resolution

* Capture the Chocolatey and Cygwin installer logs when provisioning fails, including runner image and package versions.
* Update or replace the obsolete provisioning path after reviewing compatibility with current Windows runner images.
* Stop and report failed prerequisite commands rather than silently continuing after a downgrade failure.
* Preserve Cygwin coverage of the Windows shims rather than disabling the job.

If installer diagnostics establish a second independent cause, split that cause with evidence instead of filing separate tickets merely for each error line.

## Acceptance criteria

* Cygwin provisions on the supported runner image and the Windows shim tests actually run.
* Provisioning failures expose the installer diagnostics needed to distinguish dependency, download, and installation failures.
* Any workflow changes also update the generating template and are assessed for both release branches.

## Scope boundary

This is a runner-provisioning failure, not evidence of an npm shim regression. It is separate from #10016, #10020, the npm 12 integration policy failures, and the `latest` live-registry smoke-test reset.

{"repository": "npm/cli", "task_candidate_id": 17974, "repository_id": 185, "issue_number": 10025, "github_issue_id": 5558387445, "html_url": "https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/10025", "created_at": "2026-09-23T19:26:30+00:00", "author_association": "CONTRIBUTOR", "title": "ci: Cygwin provisioning fails before Windows shim tests run", "body_text": "## Summary

The `release/v11` Windows Shims Tests job fails during Cygwin provisioning, before the shim tests execute. The setup action attempts a Chocolatey downgrade that conflicts with an installed runner package, continues, and then receives exit code 1 from the Cygwin installer.

This issue tracks the provisioning incident, including both observed failures. The available logs do not prove that the failed downgrade caused the Cygwin installer failure. Keep that causal uncertainty explicit rather than treating adjacent errors as a proven chain.

## Affected run

Branch: `release/v11`, commit `d12b9434dd010b5fb7044c3cc149cdda317813f8`, npm `11.20.0`.

Workflow: https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787154762

Failing job: [Windows Shims Tests](https://github.com/npm/cli/actions/runs/35787154762/job/106946629063)

Failing step: `Setup Cygwin`, using `egor-tensin/setup-cygwin@v4.0.1`.

The other 16 jobs in this CI run passed.

## Evidence

The action attempts to downgrade Chocolatey 2.7.4 to 1.1.0:

```text
Unable to resolve dependency 'chocolatey': Unable to resolve dependencies.
'chocolatey 1.1.0' is not compatible with
'apache-httpd 2.4.55 constraint: chocolatey (>= 1.2.0)'.
```

The action continues using Chocolatey 2.7.4, installs the Cygwin 3.6.10 package files, and runs its setup executable. That operation fails:

```text
Installing 64-bit Cygwin...
ERROR: Running [...] was not successful. Exit code was '1'.
See log for possible error messages.
The upgrade of Cygwin was NOT successful.
```

The installer invocation selects `http://mirrors.kernel.org/sourceware/cygwin/`. The workflow log names the mirror but does not establish that it was unavailable.

The action's downgrade workaround references chocolatey/choco#2953. The recorded [action source](https://github.com/egor-tensin/setup-cygwin/blob/d2c752bab416d4b0662591bd366fc2686297c82d/action.yml) and the [v11 workflow](https://github.com/npm/cli/blob/d12b9434dd010b5fb7044c3cc149cdda317813f8/.github/workflows/ci.yml) identify the provisioning path.

## Root-cause status

Confirmed: the bootstrap's requested Chocolatey downgrade is incompatible with an installed runner dependency, and the subsequent Cygwin installation fails. The Windows shim assertions never execute.

Unresolved: why `setup-x86_64.exe` exits 1 and whether the downgrade failure contributes. The referenced Chocolatey and Cygwin setup logs are not included in the captured job output. Cache-service warnings elsewhere in the job are not sufficient evidence of the cause.

## Proposed resolution

* Capture the Chocolatey and Cygwin installer logs when provisioning fails, including runner image and package versions.
* Update or replace the obsolete provisioning path after reviewing compatibility with current Windows runner images.
* Stop and report failed prerequisite commands rather than silently continuing after a downgrade failure.
* Preserve Cygwin coverage of the Windows shims rather than disabling the job.

If installer diagnostics establish a second independent cause, split that cause with evidence instead of filing separate tickets merely for each error line.

## Acceptance criteria

* Cygwin provisions on the supported runner image and the Windows shim tests actually run.
* Provisioning failures expose the installer diagnostics needed to distinguish dependency, download, and installation failures.
* Any workflow changes also update the generating template and are assessed for both release branches.

## Scope boundary

This is a runner-provisioning failure, not evidence of an npm shim regression. It is separate from #10016, #10020, the npm 12 integration policy failures, and the `latest` live-registry smoke-test reset.
